scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: The BIS panel regression explains private credit loan origination (45 countries, 2010–2019) with four drivers: policy rate, bank-efficiency (FI) index, bank regulatory stringency and corporate leverage. The policy rate falls by **one standard deviation**, all else equal.
scenarios.ask: Roughly how large is the associated change in private credit origination?

options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Sibling swap: under 1% is the corporate-leverage effect, the weakest driver.
Sibling swap: ~2–4% per SD is the regulatory-stringency effect.

working.label: Policy-rate coefficient
working.display: negative ($\approx -0.03$): lower rate $\Rightarrow$ more private credit

scenarios.takeaway: Per 1 SD: FI index ~33% > policy rate ~12% > stringency 2–4% > leverage <1%.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: BIS regression, per one standard deviation: the policy rate moves private credit origination by about 12%, and bank regulatory stringency moves it by about 2–4% (use 3%). A country **cuts** its policy rate by 1 SD and at the same time **loosens** bank regulation by 1 SD.
scenarios.ask: Net change in private credit origination: positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Lets the stringency leg dominate; at ~3% it only trims the ~12% rate-cut effect.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The legs are ~12% vs ~3%, a 4× gap: not close.

scenarios.takeaway: Stringency coefficient is POSITIVE: looser bank rules pull borrowers back to banks, but the rate effect is ~4× bigger.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: BIS regression, per one standard deviation: the policy rate moves private credit origination by about 12%; the FI index (how effectively banks meet loan demand) moves it by about 33%. A country's policy rate **rises** 1 SD while its FI index **falls** 1 SD.
scenarios.ask: Net change in private credit origination: positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Reads a falling FI index as bad for private credit; the coefficient is negative, so weaker banks mean MORE private credit.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The legs are −12% and +33%: the FI leg is nearly 3× larger.

scenarios.takeaway: Both the policy rate and the FI index carry NEGATIVE signs: weaker banks → more private credit, and FI is the biggest driver.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: Policy rates stay low for years. Banks hold largely floating-rate assets funded by sticky, slow-repricing deposits. Private credit funds (PCFs) are floating-rate on both assets and liabilities.
scenarios.ask: What happens to lending margins?

options.label: PCF margins compress; banks escape
options.why: Role swap: the mismatched (floating vs sticky) structure is the BANK's; PCFs are matched.

options.label: Bank margins compress; PCFs largely escape
Both widen
options.why: Reverses the margin effect: low rates squeeze the lender whose asset yields fall faster than its funding costs.

working.label: Bank asset yields vs deposit costs
working.display: asset yields fall faster than sticky deposit costs

working.label: Result
working.display: bank margins squeezed; PCFs (floating/floating) unaffected $\Rightarrow$ room for PCFs to lend

scenarios.takeaway: Low rates squeeze banks (floating assets, sticky deposits); matched-floating PCFs slip through and fill the gap.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: From 2010 to 2019 bank cost of equity rose sharply (market risk, stricter regulation) while BDCs swapped expensive equity for cheaper debt. Banks' traditional cost-of-capital advantage over BDCs eroded.
scenarios.ask: By roughly how much did the advantage narrow?

options.label: ≈ 8.3 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 25 bp
options.why: Decimal slip: 2.5 percentage points read as 0.25; a quarter point would be noise.

options.label: ≈ 80 bp
options.why: Scale slip (≈0.3× the truth).

scenarios.takeaway: Banks' funding edge over BDCs shrank by ~250 bp (2.5 pp) over 2010–2019.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: The ≈250 bp erosion of banks' funding advantage over BDCs (2010–2019) splits into three channels: BDCs' lower cost of equity, BDCs' increased leverage, and the cost-of-debt difference. The cost-of-debt difference stayed small, contributing ≈0 bp.
scenarios.ask: Compare the cost-of-equity channel with the leverage channel: which contributed more?

options.label: Cost-of-equity channel clearly bigger
options.why: Drops the co-equal leverage channel; the reading splits the erosion roughly evenly.

options.label: Leverage channel clearly bigger
options.why: Overweights leverage; the lower BDC cost of equity pulled just as hard.

scenarios.takeaway: Gap erosion: CoE and leverage ~50/50; the CoD DIFFERENCE barely moved the gap (even though cheap debt cut BDCs' own WACC).

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: BDCs replace part of their equity with debt. Their debt costs a bit more than bank debt but much less than their own equity. The extra leverage nudges BDCs' cost of equity up modestly.
scenarios.ask: BDCs' overall cost of capital:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Lets the modest cost-of-equity uptick dominate; the cheaper-debt benefit more than offsets it.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: "Fully cancelled" contradicts the stated net decline in BDC cost of capital.

working.label: Substitution
working.display: expensive equity $\to$ cheaper debt: pulls WACC down

working.label: Offset
working.display: cost of equity rises modestly: pushes WACC up a little

scenarios.takeaway: Debt only has to beat BDCs' OWN equity, not bank debt; the substitution lowers WACC net of the CoE uptick.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: The Global Drivers of Private Credit
scenarios.setup: Policy rates rise and stay high. BDC funding costs track policy rates closely; bank deposit costs reprice slowly.
scenarios.ask: Effect on the bank-vs-BDC competitive balance?

options.label: BDC cost of capital falls; BDCs gain further ground
options.why: Reverses the regime shift: BDCs' cheap-debt benefit was a low-rate phenomenon.

options.label: Banks lose most, as deposit costs reprice fastest
options.why: Deposits reprice SLOWEST, which is why rising rates favor banks.

options.label: BDC cost of capital rises; the edge shifts back toward banks

working.label: BDC debt
working.display: floats with policy rates $\Rightarrow$ funding cost up quickly

working.label: Balance
working.display: BDC cost of capital rises relative to banks'

scenarios.takeaway: Higher-for-longer rates erode BDCs' cheap-debt edge; sticky deposits shelter banks.

scenarios.reading: Reading 100: Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Markets

options.label: Roughly unchanged

working.display: withdraw $\Rightarrow$ less standing activity $\Rightarrow$ fewer cancellations

working.label: Institutions (for contrast)
working.display: use MORE hidden orders to avoid moving a thin market

scenarios.reading: Reading 100: Advances in Artificial Intelligence: Implications for Capital Markets
scenarios.setup: Better computing hardware and algorithmic efficiency have cut the cost per unit of compute used to train AI models. At the same time, frontier models keep getting more complex.

options.label: Falls

scenarios.reading: Reading 106: Tokenization and Financial Market Inefficiencies

scenarios.setup: A major global geopolitical shock sends energy prices sharply higher. Consider a country that imports most of its energy.

options.label: Currency strengthens; spreads tighten
options.why: That is the exporter's side of the asymmetry, reversed onto the importer.

working.display: importer pays more per barrel $\Rightarrow$ worsens

scenarios.setup: A major global geopolitical shock hits. Investors pile into US, UK, German, Swiss and Japanese government bonds.

options.label: Rise

options.label: Roughly unchanged

scenarios.setup: Russia invades Ukraine in 2022. Defense and energy stocks rally in most countries on expectations of higher defense spending and energy prices. Consider a defense firm that earns a large share of its revenue in Russia and Ukraine.
scenarios.ask: This firm's share price:

options.label: Roughly unchanged, the two forces cancel
options.why: The documented outcome was a sharp decline, not an offset.

scenarios.setup: An asset is expected to GAIN value whenever geopolitical risk rises: it pays off in exactly the bad states investors fear.
scenarios.ask: Its risk premium under modern asset-pricing theory:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Reverses the convention: positive premiums compensate assets that LOSE value when risk rises.

options.label: Zero, geopolitical risk is not priced
options.why: Geopolitical risk is priced in both equity and option markets.

working.label: Payoff profile
working.display: gains in bad states $\Rightarrow$ acts as insurance

working.label: Premium
working.display: investors accept a lower (even negative) premium for insurance

scenarios.takeaway: Hedges carry negative premiums; assets that crater in bad states carry positive ones.

Sibling swap: applies the ~20× global multi-country-shock multiple.

scenarios.reading: Reading 104: Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Safeguarding Stability and Trust

scenarios.reading: Reading 104: Monetary and Fiscal Policy: Safeguarding Stability and Trust
scenarios.setup: Banks operate with an implicit government backstop: the sovereign would support them in distress.
scenarios.ask: Effect of the backstop on bank credit ratings:

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: A two-bond portfolio. Bond 1: USD 500,000, $PD = 5\%$, recovery 50%. Bond 2: USD 300,000, $PD = 3\%$, recovery 30%. Joint default probability 2%, default correlation 25%, credit VaR defined at 99% over one year.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio expected credit loss is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 57,000
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 460,000
options.why: Forgot PD: $500{,}000 \times 0.5 + 300{,}000 \times 0.7$ is the loss if both bonds default for certain, not an expectation.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,900,000
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: EL = Σ exposure × PD × (1 − recovery); correlation, joint PD and the confidence level belong to UL/VaR.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Building portfolio EL bond by bond. Bond 1: USD 500,000, $PD = 5\%$, recovery 50%. Bond 2: USD 300,000, $PD = 3\%$, recovery 30%.
scenarios.ask: Which bond contributes more expected loss?

options.label: Bond 2, clearly
options.why: Bond 2's higher loss rate (70%) does not make up for its smaller size and lower PD: 6,300 vs 12,500.

scenarios.takeaway: Size each EL leg as exposure × PD × (1 − recovery); convert recovery to loss rate first.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Two-bond portfolio with expected loss USD 18,800 at a default correlation of 25%. Bond 1: USD 500,000, $PD = 5\%$, recovery 50%. Bond 2: USD 300,000, $PD = 3\%$, recovery 30%. The desk re-estimates default correlation at 50%; individual PDs and recoveries are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio expected loss: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: Higher correlation widens the loss distribution (UL, credit VaR), not its mean.

options.label: Falls
options.why: Correlation never enters EL at all; EL is the sum of the individual ELs.

working.label: EL is additive
working.display: $EL_P = \sum_i EAD_i \times PD_i \times LGD_i$ with no $\rho$ term

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation moves UL and credit VaR, never EL.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: A loan has a total commitment of USD 100,000, of which 80% is drawn. Drawdown on default (usage given default) is 70% of the undrawn amount. $PD = 2\%$, $LGD = 40\%$.
scenarios.ask: Before computing EL, where must the adjusted exposure land?

options.label: Below USD 80,000
options.why: Drawdown before default adds to the balance already drawn; exposure cannot fall below the 80,000 outstanding.

options.label: Above USD 100,000
options.why: That comes from adding 70% of the full commitment instead of the undrawn part: $80{,}000 + 0.70 \times 100{,}000 = 150{,}000$. Only the undrawn 20,000 is drawn down, and exposure cannot exceed the commitment.

scenarios.takeaway: Adjusted exposure = outstanding + UGD × undrawn; it always sits between outstanding and commitment.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: A loan with a USD 120m commitment has USD 80m outstanding; no drawdown factor is given. $PD = 2\%$, loss rate $LR = 25\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 14\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 15\%$.
scenarios.ask: Unexpected loss on this loan today is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 9.9m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 33m
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 99m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

working.label: Adjusted exposure
working.display: $AE = OS = 80$ (no drawdown factor, so the USD 120m commitment is a red herring)

scenarios.takeaway: UL = AE × √(PD·σ²_LR + LR²·σ²_PD); finish by multiplying by exposure.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Same loan: exposure USD 80m, $PD = 2\%$, $LR = 25\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 14\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 15\%$. You have the per-unit UL: $\sqrt{PD\,\sigma^2_{LR} + LR^2\sigma^2_{PD}} = 0.0409$.
scenarios.ask: Which is bigger for this loan: UL or EL?

options.label: EL
options.why: Per unit, EL is $PD \times LR = 0.005$, far below 0.0409.

options.label: About equal
options.why: 0.0409 vs 0.005: UL is roughly 8× EL.

scenarios.takeaway: For a single loan, UL is typically a multiple of EL: compare √(variance) with PD × LR.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Adjusted exposure USD 30m, $PD = 4\%$, $LGD = 40\%$, $\sigma_{LGD} = 40\%$. No $\sigma_{PD}$ is given, so use the binomial $\sigma^2_{PD} = PD(1-PD)$. $UL = AE\sqrt{PD\,\sigma^2_{LGD} + LGD^2\,\sigma^2_{PD}}$.
scenarios.ask: Inside the root, which term is bigger: $PD\,\sigma^2_{LGD}$ or $LGD^2\,\sigma^2_{PD}$?

options.label: $PD\,\sigma^2_{LGD}$, clearly
options.why: It is bigger, but only by 4%: 0.0064 vs 0.006144.

options.label: $LGD^2\,\sigma^2_{PD}$, clearly
options.why: 0.006144 is slightly below 0.0064, not above it.

scenarios.takeaway: When σ_PD is missing, derive it as √(PD(1−PD)); here both variance terms pull equally.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Adjusted exposure USD 30m, $PD = 4\%$, $LGD = 40\%$, $\sigma_{LGD} = 40\%$; no $\sigma_{PD}$ is given. The correct UL uses the binomial $\sigma_{PD} = \sqrt{PD(1-PD)}$. An analyst instead plugs $\sigma_{LGD} = 40\%$ in as $\sigma_{PD}$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the correct UL, the analyst's UL is: higher, lower, or the same?

options.label: Lower
options.why: The binomial $\sigma_{PD} = \sqrt{0.04 \times 0.96} \approx 19.6\%$ is well below 40%, so the swap inflates the default term.

options.label: The same
options.why: $\sigma_{PD}$ enters squared: going from 19.6% to 40% roughly quadruples the default term.

scenarios.takeaway: Binomial σ_PD = √(PD(1−PD)) is small for low PD; borrowing σ_LGD overstates UL.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks

scenarios.ask: The variance of the number of defaults is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Count variance np(1−p); single-loan p(1−p); default-rate p(1−p)/n. Read the units of the options.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Same 500 independent loans, $p = 1.5\%$ each. The expected number of defaults is $np = 7.5$.
scenarios.ask: The binomial variance of the default count is: below 7.5, above 7.5, or exactly 7.5?

options.label: Above 7.5
options.why: Variance is $np(1-p)$, and $1 - p = 0.985 < 1$ pulls it under the mean.

options.label: Exactly 7.5
options.why: Variance equal to the mean is Poisson; the binomial carries the extra $(1-p)$ factor.

scenarios.takeaway: Rare-event binomial: variance sits just below the mean.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Two credit assets: $UL_X$ = USD 556,417, $UL_Y$ = USD 387,732, default correlation $\rho = 0.4$. Risk contribution $RC_X = UL_X\,(UL_X + \rho\,UL_Y)/UL_P$.
scenarios.ask: Is $X$'s risk contribution below, equal to, or above its standalone UL of USD 556,417?

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only at $\rho = 1$ does a contribution equal standalone UL.

options.label: Above
options.why: With $\rho < 1$, diversification pulls every contribution below standalone UL.

scenarios.takeaway: ρ < 1 ⇒ each risk contribution < standalone UL, and contributions sum to UL_P.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Two assets, each with standalone UL of USD 8.0m. At $\rho = 0$, portfolio UL is USD 11.31m and each asset's UL contribution (ULC) is USD 5.66m. The board asks what happens as default correlation rises toward 1.
scenarios.ask: Each asset's ULC: rises, falls, or stays unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher correlation removes diversification; at $\rho = 1$ each ULC climbs to its standalone 8.0m.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: $ULC = UL\,(1+\rho)/\sqrt{2+2\rho} = UL\sqrt{(1+\rho)/2}$, which increases with $\rho$.

scenarios.takeaway: More correlation ⇒ larger UL_P and larger ULCs; at ρ = 1 ULC = standalone UL.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: A bank targets a 99.97% confidence level, consistent with a AA senior-debt rating. Economic capital is $EC = CM \times UL_P$, with the capital multiplier $CM$ read off the fitted loss distribution at the target confidence level. The board considers targeting a lower rating, say A.
scenarios.ask: The capital multiplier: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: A lower rating means a lower confidence level, a less extreme quantile, and so a smaller CM. A weaker rating needs less cushion, not more.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: CM is not a fixed Basel constant; it depends on the confidence level and on portfolio quality.

working.label: Rating → confidence
working.display: Lower target rating → lower confidence level

working.label: Confidence → CM
working.display: Lower confidence → quantile closer to the body of the loss distribution → smaller CM → less EC

scenarios.takeaway: Higher target rating → higher confidence → higher CM → more economic capital.

scenarios.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: One-year loan of EUR 420m at 6%. Funding cost 0.5%, expected loss 3%, operating costs 1% (all of face), transaction costs EUR 1m. Economic capital is 5% of the loan and earns 2% pre-tax. Tax rate 35%.
scenarios.ask: After-tax RAROC is closest to?

options.why: Forgot to deduct expected loss (EUR 12.6m); EL is a cost line in the numerator.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: RAROC = (revenue − funding − EL − opex − transaction + return on EC)(1 − t) / economic capital.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: Merton set-up: a firm's only debt is a zero-coupon bond with face value USD 60m due at $T$. At $T$ its assets are worth USD 50m. You have computed $V_T - F = -10$.
scenarios.ask: The value of equity at $T$ is: negative, zero, or positive?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Limited liability: $E_T = \max(V_T - F, 0)$ is floored at zero; shareholders do not owe the shortfall.

options.label: Positive
options.why: A USD 10m positive figure is the creditors' loss (the put they wrote finishing in the money), not an equity value.

scenarios.takeaway: Equity = max(V − F, 0): a call, floored at zero; debt = F − put.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: A 5-year zero-coupon bond with face value USD 100m trades at USD 88m. The continuously compounded risk-free rate is 1.5%.
scenarios.ask: The credit spread is closest to?

options.why: Forgot to subtract $r$ and then read the decimal yield 0.0256 as a percent.
Scale slip (0.3×).
Did not divide $\ln(0.88)$ by $T = 5$: 12.8% − 1.5% is a five-year total, not a per-annum spread.

scenarios.takeaway: Spread = −ln(D/F)/T − r; divide by T, then subtract the risk-free rate.

scenarios.setup: Merton: assets $V_0$ = USD 240m, equity $E_0$ = USD 150m, equity volatility $\sigma_E = 30\%$, $N(d_1) = 0.95$. The link is $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$.
scenarios.ask: Before solving: is asset volatility $\sigma_V$ above, below, or equal to 30%?

options.label: Above
options.why: That reverses leverage: equity is the levered claim on the assets, so equity is the more volatile one.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only for an unlevered firm with $N(d_1) = 1$; here $V/E = 1.6$.

scenarios.takeaway: Levered firm: σ_V < σ_E, scaled down by N(d1)·V/E.

scenarios.setup: Merton: $V_0$ = USD 240m, $E_0$ = USD 150m, $\sigma_E = 30\%$, with $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$. At $N(d_1) = 0.95$ the implied $\sigma_V$ is about 19.7%. The model is re-run with $N(d_1) = 0.80$; the equity inputs do not change.
scenarios.ask: The implied asset volatility: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: $N(d_1)$ sits in the denominator of $\sigma_V = \sigma_E E_0 / (N(d_1) V_0)$; a smaller delta needs more asset volatility to produce the same equity volatility.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: $N(d_1)$ enters directly: $45/(0.80 \times 240) = 23.4\%$.

scenarios.takeaway: σ_V = σ_E·E / (N(d1)·V): lower delta ⇒ higher implied asset volatility.

scenarios.setup: Merton, FiberTech: assets USD 500m, debt USD 300m due in 1 year, $\sigma = 25\%$, $r = 3\%$. You have $d_1 = 2.29$, and $d_2 = d_1 - \sigma\sqrt{T}$.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: $N(-d_1)$ or $N(-d_2)$?

options.label: $N(-d_1)$
options.why: $d_2 < d_1$, so $-d_2 > -d_1$ and $N(-d_2)$ is the bigger tail: 2.08% vs 1.11%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The arguments differ by $\sigma\sqrt{T} = 0.25$, which nearly doubles the tail probability here.

scenarios.takeaway: d2 = d1 − σ√T is the distance to default; PD = N(−d2), always above N(−d1).

scenarios.setup: Merton, FiberTech: assets USD 500m, debt USD 300m due in 1 year, $r = 3\%$. At $\sigma = 25\%$, $d_2 = 2.04$ and the risk-neutral $PD = N(-d_2) = 2.08\%$. Asset volatility is re-estimated at 35%.
scenarios.ask: Risk-neutral PD: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher $\sigma$ shrinks $d_2$ (larger $\sigma\sqrt{T}$ below and larger $-\sigma^2/2$ drag above): $d_2$ drops to about 1.37, PD rises to about 8.5%.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: $\sigma$ enters $d_2$ twice; the distance to default is very sensitive to it.

scenarios.takeaway: More asset volatility ⇒ shorter distance to default ⇒ higher PD.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: Merton: $V_0$ = USD 40m, face value $F$ = USD 25m due in 5 years, $\sigma = 30\%$, risk-free $r = 7\%$, expected asset return $\mu = 10\%$. A colleague computed PD with $r$ as the drift; you switch to $\mu$ for a real-world PD.
scenarios.ask: Switching the drift from $r$ to $\mu$ makes the PD: rise, fall, or stay unchanged?

options.label: Rise
options.why: A higher drift moves expected log asset value further above the default point: $d_2$ rises from 0.89 to 1.11, and PD falls from about 19% to about 13%.

options.label: Stay unchanged
options.why: Drift enters the numerator of $d_2$ as $(\text{drift} - \sigma^2/2)T$.

scenarios.takeaway: Real-world PD uses μ; since μ > r, real-world PD < risk-neutral PD.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: Merton real-world PD: $d_2 = [\ln(V_0/F) + (\mu - \sigma^2/2)T]/(\sigma\sqrt{T})$ with $V_0 = 40$, $F = 25$, $\mu = 10\%$, $\sigma = 30\%$, $T = 5$ years.
scenarios.ask: In the numerator, which is bigger: the leverage term $\ln(V_0/F)$ or the drift term $(\mu - \sigma^2/2)T$?

options.label: The drift term
options.why: $(0.10 - 0.045) \times 5 = 0.275$ vs $\ln 1.6 = 0.470$. Forgetting $\sigma^2/2$ gives 0.50 and flips the ranking.

options.label: About equal
options.why: 0.470 vs 0.275: not close.

scenarios.takeaway: Drift scales with T but carries the −σ²/2 drag; volatility scales with √T.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: Uncollateralised swap. Expected positive exposure is constant at 5% of notional; counterparty credit spread 400 bps; recovery 50%; hazard rate 6.7%; maturity about 5 years.
scenarios.ask: The CVA as a running spread is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 100 bps per annum
options.why: Multiplied by the 5-year maturity: that points toward an upfront CVA, not a per-annum spread.

options.label: ≈ 400 bps per annum
options.why: That is the counterparty spread itself; EPE (5%) scales it down.

options.label: ≈ 2,000 bps per annum
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

working.label: Shortcut
working.display: $CVA_{spread} \approx EPE \times s$ (recovery and hazard rate are already inside $s$)

scenarios.takeaway: CVA running spread ≈ EPE × counterparty spread; nothing else.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: A trader wants a quick CVA estimate. Expected positive exposure is 13%; the counterparty's credit spread is about 225 bps per annum.
scenarios.ask: The CVA as a running spread, in percent (ignoring sign), is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip (0.1×): divided by 1,000 instead of 100.
Divided EPE by the spread (13 / 2.25) instead of multiplying.
29.25 is in basis points; divide by 100 to get percent.

working.label: CVA in percent
working.display: $29.25 / 100 = 0.29\%$ (quoted as −0.29% when written as a value adjustment)

scenarios.takeaway: 1 bp = 0.01%; carry units at every step.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: CVA running spread ≈ −EPE × counterparty spread. Today EPE is 13% and the spread 225 bps, so CVA ≈ −29 bps. The counterparty's spread widens to 450 bps; EPE is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The CVA charge: roughly doubles, rises by much less than double, or is unchanged?

options.label: Rises by much less than double
options.why: The approximation is linear in the spread: $0.13 \times 450 = 58.5$ bps.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The spread is a direct multiplier; fixed EPE does not freeze CVA.

scenarios.takeaway: CVA scales linearly in both EPE and the counterparty spread.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: An interest rate swap on USD 10m notional has a risky duration of 3 years. The upfront CVA is 0.75% of notional.
scenarios.ask: The CVA as a running spread is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 0.83 bps
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 2.5 bps
options.why: Read 0.75% as 7.5 bps (it is 75 bps), then divided by 3.

options.label: ≈ 8.3 bps
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Running spread ≈ upfront CVA ÷ risky duration.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: Same swap: upfront CVA is 0.75% of notional, which is 75 bps, and the risky duration is 3 years.
scenarios.ask: The equivalent running spread must be: below 75 bps, above 75 bps, or equal to 75 bps?

options.label: Above 75 bps
options.why: An annual charge paid for about 3 years must be smaller than the one-off equivalent: 75 / 3 = 25.

options.label: Equal to 75 bps
options.why: Only if the risky duration were 1 year.

scenarios.takeaway: A running spread over several years is always smaller than the upfront charge.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: From CityBank's side of a swap: EPE 6.00%, ENE 4.20%. The counterparty FinCorp's spread is 250 bps; CityBank's own spread is 110 bps. You have the CVA leg: $-0.06 \times 250 = -15.00$ bps. The DVA leg (ENE × own spread) pulls the other way.
scenarios.ask: The net bilateral CVA spread is: negative (a charge), positive (a benefit), or too close to call?

options.label: Positive (a benefit)
options.why: DVA is $0.042 \times 110 = +4.62$ bps, less than a third of the 15 bp CVA leg.

scenarios.takeaway: BCVA ≈ −EPE × counterparty spread + ENE × own spread; size each leg before netting.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: CityBank vs FinCorp swap, from CityBank's side: EPE 6.00%, ENE 4.20%, FinCorp spread 250 bps, CityBank's own spread 110 bps, maximum PFE 18.0%.
scenarios.ask: The bilateral CVA, as a charge in bps per annum, is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 1.0 bps
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).

options.label: ≈ 3.9 bps
options.why: Swapped the spread pairing (EPE × own, ENE × counterparty); done that way it even flips to a benefit.

options.label: ≈ 40 bps
options.why: Used the maximum PFE (18%) in place of EPE. PFE is a tail measure for limits; valuation uses expected exposure.

scenarios.takeaway: EPE pairs with the counterparty's spread, ENE with your own; PFE never enters CVA.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: CityBank vs FinCorp, from CityBank's side: EPE 6.00%, ENE 4.20%, FinCorp spread 250 bps. With CityBank's own spread at 110 bps, BCVA is about −10.4 bps. CityBank's own spread then widens to 200 bps; nothing else changes.
scenarios.ask: CityBank's BCVA charge becomes: larger, smaller, or unchanged?

options.label: Larger
options.why: The own spread drives DVA, which is a benefit. DVA rises to $0.042 \times 200 = 8.4$ bps and the net charge shrinks to 6.6 bps.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The own spread enters through the DVA leg.

scenarios.takeaway: Own spread widening ⇒ bigger DVA ⇒ smaller BCVA charge (the DVA paradox).

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: Bilateral CVA from VXR's side, with EPE = ENE, both unchanged. VXR's own spread widens from 74 to 154 bps; counterparty Excellence Bank's spread widens from 128 to 176 bps.
scenarios.ask: VXR's BCVA: improves (moves in VXR's favour), deteriorates, or unchanged?

options.label: Deteriorates
options.why: Only the counterparty widening is adverse (CVA leg, −48 bps). VXR's own widening feeds DVA, a benefit of +80 bps. Net +32.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The two widenings are different sizes (80 vs 48), so they do not cancel.

scenarios.takeaway: Own spread and counterparty spread move BCVA in opposite directions; net the changes.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Three exposures with UL of USD 597,000, 840,000 and 1,023,500; pairwise default correlation 0.40; portfolio UL USD 1,920,250; capital multiplier 5.50. Exposure 1's risk contribution is USD 417,348, giving EC of about USD 2.30m.
scenarios.ask: Economic capital for Exposure 2 is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 11m
options.why: That is $UL_P \times CM$, the whole portfolio's economic capital.

options.label: ≈ USD 36m
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 108m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: EC_i = CM × ULC_i; finish the chain the worked example shows.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Three exposures with UL of USD 597,000, 840,000 and 1,023,500; pairwise correlation 0.40; $UL_P$ = USD 1,920,250; CM = 5.50, so $CM \times UL_P$ = USD 10.56m. Each exposure gets $EC_i = CM \times ULC_i$, with $ULC_i = UL_i(UL_i + \rho\sum_{j \ne i} UL_j)/UL_P$.
scenarios.ask: Before adding up: $EC_1 + EC_2 + EC_3$ comes in below, equal to, or above USD 10.56m?

options.label: Above
options.why: That happens if you sum standalone UL × CM ($2{,}460{,}500 \times 5.5 \approx 13.5$m). Risk contributions sum exactly to $UL_P$.

options.label: Below
options.why: The allocation leaves no residual: $\sum ULC_i = UL_P$ by construction.

scenarios.takeaway: Risk contributions are additive to UL_P, so allocated EC sums to portfolio EC with no residue.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: Credit card receivables aging (USD m): 0–30 days 600; 31–60 days 250; 61–90 days 170; 91–120 days 130; 121+ days 60; total 1,210. Written off this period: 35.
scenarios.ask: The delinquency ratio is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).
Only the 121+ bucket; delinquency counts everything more than 90 days past due.
Counted everything more than 30 days past due; the cut-off is 90 days.

scenarios.takeaway: Delinquency = >90 days past due / pool; default = written off / pool.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: Credit card receivables aging (USD m): 0–30 days 600; 31–60 days 250; 61–90 days 170; 91–120 days 130; 121+ days 60; total 1,210. Written off this period: 35.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger for this pool: the delinquency ratio (>90 days past due ÷ pool) or the default ratio (written off ÷ pool)?

options.label: Default ratio
options.why: Write-offs are 35 vs 190 more than 90 days late; not every seriously late balance gets charged off.

options.label: About equal
options.why: 15.7% vs 2.9%: more than five times apart.

scenarios.takeaway: Delinquency leads defaults; in a working pool it is the larger ratio.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: A securitisation's collateral pool: each asset's default probability is held fixed. The structurer considers a rise in default correlation across the pool.
scenarios.ask: The risk of the equity (first-loss) tranche: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: Pool EL is unchanged. Higher correlation makes the 'almost nothing defaults' outcome more likely, and that is the equity tranche's only good state. Risk shifts up to the senior tranche.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Pool EL is fixed, but correlation reshapes the loss distribution and so moves risk between tranches.

working.label: Pool EL
working.display: Linear in the PDs: unaffected by correlation

working.label: Distribution shape
working.display: Higher ρ fattens both tails: more zero-default outcomes and more mass-default outcomes

working.label: Tranches
working.display: Equity gains from the zero-default tail (safer); senior is hit by the mass-default tail (riskier)

scenarios.takeaway: Higher correlation: senior tranche riskier, equity tranche safer, pool EL unchanged.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Portfolios A and B hold the same number of bonds with the same individual PDs and the same total notional. A's bonds are uncorrelated; B's are highly correlated.
scenarios.ask: B's credit VaR relative to A's is: higher, lower, or the same?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Correlated names default together, which fattens the loss tail; correlation removes diversification rather than adding it.

options.label: The same
options.why: EL is the same, but dispersion (UL, credit VaR) is not; the tail is what VaR reads.

working.label: Expected loss
working.display: Identical: n × PD × EAD × LGD for both

working.label: Dispersion
working.display: Loss variance rises with every pairwise ρ, so B's distribution is much wider

scenarios.takeaway: Same EL, more correlation ⇒ wider loss distribution ⇒ higher credit VaR and capital.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: Under a CSA, exposure below the threshold is not collateralised: collateral required $= \max(0, \text{Exposure} + IA - \text{Threshold})$. A firm lowers the threshold it grants a counterparty.
scenarios.ask: The firm's credit risk to that counterparty: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: A lower threshold means collateral is called sooner, so less exposure is left uncollateralised. It is the operational burden that rises, not credit risk.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The threshold moves uncollateralised exposure one for one.

working.label: Threshold's role
working.display: An unsecured credit line: exposure up to it is uncollateralised

working.label: Lower threshold
working.display: More collateral called, less uncollateralised exposure → lower credit risk (more margin calls)

scenarios.takeaway: Lower threshold ⇒ more collateral ⇒ less credit risk, more operational work.

scenarios.setup: An economic downturn pushes corporate bond default rates sharply higher.
scenarios.ask: Average recovery rates on defaulted bonds: rise, fall, or unchanged?

options.label: Rise
options.why: Many simultaneous defaults flood the distressed-debt market while collateral values are depressed; recovery and default rates are negatively correlated.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Hull documents a strong negative relationship, which is why regulators require a downturn LGD.

working.label: Supply effect
working.display: Many defaulted securities hit a thin buyer base → prices fall

working.label: Valuation effect
working.display: The same macro shock depresses collateral and going-concern values

scenarios.takeaway: Downturn: PD up and recovery down together, so EL rises more than proportionally.

scenarios.setup: For one rating category you estimate default probability two ways: from bond credit spreads via $\lambda \approx s/(1-R)$, and from historical default data.
scenarios.ask: The spread-implied PD relative to the historical PD is: higher, lower, or about the same?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Spreads also pay for illiquidity and systematic (non-diversifiable) default risk; the conversion treats those premia as default.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The gap is systematic and large, often several times, and widest for high grades.

working.label: Spread decomposition
working.display: Spread = expected default loss + liquidity premium + systematic risk premium + frictions

working.label: Implication
working.display: λ = s/(1−R) attributes the whole spread to default → risk-neutral PD > real-world PD

scenarios.takeaway: Risk-neutral (spread-implied) PD > historical PD: use it for valuation, not loss forecasting.

scenarios.reading: Reading 82: Schroeck, Capital Structure in Banks
scenarios.setup: Economic capital is read from the tail of a beta distribution fitted to two moments, $EL_P$ and $UL_P$. A large, high-quality, well-diversified portfolio has $EL_P > UL_P$.
scenarios.ask: For this portfolio, beta-based economic capital is likely: overstated, understated, or about right?

options.label: Understated
options.why: That is the low-quality case ($EL_P < UL_P$, tail too thin). Here the fitted beta tail is too fat.

options.label: About right
options.why: A two-moment fit calibrates the body, not the tail; the direction of the misfit depends on $EL_P / UL_P$.

working.label: Fit
working.display: Beta matched on mean = EL_P and standard deviation = UL_P

scenarios.takeaway: Beta fit: high quality ⇒ tail too fat ⇒ EC overstated; low quality ⇒ the reverse.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A 10-year uncollateralised interest rate swap. Two effects drive its expected exposure over time: diffusion (uncertainty about rates grows with the horizon) and amortisation (fewer cash flows remain as maturity approaches).
scenarios.ask: Over the final few years before maturity, expected exposure: rises, falls, or stays flat?

options.label: Rises
options.why: Diffusion dominates early; amortisation wins late. At maturity no cash flows remain, so exposure goes to zero however far rates have moved.

options.label: Stays flat
options.why: The two effects do not balance late in the life; amortisation takes exposure to zero at maturity.

working.label: Late life
working.display: Amortisation dominates → exposure falls to zero at maturity

working.label: Shape
working.display: Hump, peaking roughly a third of the way through

scenarios.takeaway: Swap exposure is hump-shaped: diffusion up, amortisation down, zero at maturity.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: A dealer values an OTC position with a unilateral CVA only, a charge for counterparty default. It then adds DVA, the term for its own default against its expected negative exposure.
scenarios.ask: The risky value of the position: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: DVA ≈ ENE × own spread is a benefit, so bilateral CVA is a smaller deduction than CVA alone.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: DVA is non-zero whenever ENE > 0 and the dealer's own spread > 0.

working.label: Bilateral
working.display: Value = risk-free value − CVA + DVA → higher

scenarios.takeaway: DVA is a benefit from your own default risk on negative exposure; adding it raises value.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: A CMBS pool's properties earn net operating income (NOI) of USD 68m a year. Debt service on the notes is USD 54m a year. The pool's assets are worth about USD 5bn.
scenarios.ask: NOI falls 25% and debt service stays the same. The DSCR ends up:

options.label: Still above 1.0
options.why: A DSCR of 1.26 means income covers debt service with 26% to spare, but that doesn't mean income can fall 26%. Income can only fall $1 - 1/1.26 \approx 20.6\%$ before coverage is lost, so a 25% fall goes past that point.

options.label: Unchanged, because DSCR depends on pool value
options.why: DSCR is a flow ratio: NOI divided by debt service. The USD 5bn pool value belongs in loan-to-value, not DSCR.

scenarios.takeaway: A DSCR of $D$ lets income fall $1 - 1/D$ before cover is lost, not $D - 1$: at 1.26 that's about 21%, not 26%.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: An MBS has four pools (USD m, coupon): apartments 24 at 8.4%, villas 32 at 7.0%, penthouses 16 at 6.8%, farmhouses 8 at 5.6%. The simple average of the four coupons is 6.95%.
scenarios.ask: Will the balance-weighted WAC come out above the 6.95% simple average, below it, or about the same?

options.label: Below
options.why: For that, the low-coupon pools would have to be the big ones. Here the 8.4% and 7.0% pools hold 70% of the balance, so they pull the WAC up.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The weights are 30/40/20/10, nowhere near equal. Weighting moves the answer by about 0.3 percentage points.

scenarios.takeaway: A weighted average leans toward its biggest pools. If the big pools have the high coupons, WAC sits above the simple average.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: A commercial mortgage pool has four parts (USD m, days to maturity): superstores 26 at 82 days, offices 67 at 169 days, cinemas 22 at 253 days, restaurants 17 at 336 days. The simple average maturity is 210 days.
scenarios.ask: Will the balance-weighted WAM come out above 210 days, below it, or about the same?

options.label: Above
options.why: The two long pools (253 and 336 days) hold only 29.5% of the balance. The office pool holds just over half, at 169 days, and it dominates.

options.label: About the same
options.why: With one pool at 51% of the balance, weighting matters. WAM comes out about 23 days below the simple average.

scenarios.takeaway: Find the pool that holds most of the balance first: WAM sits just above its 169 days, well below the 210-day simple average.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds 100 equal credits. Each has PD 3% and zero recovery, and default correlation is zero. The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 4.
scenarios.ask: The 95% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 40,000
options.why: That's the 95% quantile loss (4 defaults × USD 10,000). Credit VaR then subtracts the USD 30,000 expected loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 100,000
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 300,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Credit VaR is the quantile loss minus expected loss. With 100 independent credits the 95th percentile is only one default above the mean.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: A USD 1m portfolio holds 100 equal credits. Each has PD 3% and zero recovery, and default correlation is zero. The 95th percentile of the number of defaults is 4. So far you have: position size USD 10,000, and expected number of defaults $np = 3$.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: the 95% credit VaR or the expected loss?

options.label: Credit VaR
options.why: Credit VaR is only the loss beyond the mean: $(4 - 3) \times 10{,}000 = 10{,}000$. Expected loss is $3 \times 10{,}000 = 30{,}000$.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The quantile is 4 defaults and the mean is 3, so VaR covers one default and EL covers three. EL is three times VaR.

scenarios.takeaway: In a granular, independent portfolio, credit VaR can be smaller than EL. EL is paid through the spread, and only the tail beyond it needs capital.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Portfolio Y has USD 1m notional across 30 positions, all exposures to the same obligor, so default correlation is 1. PD is 3% and recovery is zero.
scenarios.ask: The 99% credit VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.03m
options.why: That's the expected loss ($0.03 \times 1\text{m}$). You stopped before subtracting it from the quantile loss.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.3m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 29m
options.why: Treated each of the 30 positions as a USD 1m exposure: $30 \times (1 - 0.03)$. The portfolio can't lose more than its USD 1m notional.

working.label: P(no default)
working.display: $1 - 0.03 = 97\% < 99\%$, so the 99th percentile lands in the default state

scenarios.takeaway: At correlation 1, the portfolio behaves like one loan. Compare $1 - PD$ with the confidence level: if the quantile falls in the default state, VaR is close to the full notional.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Portfolio Y has USD 1m notional across 30 positions, all exposures to the same obligor, so default correlation is 1. PD is 3% and recovery is zero. At 99% confidence, credit VaR is USD 970,000.
scenarios.ask: The confidence level drops from 99% to 95%. Credit VaR:

options.label: Falls only slightly and stays near USD 0.9m
options.why: With $P(\text{no default}) = 97\% > 95\%$, the 95th percentile falls in the no-default state. The quantile loss is 0, so VaR is floored at zero.

options.label: Rises
options.why: A lower confidence level can never push a quantile up. Here it moves the quantile from the default state to the no-default state.

working.label: Where the 95th percentile sits
working.display: $97\% > 95\%$, so it falls in the no-default state (loss 0)

scenarios.takeaway: With a single all-or-nothing credit, check whether $1 - PD$ is above or below the confidence level before computing anything: the answer is either close to the full notional or zero.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.025$ and $\pi_2 = 0.035$, and default correlation $\rho_{12} = 0.05$. The joint default probability is $\pi_{12} = \pi_1\pi_2 + \rho_{12}\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\,\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$.
scenarios.ask: Which term is larger: the independence term $\pi_1\pi_2$ or the correlation term?

options.label: The independence term
options.why: The product of two small PDs is tiny, at 0.0875%. The standard-deviation product is about 2.87%, so even a 0.05 correlation gives 0.1435%.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The correlation term is about 1.6 times the independence term. Even a small $\rho$ more than doubles the joint PD compared with independence.

scenarios.takeaway: For small PDs, $\pi_1\pi_2$ is second-order small but the SD product is first-order. That's why even a tiny default correlation dominates the joint default probability.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.025$ and $\pi_2 = 0.035$, and default correlation $\rho_{12} = 0.05$.
scenarios.ask: Their joint default probability is closest to:

options.why: That's just $\pi_1\pi_2$, the independence case. You dropped the correlation term.
Decimal slip on the correlation term, reading 0.001435 as 0.01435. The joint PD should sit near the independence value when $\rho$ is small.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The joint PD must lie between $\pi_1\pi_2$ and $\min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$, and near the bottom of that range when $\rho$ is small.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Two credits have PDs $\pi_1 = 0.003$ and $\pi_2 = 0.004$. Capping the joint PD at $\min(\pi_1, \pi_2)$ gives a maximum permissible default correlation of 0.866.
scenarios.ask: Credit 2's PD moves from 0.004 to 0.0035, closer to credit 1's. Credit 1 is unchanged. The maximum permissible default correlation:

options.label: Falls
options.why: The bound reaches 1 only when the two PDs are equal. Moving them closer relaxes the bound, from 0.866 to 0.926.

options.label: Unchanged, because the joint PD cap is still 0.003
options.why: The cap on $\pi_{12}$ is still 0.003, but the denominator $\sqrt{\pi_1(1-\pi_1)\pi_2(1-\pi_2)}$ shrinks as $\pi_2$ falls, so $\rho_{max}$ rises.

scenarios.takeaway: Maximum default correlation is below 1 whenever the two PDs differ. It rises toward 1 as they converge.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: Over the same horizon, a BBB credit has PD 0.003 and a CCC credit has PD 0.005. The probability that both default is 0.0002.
scenarios.ask: The implied default correlation is closest to:

options.why: That's the joint default probability itself, not a correlation.
Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (10×).

scenarios.takeaway: A joint PD 13 times the independence value implies a default correlation of only about 0.05. Low default correlations still cluster defaults a lot.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
scenarios.setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$.
scenarios.ask: The economy turns down and $m = -1.41$. Compared with the 5% unconditional PD, the conditional PD is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Sign slip. With $m < 0$, the term $-\beta m = +0.846$ makes the numerator less negative, which pushes the PD up.

options.label: Unchanged, because $m$ only drives correlation
options.why: $m$ enters the conditional PD directly. Only at $m = 0$ does $p(m) = N(k) = 5\%$.

scenarios.takeaway: In the one-factor copula a negative $m$ raises the conditional PD. The check: $m = 0$ gives back $N(k)$.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
scenarios.setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$. The market factor falls to $m = -1.41$.
scenarios.ask: The conditional PD is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: A 1.4σ downturn with β = 0.6 roughly triples a 5% PD. Conditioning on $m$ is how the model makes defaults cluster.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives: Credit Derivatives
scenarios.setup: In a one-factor Gaussian copula, a firm has $\beta = 0.60$ and default threshold $k = -1.645$, so its unconditional PD is 5%. Its PD conditional on the market factor is $p(m) = N\!\left[\dfrac{k - \beta m}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}}\right]$. With $m = -1.41$ you have the numerator $k - \beta m = -0.799$. A colleague divides it by $1 - \beta^2 = 0.64$ instead of $\sqrt{1-\beta^2} = 0.80$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the correct conditional PD, the colleague's figure is:

options.label: Too high
options.why: Dividing a negative numerator by a smaller number makes the argument more negative ($-1.25$ vs $-1.00$), so $N(\cdot)$ gets smaller.

options.label: The same, because the scaling cancels
options.why: Nothing cancels. The divisor sets how many standard deviations the threshold sits from the conditional mean.

scenarios.takeaway: The idiosyncratic part has standard deviation $\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$, not variance $1-\beta^2$. Using the variance understates a stressed PD.

scenarios.setup: US municipal defaults arrive as a Poisson process with an average of 6.0 per year.
scenarios.ask: The probability that the next default happens within one month is closest to:

options.why: Converted to monthly twice: $\lambda t = 6/12/12 = 0.042$.
Scale slip (0.3×).
Forgot the time conversion. With $t = 1$ year, $1 - e^{-6} = 99.8\%$.

scenarios.takeaway: Half a default is expected per month, so a 30–40% chance of at least one is the right size.

scenarios.setup: Municipal defaults arrive as a Poisson process at 6.0 per year. Over one month, $\lambda t = 6.0 \times 1/12 = 0.5$.
scenarios.ask: Is the probability of at least one default within the month above 50%, below it, or exactly 50%?

options.label: Exactly 50%
options.why: $\lambda t$ is the expected number of defaults, not a probability. For $x > 0$, $1 - e^{-x} < x$.

options.label: Above 50%
options.why: $e^{-0.5} = 60.7\%$ is the survival probability, the chance of no default. The default probability is the other 39.3%.

scenarios.takeaway: $1 - e^{-\lambda t}$ is always below $\lambda t$. The expected count overstates the probability of at least one event.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: Moody's average cumulative default rates for Caa-C: 36.908% by year 3 and 44.128% by year 4.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: the year-4 marginal PD (seen from today) or the year-4 PD conditional on surviving to the end of year 3?

options.label: The marginal PD
options.why: The conditional PD divides the marginal by the survival probability, 0.631. Dividing by less than 1 makes it bigger.

options.label: About equal
options.why: They'd match only if survival to year 3 were close to 100%. For Caa it's only 63%.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditional PD is marginal PD divided by survival, so it's always at least the marginal, and much larger for weak credits.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Rating Migration Matrices and Default Probability Measures
scenarios.setup: Moody's average cumulative default rates for Caa-C: 36.908% by year 3 and 44.128% by year 4.
scenarios.ask: The PD for year 4, conditional on no earlier default, is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).
That's the four-year cumulative PD: default at any time in years 1–4, not in year 4 alone.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Cumulative, then difference, then divide by survival. About one in nine Caa bonds still alive after year 3 defaults in year 4.

scenarios.setup: One-year migration matrix, where default (D) is absorbing. From A: to A 0.90, to B 0.09, to D 0.01. From B: to A 0.05, to B 0.85, to D 0.10. A credit is rated A today.
scenarios.ask: Of the two year-2 default paths, A→A→D and A→B→D, which adds more to the two-year PD?

options.label: A→A→D, staying in A
options.why: $0.90 \times 0.01 = 0.90\%$. But the rare downgrade meets a PD 10 times higher: $0.09 \times 0.10 = 0.90\%$ as well.

options.label: A→B→D, through the downgrade
options.why: Close, but not bigger: both paths come to exactly 0.90%.

scenarios.takeaway: Migration isn't second-order: a small downgrade probability times a much higher PD can match the stay-put path. That's why the two-year PD is above twice the one-year PD.

scenarios.setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp and expected recovery is 40%. Its bonds trade near par with 3y/5y/10y spreads of 50/60/100bp. Assume a constant hazard rate, with $s \approx \lambda(1-R)$.
scenarios.ask: Is the implied hazard rate higher than the 240bp CDS spread, lower, or equal to it?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Slip: multiplied by LGD instead of dividing. A spread pays for loss, so dividing by $1 - R = 0.6$ scales it up.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only if recovery were zero. With 40% recovery, each default costs 60%, so more defaults are needed to justify the spread.

scenarios.takeaway: $\lambda = s/(1-R)$: the hazard rate is always at least the spread, because each default loses only a fraction of par.

scenarios.setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp. With a 40% recovery assumption, the implied constant hazard rate is $\lambda = s/(1-R) = 4.0\%$.
scenarios.ask: Keep the spread at 240bp but assume 60% recovery instead. The implied hazard rate:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Higher recovery means each default costs less, so more frequent defaults are needed to justify the same spread: $0.024/0.40 = 6.0\%$.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: $\lambda$ depends on LGD directly. Only CVA with the same $R$ used on both sides is roughly recovery-neutral.

scenarios.takeaway: For a fixed spread, a higher recovery assumption means a higher implied default intensity.

scenarios.setup: GlobalTech's 5-year CDS spread is 240bp and expected recovery is 40%. Its bonds trade near par with 3y/5y/10y spreads of 50/60/100bp. Assume a constant hazard rate, with $s \approx \lambda(1-R)$.
scenarios.ask: The 5-year cumulative default probability is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (3×).
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Spread over LGD gives the annual intensity. Over $T$ years the cumulative PD is $1 - e^{-\lambda T}$, a bit under $\lambda T$.

scenarios.setup: Two-way CSA. The dealer's exposure to the counterparty is USD 48m. The counterparty owes an independent amount of USD 5m and has a threshold of USD 20m. The dealer already holds USD 29.5m of collateral after haircuts. The minimum transfer amount (MTA) is USD 1m.
scenarios.ask: The resulting margin call is:

options.label: The counterparty must post more collateral
The dealer must return collateral
options.why: The requirement is $48 + 5 - 20 = 33$. That exceeds the 29.5 held, so the counterparty is short, not over-collateralised.

options.label: No transfer, because the gap is inside the MTA
options.why: The gap is USD 3.5m, well above the USD 1m MTA.

scenarios.takeaway: Independent amount adds, threshold subtracts. Net against collateral already held, then test against the MTA.

scenarios.setup: Two-way CSA: exposure USD 48m, independent amount USD 5m, threshold USD 20m, collateral held USD 29.5m after haircuts, MTA USD 1m. Right now the counterparty owes a delivery of USD 3.5m.
scenarios.ask: The threshold is renegotiated from USD 20m to USD 25m, with everything else unchanged. The margin call:

options.label: Shrinks, but the counterparty still posts
options.why: Raising the threshold cuts the requirement by the full USD 5m: $3.5 - 5 = -1.5$. The dealer now holds USD 1.5m too much, which is above the MTA.

options.label: Flips, and the dealer must return collateral
Grows
options.why: The threshold is subtracted from exposure, so raising it lowers the requirement.

scenarios.takeaway: A threshold change moves the call one-for-one. If the old call was smaller than the change, the direction flips.

scenarios.setup: One-way CSA with no threshold. The requirement is the bank's full exposure of USD 62m, and the MTA is USD 0.5m. No collateral is held yet. The hedge fund offers USD 40m of government bonds (4% haircut) and USD 25m of corporate bonds (12% haircut), which is USD 65m at market value.
scenarios.ask: After haircuts, the position is:

options.label: A surplus
options.why: At market value it's +3.0m, but the haircuts take off $1.6 + 3.0 = 4.6$m. That leaves 60.4m of credit against the 62m required.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The −1.6m gap is clear, and more than three times the 0.5m MTA.

scenarios.takeaway: Haircuts only ever reduce the collateral credit. A 3m surplus at market value can turn into a shortfall once 4.6m of haircuts come off.

scenarios.setup: One-way CSA with no threshold. The requirement is the bank's full exposure of USD 62m, and the MTA is USD 0.5m. The hedge fund offers USD 40m of government bonds (4% haircut) and USD 25m of corporate bonds (12% haircut), which is USD 65m at market value.
scenarios.ask: The total haircut deduction, meaning market value minus collateral credit given, is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 14m
options.why: Scale slip (3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 46m
options.why: Percent-vs-decimal slip: read the 4% and 12% haircuts as 0.4 and 1.2.

options.label: ≈ USD 138m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Size the haircut first: 4.6m against a 3m headline surplus tells you the sign of the answer.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A netting set is simulated at four annual points (USD m). Expected MtM: +2, +1, −1, −3. Expected exposure (EE): 5, 7, 6, 3. 97.5% PFE: 14, 19, 16, 9.
scenarios.ask: Maximum exposure over the four years is closest to:

options.why: That's the peak EE, the mean profile. Maximum exposure is the worst case, read from the PFE profile.
Added the four PFEs together. Maximum exposure is the largest single PFE, not their sum.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Maximum exposure is the peak of the PFE profile, well above any EE.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A netting set is simulated at four annual points (USD m). Expected MtM: +2, +1, −1, −3. Expected exposure (EE): 5, 7, 6, 3. 97.5% PFE: 14, 19, 16, 9. Effective EE is the running maximum of EE.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: EPE (the time average of EE) or effective EPE?

options.label: EPE
options.why: The running maximum can never fall below EE, so effective EPE is always at least EPE.

options.label: Equal
options.why: They're equal only if EE never declines. Here EE falls after year 2, and the running maximum locks in 7.

scenarios.takeaway: Effective EPE ≥ EPE, and the gap is strictly positive as soon as the EE profile turns down.

scenarios.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2bn.
scenarios.ask: The capital adequacy (total capital) ratio is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Tier 2 on its own over RWA. Tier 2 is never used alone as a capital adequacy measure.

scenarios.takeaway: CAR, the Tier 1 ratio and the CET1 ratio all divide by RWA. Only the numerator changes.

scenarios.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: A bank has Tier 1 capital of USD 200m, Tier 2 capital of USD 100m and risk-weighted assets of USD 2bn. Its total capital ratio is 15% and its Tier 1 ratio is 10%.
scenarios.ask: The bank issues USD 50m of Tier 2 subordinated debt, and RWA doesn't change. Its Tier 1 ratio:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Only the total capital ratio rises, to 17.5%. The Tier 1 ratio's numerator excludes Tier 2 entirely.

options.label: Falls
options.why: RWA is unchanged and Tier 1 is unchanged, so nothing pushes the ratio down.

scenarios.takeaway: The capital ratios share a denominator. Check which numerator the new capital actually enters.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A portfolio has MtM +15. You hold variation margin of 10, and each side has posted segregated initial margin of 6. Ignore close-out costs.
scenarios.ask: Before the zero floor, is the counterparty-credit residual $MtM - VM_{held} - IM_{held}$ positive, negative or zero?

options.label: Positive
options.why: Dropped the initial margin held: $15 - 10 = 5$. The IM you hold is also a buffer against the counterparty defaulting.

options.label: Zero
options.why: $15 - 10 - 6 = -1$. The position is slightly over-collateralised.

working.label: Funding exposure
working.display: $15 - 10 + 6 = 11$ (posted IM is locked away and must be funded)

scenarios.takeaway: Initial margin held reduces credit exposure. Segregated initial margin posted adds to funding exposure. Same number, opposite signs.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A portfolio has MtM +15. You hold variation margin of 10. Each side has posted segregated initial margin of 6, which can't be reused. Counterparty credit exposure is 0 and funding exposure is 11.
scenarios.ask: Both sides raise their segregated initial margin from 6 to 8. Your funding exposure:

options.label: Falls
options.why: IM held reduces credit exposure. IM you post that is segregated must be funded, so it adds to funding exposure.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Credit exposure stays at its floor of 0, but funding exposure goes from 11 to 13.

scenarios.takeaway: More segregated IM reduces counterparty risk but costs funding. That trade-off is what MVA prices.

scenarios.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
scenarios.setup: Three swaps on identical terms, each listed as fixed payer → fixed receiver: (1) Bank A → Bank B, USD 250m; (2) Bank B → Bank C, USD 180m; (3) Bank C → Bank A, USD 130m. Count paying fixed as + and receiving fixed as −.
scenarios.ask: Across its two swaps, Bank B's net fixed-rate position is:

options.label: Flat, since B sits in the middle of the chain
options.why: B receives fixed on 250 (from A) and pays fixed on only 180 (to C). That nets to receiving 70, not zero.

options.label: A net payer of fixed
options.why: Sign slip. B pays on 180 but receives on 250.

working.label: Notional after compression
working.display: A pays fixed on 120 in total (70 to B, 50 to C), down from 560 gross

scenarios.takeaway: Net every bank with a fixed sign convention. The nets must sum to zero, and a middle-of-the-chain bank isn't flat unless its two notionals match.

scenarios.reading: Reading 94: Gregory, ISDA Master Agreement, Netting and Close-out
scenarios.setup: Three swaps on identical terms, each listed as fixed payer → fixed receiver: (1) Bank A → Bank B, USD 250m; (2) Bank B → Bank C, USD 180m; (3) Bank C → Bank A, USD 130m. A multilateral compression cuts gross notional from USD 560m to USD 120m.
scenarios.ask: After compression, each bank's net interest-rate exposure is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: Compression removes redundant gross notional. Each bank's net position, and so its rate risk, is kept exactly.

options.label: Higher
options.why: No bank's net fixed position changes, so rate risk can't increase.

scenarios.takeaway: Compression lowers notional, operational load and leverage exposure. Market risk is unchanged.

scenarios.reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
scenarios.setup: A pool prepaid 0.55% of its scheduled balance this month (SMM). Multiplying by 12 gives 6.60%.
scenarios.ask: Is the compounded annual rate $CPR = 1 - (1 - SMM)^{12}$ higher than 6.60%, lower, or equal?

options.label: Higher
options.why: Survival compounds: each month's prepayment applies to a smaller surviving balance, so 12 × SMM overstates the annual rate.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only to first order. The compounding shortfall is about 0.2 percentage points here.

scenarios.takeaway: Annualising a monthly rate by compounding survival always gives less than 12 times the rate. It's the same idea as a hazard rate against a cumulative PD.

scenarios.reading: Fabozzi, Securitisation Cash Flows and Structures
scenarios.setup: A pool 20 months seasoned prepaid 0.55% of its balance this month (SMM), which is a CPR of 6.40%. The 100 PSA benchmark ramps CPR up by 0.2% a month to 6% at month 30, then stays flat.
scenarios.ask: Relative to 100 PSA, this pool is prepaying:

options.label: Slower
options.why: At month 20 the benchmark is only $6\% \times 20/30 = 4.00\%$. A CPR of 6.40% beats it.

options.label: At about 100 PSA
options.why: 6.40% is close to the terminal 6%, but the benchmark at month 20 is 4.00%: $6.40/4.00 = 160$ PSA.

scenarios.takeaway: PSA is a ramp: compare with the benchmark at the pool's seasoning month, not with the 6% plateau.

scenarios.reading: Reading 98: Gregory, Credit and Debt Value Adjustments
scenarios.setup: CVA on an uncollateralised swap uses a hazard rate implied from the counterparty's CDS spread, $\lambda \approx s/(1-R)$. The same recovery $R$ also sets the loss given default in CVA. The EPE profile is fixed.
scenarios.ask: The recovery assumption rises from 40% to 60% and the CDS spread doesn't move. CVA:

options.label: Falls
options.why: LGD does fall, but the implied $\lambda$ rises by the same factor. The two $(1-R)$ terms cancel.

options.label: Rises
options.why: The higher implied default intensity is exactly offset by the smaller loss per default.

working.label: Result
working.display: No $R$ left, so CVA is about recovery-neutral (if the same $R$ is used both times)

scenarios.takeaway: CVA rises with the spread but hardly moves with recovery, because $R$ enters twice with opposite signs.

scenarios.reading: Reading 102: Choudhry, An Introduction to Securitisation
scenarios.setup: Two securitisations have identical tranche attachment points. Both pools hold assets with a 2% individual PD. Pool 1's pairwise default correlation is 0.05 and Pool 2's is 0.40.
scenarios.ask: For the same senior rating, Pool 2's senior tranche needs subordination that is:

options.label: The same, since expected loss is identical
options.why: Expected loss is the same, but correlation fattens the tail. The tail is what reaches the senior tranche.

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Higher correlation makes defaults cluster, which raises the chance of breaching any attachment point.

working.label: Senior tranche
working.display: Higher chance of breaching the attachment point, so more subordination is needed

scenarios.takeaway: PD moves the whole loss distribution. Correlation moves only its shape, and the shape is what sets senior subordination.

scenarios.reading: Reading 89: Malz, Default Correlation and Portfolio Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: A credit portfolio's PDs, exposures and LGDs are all held fixed. Pairwise default correlation between the obligors rises.
scenarios.ask: The portfolio's expected loss:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Correlation raises unexpected loss and credit VaR, not EL. $EL = \sum PD_i \cdot EAD_i \cdot LGD_i$ has no correlation term.

options.label: Falls
options.why: EL is linear in the individual PDs, and none of them changed.

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation moves the tail (UL, credit VaR, capital), not the mean (EL, spread).

scenarios.setup: A portfolio of BBB bonds is managed over one year. It switches from buy-and-hold to monthly rebalancing: any bond downgraded below BBB is sold and replaced with a BBB bond.
scenarios.ask: The probability of large default losses (the far tail):

options.label: Rises
options.why: Rebalancing does make small downgrade losses realised and more frequent. But it cuts off the migration path that leads to default.

options.label: Unchanged, since the average rating is BBB either way
options.why: The average rating is the same, but the loss distribution isn't: rebalancing gives a shorter tail and a thicker body.

working.label: Path to default
working.display: Credits reach default by migrating downward, and rebalancing sells them on the first downgrade

working.label: Tail
working.display: Default losses in the portfolio become much rarer

working.label: Body
working.display: Every downgrade is realised as a small permanent loss

scenarios.takeaway: Constant-risk rebalancing trades tail risk for more frequent small losses.

scenarios.reading: Reading 83: Doumpos, Fundamentals of Credit Risk
scenarios.setup: For one rating category, a risk manager backs default probabilities out of corporate bond spreads with $\lambda = s/(1-R)$ and compares them with historical default rates.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the historical PDs, the spread-implied PDs are typically:

options.label: Lower
options.why: The spread carries liquidity and systematic-risk premia on top of expected default loss, and $s/(1-R)$ counts all of it as default.

options.label: About the same
options.why: The gap is large, often several times, and widest for high-grade issuers where the premia dwarf the expected loss.

working.label: Implied PD
working.display: Counts the whole spread as default compensation, so it's inflated compared with the real-world PD

scenarios.takeaway: Risk-neutral PDs are above real-world PDs. Use risk-neutral for valuation and CVA, real-world for loss forecasting and capital.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: A bank has a currency swap and an interest-rate swap with one counterparty under a single enforceable netting agreement.
scenarios.ask: The correlation between the two trades' values moves from strongly positive to strongly negative. The netting benefit:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Netting pays off when trade values have opposite signs, and negative correlation makes that the usual state.

options.label: Unchanged, since netting is a legal mechanism
options.why: The legal right is the same, but how much it saves depends on how often the trades offset each other.

working.label: Strong positive correlation
working.display: Values usually share a sign, so the benefit is small

working.label: Strong negative correlation
working.display: Values usually offset, so the benefit is largest

scenarios.takeaway: Netting benefit is largest for negatively correlated trades and close to zero for strongly positive ones.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: An investment firm trades derivatives in volatile markets under a collateral agreement that remargins every 3 days.
scenarios.ask: The remargining period is cut from 3 days to 1 day. Residual uncollateralised exposure:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Less time passes between calls, so the position has less room to move against the firm before collateral arrives.

options.label: Unchanged, because the threshold and MTA fix it
options.why: The threshold and MTA add to residual exposure, and so does the move over the margin period of risk, which scales with $\sqrt{\tau}$.

scenarios.takeaway: Shorter remargining means a shorter margin period of risk. The exposure that builds up in that window shrinks roughly with $\sqrt{\tau}$.

scenarios.reading: Reading 97: Gregory, Credit Exposure and Funding
scenarios.setup: At a future date, a netting set has three equally likely values: +12, 0 and −12.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: the expected MtM or the expected exposure?

options.label: Equal, because the distribution is symmetric
options.why: Exposure floors each scenario at zero before averaging, so the −12 counts as 0, not −12.

options.label: Expected MtM
options.why: Expected exposure averages non-negative numbers, so it can't be below the expected MtM.

scenarios.takeaway: $EE = E[\max(V, 0)] \ge \max(E[V], 0)$. The floor goes inside the expectation.

scenarios.reading: Reading 87: Jorion, Portfolio Risk: Analytical Methods
scenarios.setup: A pension fund has USD 20m in three sleeves: 30% US stocks ($\sigma = 12\%$), 40% US bonds ($\sigma = 5\%$), 30% non-US stocks ($\sigma = 18\%$). Portfolio volatility is 10%. One-year horizon, 99% ($z = 2.33$).
scenarios.ask: Roughly how big is the fund's **undiversified** VaR?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.47m
options.why: That is the diversification benefit (undiversified minus diversified VaR), not the undiversified VaR itself.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.7m
options.why: Stopped after one sleeve. That is the US-stock individual VaR alone, not the sum across all three.

options.label: ≈ USD 16m
options.why: Applied each sleeve's volatility to the full USD 20m. The weights were dropped, so every sleeve was counted at 100% of the fund.
