options.label: ≈ USD 0.50bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 4.1bn
options.why: Gross revenue divided by NIM (100 / 0.0245). The numerator is net.

scenarios.takeaway: Earning assets = net interest income / NIM. Net in the numerator, decimal in the denominator.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Total assets USD 1,212m, zero equity. Rate-sensitive assets USD 542m earn 5% and the remaining fixed assets earn 10%. Rate-sensitive liabilities USD 156m cost 4% and the remaining fixed liabilities cost 6%.
scenarios.ask: Which block contributes more to net interest income: the rate-sensitive block (RSA income − RSL cost) or the fixed block (FA income − FL cost)?

options.label: The fixed block: fixed assets earn 10%
options.why: Fixed assets (670m) earn 67.0m, but fixed liabilities (1,056m at 6%) cost 63.4m, so the fixed block nets only about 3.6m.

options.label: About equal
options.why: It is 20.9m vs 3.6m.

scenarios.takeaway: NII is a whole-balance-sheet quantity. The rate-sensitive block alone (20.86) is a trap answer.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: National Bank's cumulative interest-sensitive gap for the coming year is +USD 128m. Market rates are expected to fall by 1.5 percentage points.
scenarios.ask: Net interest income over the year:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Sign slip: a positive gap helps only when rates rise. Here asset yields reprice down more than funding costs.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: Only a zero gap insulates NII. A positive gap is exposed to falling rates.

scenarios.takeaway: Positive gap + falling rates → NII falls. The sign of ΔNII is the sign of gap × Δr.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bank's cumulative interest-sensitive gap is +USD 128m and market rates fall by 1.5 percentage points.
scenarios.ask: The size of the change in net interest income is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.19m
options.why: You read 1.5 percentage points as 0.15% (0.0015).

options.label: ≈ USD 19m
options.why: You read 1.5 percentage points as 15% (0.15).

options.label: ≈ USD 190m
options.why: You multiplied by 1.5 without converting to a decimal.

scenarios.takeaway: ΔNII = Δr (as a decimal) × gap. 1.5 pp = 0.015.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A three-year USD 1,000 loan pays an 8% annual coupon and yields 8%, so it is priced at par. The present values of its cash flows are 74.07, 68.59 and 857.34.
scenarios.ask: Its duration, compared with its three-year maturity, is:

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only zero-coupon or single-payment instruments have duration equal to maturity.

options.label: Longer
options.why: Duration is a PV-weighted average of the cash-flow times, and none of those times is later than year 3.

scenarios.takeaway: Anything that pays cash before maturity has duration < maturity.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bond has duration 6.5 years and price USD 980. Rates on comparable bonds rise from 6.00% to 6.75%. Use $\Delta P / P = -D \, \Delta i / (1 + i)$.
scenarios.ask: The size of the percentage price change is closest to:

options.why: Basis-point slip: you treated the 75bp move as 7.5bp (0.00075).
Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (3×). Skipping the (1 + i) only nudges it to 4.9%.

scenarios.takeaway: Duration × relative rate change: 6.5 × ~0.7% ≈ 4.6%. A 75bp move can't cost 41%.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Duration 6.5 years; rates rise from 6.00% to 6.75%. You have the relative rate change: $\Delta i / (1 + i) = 0.0075 / 1.06 = 0.00708$.
scenarios.ask: Is the bond's price loss bigger than 5%, smaller than 5%, or too close to call?

options.label: Bigger than 5%
options.why: 6.5 × 0.00708 = 0.046. Only a duration above about 7.1 would push it past 5%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 4.6% vs 5% is a clear gap. Even skipping the (1 + i) only gets you to 4.9%.

scenarios.takeaway: Multiply duration by the relative rate change. Here the loss lands just under 5%.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Green House National Bank: asset duration $D_A = 4.40$ years on assets of USD 648m, liability duration $D_L = 2.16$ years on liabilities of USD 401m. The unadjusted gap $D_A - D_L$ is 2.24 years.
scenarios.ask: The leverage-adjusted duration gap is:

options.label: Smaller than 2.24 years
options.why: The adjustment multiplies $D_L$ by $L/A = 0.62 < 1$. That shrinks the amount subtracted, so the gap grows.

options.label: Equal to 2.24 years
options.why: It would be equal only if L = A (zero equity) or $D_L = 0$. Neither holds here.

scenarios.takeaway: L < A, so the leverage-adjusted gap is always larger than D_A − D_L.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Green House National Bank has asset duration 4.40 years, liability duration 2.16 years, assets USD 648m and liabilities USD 401m. Rates rise by 1 percentage point (ignore the $1 + r$ discount).
scenarios.ask: Net worth:

options.label: Rises
options.why: A positive leverage-adjusted gap means assets lose more value than liabilities when rates rise.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The gap is +3.06 years. That is far from immunised: ΔNW ≈ −3.06 × 648 × 0.01 ≈ −USD 20m.

scenarios.takeaway: Positive leverage-adjusted gap → net worth falls when rates rise.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Millennial National Bank: $D_A = 2.53$, $D_L = 0.65$, A = USD 367m, L = USD 219m. Rates rise from 5.0% to 8.5%. You have the asset leg: $-2.53 \times \tfrac{0.035}{1.05} \times 367 = -$USD 30.95m. The liability leg offsets part of it.
scenarios.ask: Is the net change in net worth positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Positive
options.why: The liability leg is only +4.75m (0.65 × 0.0333 × 219). It can't offset 30.95m.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The net is about −26.2m, far from zero.

scenarios.takeaway: Short, small liabilities offset little. Net worth follows the asset leg down.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A = USD 367m ($D_A = 2.53$), L = USD 219m ($D_L = 0.65$). Rates rise from 5.0% to 8.5%.
scenarios.ask: The loss in net worth is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.87m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 2.6m
options.why: You treated the 3.5-point rise as 35bp (0.0035).

options.label: ≈ USD 8.7m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: ΔNW = −(D_A·A − D_L·L) × Δr/(1 + r). Check the size of Δr as a decimal before multiplying.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Stress test: rates rise 300bp from 3.0%. Assets (USD m, duration): cash 75 (0), fed funds 130 (1), government securities and mortgages 160 (4), loans 240 (2). Liabilities: deposits 300 (0.5), borrowings 270 (3). Equity 35.
scenarios.ask: The fall in net worth is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 36m
options.why: Asset leg only. The liability leg gives back about 28m.

options.label: ≈ USD 255m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 850m
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Shortcut: ΔNW = −(ΣD·A − ΣD·L) × Δr/(1 + r). Both legs are needed.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: ABC Bank: A = USD 180m ($D_A = 4$), L = USD 150m ($D_L = 3$), so net worth starts at USD 30m. Rates jump from 9% to 13%. Asset leg: −USD 26.42m. Liability leg: +USD 16.51m.
scenarios.ask: After the shock, the bank's net worth is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: Even the asset leg alone (−26.42) leaves 3.6m of equity. The liability leg gives back 16.51, so ΔNW = −9.91 and NW ≈ 20.1m.

options.label: Too close to zero to call
options.why: That is the asset-leg-only slip: 30 − 26.42 = 3.6m. Add back the liability leg (+16.51) and NW ≈ 20.1m, about two-thirds of the starting equity.

scenarios.takeaway: The duration formula gives a change. If the question asks for a level, add it back to the starting net worth.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Harrier Bank: asset duration $D_A = 3.60$ years, assets USD 840m, liabilities USD 760m. It wants to immunise net worth by setting the leverage-adjusted duration gap to zero.
scenarios.ask: The liability duration it needs is:

options.label: Equal to 3.60 years
options.why: That is naive matching, and it ignores that L < A.

options.label: Shorter than 3.60 years
options.why: Ratio inversion: $D_L = D_A \times A/L$, and $A/L > 1$.

scenarios.takeaway: To immunise net worth, D_L = D_A × A/L, which is longer than D_A because fewer liability dollars must absorb the asset move.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: ABC Bank, 2019: high-quality liquid assets 1,458; average monthly withdrawals 2,458; expected 30-day net cash outflows under the stress scenario 1,700. (In 2018 HQLA was 2,100 against stressed outflows of 1,600.)
scenarios.ask: In 2019, does the bank meet the liquidity coverage ratio requirement?

options.label: Yes: LCR is above 100%
options.why: Inverted ratio: 1,700 / 1,458 = 117%. LCR = HQLA / stressed net outflows.

options.label: Borderline
options.why: 86% is a clear breach, and it fell from 131% in 2018.

scenarios.takeaway: LCR = HQLA / 30-day stressed net outflows ≥ 100%. Average withdrawals are bait.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: A trader unwinds a large illiquid position over $n$ days to minimise VaR after trading costs. The daily bid-offer spread widens with the quantity traded that day. At 95% confidence the optimal schedule front-loads, selling more than $V/n$ on day 1.
scenarios.ask: If the confidence level in the objective is lowered (say to 75%), the daily amounts become:

options.label: More front-loaded
options.why: Front-loading is driven by price risk (the λσ term). A lower confidence means a smaller λ, so there is less reason to rush.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The schedule depends on λ. Hull's example flattens from 48.9 / 30.0 / 14.1 / 5.1 / 1.9 at 95% to 36.1 / 26.2 / 17.7 / 11.6 / 8.4 at 75%.

working.label: Comparative static
working.display: Lower confidence → smaller λ → the price-risk term shrinks → the schedule flattens. At 50% it is exactly $V/n$ per day

scenarios.takeaway: Higher confidence → sell faster. Lower confidence → spread the unwind evenly.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: In a deleveraging cycle, banks cut credit lines and leveraged investors are forced to sell, which pushes asset prices down. Measured leverage is assets ÷ equity.
scenarios.ask: As asset prices fall, investors' measured leverage:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Equity absorbs the price loss first, so the denominator shrinks proportionally faster than the numerator.

options.label: Stays the same
options.why: Assets and equity fall by the same dollar amount, not the same percentage, so the ratio moves.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Price fall → equity absorbs loss → assets/equity rises → further forced sales

scenarios.takeaway: Deleveraging is self-reinforcing: falling prices raise measured leverage and force more selling.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A lending institution runs the typical maturity profile: its loans and securities mature later than the deposits and borrowings that fund them. The yield curve flattens and then inverts, with short rates above long rates.
scenarios.ask: Its net interest margin:

options.label: Widens
options.why: A positive maturity gap earns the long-minus-short spread. Flattening removes that spread.

options.label: Is unaffected
options.why: Borrow-short / lend-long profits depend directly on the slope of the curve.

working.label: Maturity gap
working.display: Asset maturity > liability maturity → positive maturity gap

working.label: Curve effect
working.display: Upward slope pays for the gap. A flat or inverted curve gives a small or even negative margin

scenarios.takeaway: Positive maturity gap + flattening or inverting curve → NIM squeezed.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Rate-sensitive items (USD m, sensitivity weight): fed funds loans 60 (1.00), investments 40 (1.30), loans and leases 150 (1.50); interest-bearing deposits 180 (0.86), money market borrowings 90 (0.91). The unweighted gap is $250 - 270 = -20$.
scenarios.ask: The fed funds rate rises 2 points. Allowing for the weights, net interest income:

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is the unweighted reading (−20 × 0.02 = −0.40m). The weights flip the gap to +100.3.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The weighted gap is +100.3m, so ΔNII ≈ +2.0m.

scenarios.takeaway: Basis risk can flip the sign of the gap. Weight before you call the direction.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: Two bonds have the same maturity and the same yield. One carries a higher promised coupon rate.
scenarios.ask: The higher-coupon bond's convexity is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: More coupon means more cash early, so duration is shorter and curvature is less. Convexity falls as the coupon rises.

options.label: The same
options.why: Maturity and yield are held fixed, but the coupon still changes the timing of the cash flows and so the curvature.

working.label: Rule
working.display: Maturity and yield fixed: higher coupon → lower convexity. Convexity also rises with duration

scenarios.takeaway: Convexity rises with duration and falls with coupon.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bank estimates the change in value of a positively convex bond portfolio with the linear rule $\Delta P / P = -D\,\Delta i/(1+i)$. Rates then jump by 200bp.
scenarios.ask: Relative to the true change, the duration estimate of the loss:

options.label: Understates the loss
options.why: The true price curve lies above its tangent line, so actual prices fall by less than the line predicts.

options.label: Is exact
options.why: The linear rule is only a first-order approximation, and its error grows with the square of the rate move.

working.label: Geometry
working.display: Positive convexity → the true price–yield curve lies above the tangent (duration) line on both sides

working.label: Rate rise
working.display: True price falls by less than the line → the estimate overstates the loss. For a rate fall it understates the gain

scenarios.takeaway: Positive convexity: duration overstates losses and understates gains, and the error is bigger for bigger moves.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A USD 100 face Treasury bill is bought for USD 88 and matures in 120 days. Its bank discount rate is 36.00%, measured on a face-value base with a 360-day year.
scenarios.ask: Its yield-to-maturity equivalent yield (purchase-price base, 365-day year) is:

options.label: Lower than 36%
options.why: Both conventions push the same way. The smaller base (88) and the longer year (365) each raise the figure.

options.label: Equal to 36%
options.why: The base and the day count both push the equivalent yield up, so for any bill bought at a discount the two can't coincide.

scenarios.takeaway: The bank discount rate understates the true return: it uses the face-value base and a 360-day year.

scenarios.setup: Traders' demand to short one specific government bond issue rises sharply relative to the supply available to borrow in the repo market.
scenarios.ask: That issue's own repo rate, relative to the general collateral (GC) rate, moves:

options.label: Up, above GC
options.why: Polarity slip. Cash lenders compete to get the scarce bond and accept a lower rate on their cash.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Scarcity is priced through the repo rate. That is the special spread.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Scarce issue → cash lenders accept less interest to get it → repo rate falls

working.label: Special spread
working.display: GC rate − issue repo rate widens

scenarios.takeaway: Going special means a repo rate below GC. More shorting demand → wider special spread → cheaper financing for the bond's owner.

scenarios.setup: A bank switches its liquidity transfer pricing from matched-maturity marginal cost of funds to a zero cost-of-funds approach, where business lines are charged nothing for liquidity.
scenarios.ask: The maturity transformation on its balance sheet tends to:

options.label: Decrease
options.why: With liquidity free, long illiquid assets look more profitable and get funded with the cheapest, shortest money.

options.label: Stay the same
options.why: The internal price signal drives what business lines book. Removing it changes the balance sheet.

working.label: Ranking
working.display: Maturity transformation: zero cost > average cost > matched-maturity (none by design)

scenarios.takeaway: The cheaper liquidity looks internally, the more the bank lends long and funds short.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
scenarios.setup: Since 2008, covered interest parity has shown persistent deviations (a cross-currency basis). Banks shrink their balance sheets around regulatory reporting dates.
scenarios.ask: As a quarter-end approaches, the CIP deviation typically:

options.label: Narrows
options.why: Balance-sheet capacity is withdrawn at reporting dates, so the arbitrage that closes the basis weakens.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The calendar pattern is the key evidence that the basis prices balance-sheet capacity.

working.label: Chain
working.display: Quarter end → banks shrink balance sheets → arbitrage capacity withdrawn → basis widens → normalises afterwards

scenarios.takeaway: CIP deviations are a price for balance sheet, and they spike when balance sheet is scarcest, at quarter-ends.

scenarios.setup: A firm has sold 5–10 year fixed-price oil supply contracts and hedges them with long, short-dated oil futures that are rolled forward and margined daily. Oil prices then fall sharply.
scenarios.ask: Its near-term cash position:

options.label: Improves
options.why: The gain sits in the long-dated supply contracts and arrives only over years. The futures losses are paid in cash now.

options.label: Unaffected: the hedge is matched
options.why: It is matched in value but not in timing. The daily margin creates a cash-flow mismatch.

working.label: Futures leg
working.display: Long futures lose as oil falls → daily margin calls → cash out now

working.label: Contract leg
working.display: Fixed-price sales gain value, but the cash comes in over 5–10 years

scenarios.takeaway: A value-matched hedge can still be a liquidity mismatch: short-dated margined hedges against long-dated exposures (Metallgesellschaft).

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: An exchange's order flow becomes dominated by positive feedback traders, who sell when prices fall and buy when prices rise.
scenarios.ask: Market liquidity:

options.label: Improves
options.why: Positive feedback reinforces each move and makes the market one-sided. It is negative feedback traders who supply liquidity.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: Trader type decides whether moves are absorbed or amplified.

working.label: Positive feedback
working.display: Sell into falls, buy into rises → moves reinforced → one-sided, unstable, illiquid

working.label: Negative feedback
working.display: Buy into falls, sell into rises → prices pulled back → liquid market

scenarios.takeaway: Liquid markets are dominated by negative feedback traders. Positive feedback drains liquidity.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: Funding (JPY bn, ASF factor): capital 8,000 (100%), stable retail 20,000 (95%), less-stable retail 10,000 (90%), FI funding under 6m 25,000 (0%), other wholesale 6m–1y 12,000 (50%). Assets (RSF factor): cash 5,000 (0%), Level 1 HQLA 10,000 (5%), mortgages ≥1y 30,000 (65%), corporate loans ≥1y 20,000 (85%), other assets 6,000 (100%). You have already found available stable funding: ASF = JPY 42,000bn.
scenarios.ask: Is required stable funding (RSF) bigger than ASF, smaller, or too close to call?

options.label: RSF is smaller (NSFR above 100%)
options.why: That is what unweighted totals suggest (assets 71,000 vs funding 75,000). Weighted, the mortgages and corporate loans alone need 36,500, and RSF reaches 43,000.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The factors are exact, so the gap is exact: RSF exceeds ASF by JPY 1,000bn (about 2.4%). Small, but the sign is not in doubt.

scenarios.takeaway: Weight both sides before comparing: long-dated loans at 65–85% RSF quickly outrun funding that has 0% FI money in it.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: Funding (JPY bn, ASF factor): capital 8,000 (100%), stable retail 20,000 (95%), less-stable retail 10,000 (90%), FI funding under 6m 25,000 (0%), other wholesale 6m–1y 12,000 (50%). Assets (RSF factor): cash 5,000 (0%), Level 1 HQLA 10,000 (5%), mortgages ≥1y 30,000 (65%), corporate loans ≥1y 20,000 (85%), other assets 6,000 (100%).
scenarios.ask: Roughly how big is the gap between required and available stable funding?

options.label: ≈ JPY 33bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ JPY 100bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ JPY 300bn
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true gap.

scenarios.takeaway: An NSFR just under 100% means a shortfall of about 2% of RSF, not a large hole in the balance sheet.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: Country X has a 25% reserve requirement on transaction deposits. A customer places CNY 200m of new funds into the banking system. Ignore cash leakage and excess reserves.
scenarios.ask: Roughly how much does the money supply grow beyond the initial CNY 200m deposit?

options.label: ≈ CNY 1,800m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the true figure.

options.label: ≈ CNY 6,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ CNY 18,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: $D/r$ = 800 counts the initial deposit; 'beyond the initial deposit' is $D(1-r)/r$ = 600.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: A CNY 200m deposit enters a banking system with a 25% reserve requirement, creating CNY 600m of new money beyond the deposit. The central bank now cuts the reserve requirement to 20%. Ignore cash leakage and excess reserves.
scenarios.ask: Money created beyond the initial deposit: rises, falls, or roughly unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Polarity flip. A lower reserve ratio means less is held back each round, so more is re-lent.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The multiplier $(1-r)/r$ moves from 3 to 4, which is a 33% jump, not noise.

scenarios.takeaway: Lower reserve requirement → larger multiplier → more money created.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bond costs USD 750. It pays USD 150 a year for 4 years and is redeemed at USD 1,000. Discounting its cash flows at $y = 25\%$ gives a present value of USD 763.84.
scenarios.ask: Is the yield to maturity above 25%, below 25%, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 25%
options.why: Sign slip. The PV at 25% is above the price, so the discount rate is too low. A higher rate lowers PV toward 750.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The PV misses the price by USD 13.84 (about 1.8%), which is roughly three-quarters of a point of yield (true YTM ≈ 25.7%). The sign is clear.

scenarios.takeaway: PV above the price → raise the yield. Deep-discount bond → YTM above both the coupon rate (15%) and the current yield (20%).

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A money market security with face value USD 100 is bought for USD 95 and matures in 85 days. The desk sheet also shows a required return of 12% and a yield to maturity of 8%.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what is its bank discount rate?

options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Annualises the wrong way: multiplies by $85/360$ instead of $360/85$.
Leaves the 85-day discount un-annualised.

scenarios.takeaway: Bank discount rate uses face value as the base and a 360-day year. The 12% and 8% figures are not inputs.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A USD 100 face money market security costs USD 95 with 85 days to maturity. Its bank discount rate is $\tfrac{100-95}{100} \times \tfrac{360}{85} = 21.18\%$. You recompute using the purchase price as the base and keep the 360-day year.
scenarios.ask: Compared with 21.18%, the recomputed rate: rises, falls, or is unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: The same USD 5 gain divided by a smaller base (95 instead of 100) gives a larger return.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The base appears in the denominator, so switching from 100 to 95 changes the rate by a factor of $100/95$.

scenarios.takeaway: The discount rate understates the true return: face value is a bigger base than the price paid.

scenarios.setup: Ludska Bank repos government bonds to SKA Bank: face amount USD 1,000,000, invoice price (cash advanced) USD 1,100,000, repo rate 4.00% p.a., 90 days, actual/360.
scenarios.ask: Roughly how much repo interest does Ludska pay at settlement?

options.label: ≈ USD 1,100
options.why: Rate keyed as 0.4% instead of 4%.

options.label: ≈ USD 44,000
options.why: A full year of interest. The 4% has to be pro-rated by $90/360$.

options.label: ≈ USD 111,000
options.why: Repurchase price minus the face amount. The interest is measured against the cash actually advanced (the invoice price).

scenarios.takeaway: Repo interest accrues on the cash lent (invoice price), for the actual days over 360. The face amount only identifies the collateral.

scenarios.setup: ABC Bank repos a bond three months after a coupon date: notional GBP 10m, 3.5% annual coupon paid semiannually, clean price 97.00, haircut 3.5%, repo rate 2.00%, term 6 months. You have found the dirty value of the collateral: GBP 9,787,500.
scenarios.ask: Will ABC's cash repayment at expiry be above GBP 9,787,500, below it, or too close to call?

options.label: Above
options.why: Grows the full dirty value at the repo rate and skips the haircut, giving 9,885,375. The 3.5% haircut cut outweighs the 1% of interest added.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: Net effect ≈ $0.965 \times 1.01 - 1 = -2.5\%$, about GBP 248k below. That is clear.

scenarios.takeaway: On a short, low-rate repo, what you repay stays below the collateral's dirty value because the haircut is bigger than the interest.

scenarios.setup: ABC Bank repos a bond three months after a coupon date: notional GBP 10m, 3.5% annual coupon paid semiannually, clean price 97.00, haircut 3.5%, repo rate 2.00%, term 6 months. ABC's repayment at expiry works out to GBP 9,539,387. Suppose instead the lender had demanded a 5% haircut, with everything else unchanged.
scenarios.ask: ABC's cash repayment at expiry: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: A higher haircut is a cost today, because ABC raises less cash. But the repayment is that smaller advance plus interest, so it is lower.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The repayment is proportional to the cash advanced, and the cash advanced drops from 96.5% to 95% of the dirty value.

scenarios.takeaway: Higher haircut → less cash raised now → smaller repayment later. The liquidity pain is the funding gap today.

scenarios.setup: Bright Bank lends USD 10,000 of cash in the repo market at a spread of 0.26% for 150 days, actual/360.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what is that lending worth to the bank?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.37
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.1
options.why: Decimal slip: treats 0.26% as 0.026%.

options.label: ≈ USD 3.7
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Sanity anchor: 0.26% a year on USD 10,000 is USD 26 a year, so 150 days is a bit under half of that.

scenarios.setup: Bright Bank's USD 10,000 repo loan at a 0.26% spread for 150 days is worth $10{,}000 \times 0.0026 \times 150/360 = \text{USD } 10.83$. A junior analyst reruns it on actual/365.
scenarios.ask: The recomputed value: higher, lower, or unchanged?

options.label: Higher
options.why: A longer assumed year makes each day a smaller fraction of it, so the pro-rated amount shrinks.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The day-count denominator enters directly: the value scales by $360/365$.

scenarios.takeaway: Money market (repo) uses actual/360. Switching to 365 understates the value.

scenarios.setup: An on-the-run government bond, issued 31 March, finances in repo at a special spread of 0.30% below GC. It is expected to trade at GC from 30 September (183 days special, actual/360). An off-the-run bond with otherwise identical cash flows finances at GC.
scenarios.ask: Relative to the off-the-run bond, the on-the-run bond's price is: higher, lower, or the same?

options.label: Lower (trades cheap)
options.why: Polarity flip. Cheaper financing is a benefit to the owner (about USD 0.15 per 100 here), so buyers pay up for it.

options.label: The same
options.why: Identical cash flows, but not identical financing. The special-repo advantage is capitalised into the price.

working.label: Price effect
working.display: The owner captures the 0.15 financing benefit, so the on-the-run bond trades rich. The richness decays as the issue goes to GC.

scenarios.takeaway: Special repo rate → cheap financing for the owner → on-the-run bonds trade rich.

scenarios.setup: A bond issued on 31 March trades special at 0.30% below GC and is expected to revert to GC on 30 September. Use actual/360.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what is the financing value per USD 100 of market value?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.015
options.why: Decimal slip: uses 0.03% instead of 0.30%.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.050
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.59
options.why: Inverts the day-count fraction ($360/183$ instead of $183/360$).

scenarios.takeaway: About half a year at 30 bp is about 15 cents per 100. Count actual days (183, not 180).

scenarios.setup: A USD 80m credit line has USD 24m drawn. The bank puts the probability that the rest is drawn at 45%. The cost of term-funding the liquidity cushion is 24 bp.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what contingent liquidity charge should the facility carry?

options.label: ≈ 0.25 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 0.76 bp
options.why: Decimal slip: 10× too small, e.g. keying the 24 bp cushion cost as 2.4 bp.

options.label: ≈ 2.5 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The charge is the cushion cost scaled down twice: by the undrawn share and by the probability of drawdown.

scenarios.setup: A USD 80m credit line with USD 24m drawn carries a contingent liquidity charge of $\tfrac{56}{80} \times 0.45 \times 24 = 7.56$ bp. The customer then draws a further USD 16m (USD 40m drawn). Draw probability and cushion cost are unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The contingent liquidity charge on the facility: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: The drawn balance is funded like any other loan. The contingent charge covers only the undrawn part, and that part has shrunk.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The undrawn share drops from 0.70 to 0.50, and the charge scales with it.

scenarios.takeaway: Contingent liquidity charge ∝ undrawn share. More drawn means a smaller contingent charge.

scenarios.setup: A 4-year amortising loan is charged for funding liquidity under the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach. Term liquidity premiums for years 1–4 are 12, 17, 24 and 30 bp. Their simple average is 20.75 bp.
scenarios.ask: Is the term-weighted charge ($\sum \text{TLP}_t \cdot t / \sum t$) above 20.75 bp, below it, or equal?

options.label: Below
options.why: That would need the short-dated premiums to carry the heavy weights. Here the weights rise with $t$, and so do the premiums.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only a flat curve (or equal weights) gives the simple mean. Upward-sloping premiums with rising weights push the charge up.

scenarios.takeaway: Rising TLP curve + term weights → charge above the simple average. A flat average undercharges the long end.

scenarios.setup: A 4-year amortising loan is charged for funding liquidity under the matched-maturity marginal cost of funds approach. Term liquidity premiums for years 1–4 are 12, 17, 24 and 30 bp.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what funding liquidity charge applies to the loan?

options.label: ≈ 2.4 bp
options.why: Scale slip: one-tenth of the true charge.

options.label: ≈ 8.0 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ 83 bp
options.why: Adds the four premiums instead of averaging them.

scenarios.takeaway: A per-year charge has to sit inside the range of the premiums (12–30 bp). Anything outside that is a slip.

scenarios.setup: A 1-year bullet loan of USD 5m is priced under the matched-maturity approach. Current term liquidity premiums (bp) for 1–5 years are 5, 8, 10, 18, 35. The current average cost of funds is a flat 10 bp. Before the crisis, the 1-year premium was 1 bp.
scenarios.ask: Roughly what liquidity charge is transferred to the business unit today?

options.label: ≈ USD 25
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 83
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 500
options.why: Uses the pre-crisis 1-year premium (1 bp) instead of today's 5 bp.

scenarios.takeaway: Match the loan's tenor to the TLP row, and don't use the average cost of funds row. 1 bp on USD 5m is USD 500.

scenarios.setup: For the coming week a bank expects uses of USD 660m (new loans), USD 330m (Treasury purchases) and USD 358m (drawings on customers' credit lines). It expects sources of USD 456m (deposits received today) and USD 265m (further deposits during the week). The current funding gap is zero.
scenarios.ask: Leave out the credit-line drawings for a moment. Is the partial gap (loans + Treasuries − all expected deposits) positive, negative, or too close to call?

options.label: Positive: the bank is short of funds even before the drawings
Negative: a surplus until the drawings arrive
options.why: Sources are 721 and the loans plus Treasuries are 990. Uses already exceed sources.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The partial gap is +USD 269m, far from zero.

scenarios.takeaway: Credit-line drawings belong in uses. Dropping them hides USD 358m of the USD 627m the bank must raise.

scenarios.setup: Federal funds cost 2.10% interest plus 0.42% non-interest cost, for a total cost of 2.52%. A 10% reserve requirement applies, so only 90% of funds raised are investable.
scenarios.ask: Is the effective cost rate above 2.52%, below it, or the same?

options.label: Below 2.52%
options.why: Multiplies by 0.90 instead of dividing (gives 2.27%). The cost is spread over a smaller investable base, so it goes up.

options.label: The same
options.why: 2.52% is the intermediate result. It has not yet been adjusted for the 10% of funds that can't be invested.

scenarios.takeaway: Effective cost = total cost ÷ investable share. A reserve requirement always grosses the cost up.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 20: Covered Interest Rate Parity Lost
scenarios.setup: EUR/USD spot is 1.32 (USD per EUR) and the 1-year forward is 1.22. The 1-year USD rate is 6.00%.
scenarios.ask: Under covered interest parity, is the implied 1-year euro rate above 6%, below 6%, or equal?

options.label: Below 6%
options.why: Base/quote inversion. The euro buys fewer dollars forward (forward discount), so parity requires the euro to pay a higher interest rate.

options.label: Equal to 6%
options.why: Only a forward equal to spot implies equal rates. Here $F/S = 0.924$.

scenarios.takeaway: The currency at a forward discount is the higher-yielding one.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
scenarios.setup: Next-day projections (USD m): deposit withdrawals 129, deposit inflows 119, scheduled loan repayments 122, acceptable loan requests 90, money-market borrowings 110, sales of bank assets 61, stockholder dividends 172, non-deposit service revenue 118, repayments of bank borrowings 84, operating expenses 70. Total supplies of liquidity come to USD 530m.
scenarios.ask: Are total demands for liquidity larger than 530, smaller, or too close to call?

options.label: Larger: the bank runs a deficit
Smaller: the bank runs a surplus
options.why: Usually a sorting slip. For example, treating loan requests as cash in. Demands are withdrawals, loan requests, dividends, repayments of borrowings and opex: 545.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: These are exact cash flows. Demands of 545 against supplies of 530 is a definite USD 15m deficit.

scenarios.takeaway: Sort each item by the direction the cash moves. Loan repayments received are cash in; new loans granted are cash out.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 5: Liquidity and Reserves Management
scenarios.setup: Prime Savings projects a net liquidity surplus of USD 31m for the week. Total supply of liquidity is USD 122m. Demands excluding stockholder dividends total USD 89m.
scenarios.ask: Roughly how large are the expected dividend payments?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.067m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.20m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.6m
options.why: Scale slip: about 0.3× the true figure.

scenarios.takeaway: Net position = supplies − demands. With a surplus, demands are supplies minus the surplus, never plus.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
scenarios.setup: A 5-year bond with par USD 2,000 pays an 8% annual coupon (USD 160) and is priced at USD 1,600. The shortcut approximation gives $\tfrac{160 + 400/5}{(2{,}000 + 1{,}600)/2} = 13.33\%$.
scenarios.ask: Is the true yield to maturity above 13.33%, below it, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 13.33%
options.why: At 13.33% the PV of the cash flows comes to about USD 1,625, above the 1,600 price. The yield has to be higher.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: A USD 25 PV gap on a bond with duration ≈ 4 is about half a point of yield. You can sign it.

scenarios.takeaway: On a deep-discount bond the shortcut YTM understates the true yield because it discounts nothing.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
scenarios.setup: A taxed financial firm in the 35% bracket is looking at Aaa municipal bonds that yield 5.00% tax-exempt.
scenarios.ask: The municipals' tax-equivalent yield, compared with 5.00%: higher, lower, or the same?

options.label: Lower
options.why: Taxes the exempt yield down ($5\% \times 0.65 = 3.25\%$). The exempt yield has to be grossed up to compare with taxable yields.

options.label: The same
options.why: The same only for an untaxed investor. At a 35% rate the divisor is 0.65.

scenarios.takeaway: Tax-equivalent yield of an exempt security is always above its stated yield for a taxed holder.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 4: The Investment Function in Financial Services Management
scenarios.setup: A firm in the 35% tax bracket compares Aaa corporates yielding 8.00% (taxable) with Aaa municipals yielding 5.00% (tax-exempt). You have already found the municipals' tax-equivalent yield: 7.69%.
scenarios.ask: After tax, which holding yields more: the corporate, the municipal, or too close to call?

options.label: The municipal
options.why: Tax-exempt status doesn't make it better. The corporate nets $8\% \times 0.65 = 5.20\%$, above the muni's 5.00%. Equivalently, 7.69% < 8.00%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The gap is 20 bp after tax (31 bp on a tax-equivalent basis), and both figures are exact.

scenarios.takeaway: Gross the exempt yield up or net the taxable yield down. Either way you get the same ranking.

scenarios.reading: LR2025, Ch. 8: The Failure Mechanics of Dealer Banks
scenarios.setup: Bodrum Bank has a USD 20m OTC derivatives exposure to Aurora Bank, which has posted USD 15m of collateral. At stated values, a default would cost Bodrum USD 5m. Now suppose Aurora defaults in a market-wide stress and the same risk factors drive both the exposure and the collateral.
scenarios.ask: Bodrum's realised loss, compared with USD 5m: larger, smaller, or about the same?

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Collateral only realises at stated value in calm markets. In stress it sells for less, and the exposure also grows.

options.label: About the same
options.why: USD 5m assumes collateral is realised at stated value. Wrong-way risk moves both legs against Bodrum.

working.label: Stress adjustment
working.display: Collateral value falls and the mark-to-market exposure rises together (wrong-way), so the residual loss goes above USD 5m.

scenarios.takeaway: Collateral reduces LGD but doesn't eliminate it. In stress, exposure goes up while collateral goes down.

scenarios.reading: Hull, Risk Management and Financial Institutions, Ch. 24: Liquidity Risk
scenarios.setup: In the wholesale market between financial institutions, a dealer is asked to quote a trade well beyond its normal quoted size.
scenarios.ask: The proportional bid-offer spread on the large trade, versus a normal-size one: wider, narrower, or the same?

options.label: Narrower
options.why: That's the retail pattern: an individual doing a bigger FX deal can get a better quote. In the wholesale market, bigger is harder to hedge.

options.label: The same
options.why: Quotes are firm only up to the dealer's size limit. Beyond it, the bid slopes down and the offer slopes up.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Beyond the size limit, hedging the exposure a trade creates gets harder, so bid ↓ and offer ↑ and the spread $s$ widens.

scenarios.takeaway: Wholesale: spread widens with size. So many small positions carry less liquidity trading risk than a few large ones.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bank pays a large cash dividend out of its cash balances. Every other asset is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The value-weighted average duration of the bank's assets: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Cash has zero duration. Removing a zero-duration asset lifts the weighted average of what remains.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The weights change: cash's share falls, so the longer-duration assets carry more weight.

working.label: Effect
working.display: $D_A = \sum w_i D_i$; removing a $D = 0$ holding raises $D_A$

scenarios.takeaway: Paying out cash shrinks the balance sheet and lengthens average asset duration.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bank has assets of USD 300m with average duration $D_A = 3.047$ years and liabilities of USD 275m. It wants a zero leverage-adjusted duration gap.
scenarios.ask: Must the average liability duration be longer than 3.047, shorter, or equal?

options.label: Shorter
options.why: Polarity flip. Liabilities are the smaller base, so each dollar has to move more to offset the assets.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Matching $D_L = D_A$ still leaves a positive gap of $3.047(1 - 275/300) = 0.25$, which is exposed to rising rates.

scenarios.takeaway: With A > L, immunising net worth requires $D_L > D_A$.

scenarios.reading: Rose and Hudgins, Bank Management and Financial Services, Ch. 7: Asset-Liability Management
scenarios.setup: A bank's leverage-adjusted duration gap, $D_A - \tfrac{L}{A} D_L$, is negative. Market rates rise in a parallel shift.
scenarios.ask: Market value of net worth: rises, falls, or roughly unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: That's the positive-gap outcome. With a negative gap, liability values fall by more than asset values.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: Only a zero gap is immunised. A non-zero gap means net worth moves.

working.label: Sign rule
working.display: $\Delta NW \approx -\left(D_A - \tfrac{L}{A}D_L\right) A \tfrac{\Delta y}{1+y}$: negative gap × positive $\Delta y$ → $\Delta NW > 0$

scenarios.takeaway: Negative leverage-adjusted gap → net worth rises when rates rise and falls when they fall.

scenarios.setup: A dealer finances GBP 1bn of collateral in repo at a 2% haircut. Lenders raise the haircut to 5%. The dealer buys and sells nothing.
scenarios.ask: The cash the dealer must fund from its own resources: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: The haircut is the slice the dealer funds itself. A bigger haircut means less cash raised against the same collateral.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: No trade is needed. The terms changed, and the cash raised drops from 980m to 950m.

scenarios.takeaway: Haircut up → cash raised down → a funding need appears with no trade and no default.

scenarios.setup: A particular bond issue is in heavy demand from traders who need it to cover shorts. Cash lenders compete to get that specific issue as collateral.
scenarios.ask: The repo rate on that issue, compared with the general collateral (GC) rate: higher, lower, or the same?

options.label: Higher
options.why: Polarity flip. The scarce item is the bond. Lenders compete by accepting less interest on their cash.

options.label: The same
options.why: The GC rate applies when any bond of the class will do. Demand for a specific issue opens a special spread.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Scarce collateral → cash lenders compete → $\text{repo}_{\text{special}} = \text{GC} - \text{special spread}$

scenarios.takeaway: Special = below GC. Scarcity benefits whoever owns the bond and borrows cash against it.

scenarios.setup: A 10-year Treasury is the on-the-run issue and trades special. After the next auction it becomes the 'old' issue.
scenarios.ask: Its special spread (GC minus its repo rate): widens, narrows, or unchanged?

options.label: Widens
options.why: Scarcity doesn't grow as the bond seasons. Short interest and liquidity move to the new on-the-run issue.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Specialness is concentrated in the current issue. In the reading's data, the 10-year spread goes from 14 bp on-the-run to 2 bp old.

scenarios.takeaway: Most special = on-the-run. Specialness decays as the issue ages toward GC.

scenarios.setup: A gold miner has sold gold forward to hedge its future production, with margin recalculated daily. The gold price jumps more than 25% overnight.
scenarios.ask: The miner's cash position over the next few days: rises, falls, or roughly unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: The gain is in gold still in the ground, which is illiquid. It can't be turned into cash for tomorrow's margin call.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: Economically the hedge offsets, but the forward leg is settled in cash through margin and the offsetting gain isn't.

working.label: Forward leg
working.display: Short forward + price up → mark-to-market loss → margin calls paid in cash

working.label: Hedged asset
working.display: Gold in the ground gains value but produces no cash now

scenarios.takeaway: Hedging an illiquid asset with margined contracts converts market risk into funding liquidity risk.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: FRTB internal models. Five partial expected shortfalls on a 10-day base shock (EUR m): $ES_1, \dots, ES_5 = 40, 30, 20, 12, 6$, for liquidity horizons of 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. Each $ES_j$ with $j \ge 2$ is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10}$. The five scaled figures are then combined as the square root of the sum of their squares.
scenarios.ask: Total expected shortfall is closest to:

options.label: ≈ EUR 6.2m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 19m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The total can't be below $ES_1 = 40$ on its own, since every other term only adds under the square root.

options.label: ≈ EUR 170m
options.why: Scaled each category by its full horizon $\sqrt{LH_j/10}$ instead of the increment, then added the five figures in a straight line instead of in quadrature.

scenarios.takeaway: FRTB ES: scale by the horizon increment, then add in quadrature. The total lands above $ES_1$ but below the straight sum of the scaled partials (about 130).

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: FRTB expected shortfall. Liquidity horizons are 10, 20, 40, 60 and 120 days. Each partial $ES_j$ ($j \ge 2$) is scaled by $\sqrt{(LH_j - LH_{j-1})/10}$ before aggregation. $ES_3$ belongs to the 40-day category and $ES_4$ to the 60-day category.
scenarios.ask: Which scaling factor is larger: the one applied to $ES_3$ or the one applied to $ES_4$?

options.label: $ES_4$'s factor is larger
options.why: Scaled by the horizon level, $\sqrt{60/10} = 2.45$ against $\sqrt{40/10} = 2.00$. The formula uses the increment from the previous horizon, not the level.

options.label: $ES_3$'s factor is larger
options.why: This would need the 40→60 step to be shorter than the 20→40 step. Both increments are 20 days.

scenarios.takeaway: FRTB horizon scaling uses the increment $LH_j - LH_{j-1}$, not the horizon itself. That makes categories 3 and 4 identical.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: Currency option parity: $p = c + Ke^{-rT} - S_0e^{-qT}$. The foreign rate acts as the yield $q$. Spot is USD 0.5500, strike USD 0.5700, $T = 1$. The domestic rate is $r = 4\%$ and the foreign rate is $q = 8\%$. The call trades at USD 0.0325, with an implied vol of 14.5%.
scenarios.ask: The residual $Ke^{-rT} - S_0e^{-qT}$, which equals $p - c$, is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: Swapped the rates, discounting the strike at 8% and spot at 4%: $0.5262 - 0.5284 = -0.002$. The domestic rate discounts the domestic strike, and the foreign rate discounts spot.

options.label: Positive: the put is worth more than the call
Too close to call
options.why: The strike sits above spot and is also discounted at the lower rate. Both push $Ke^{-rT}$ above $S_0e^{-qT}$, and the gap is about 0.040, larger than the call price itself.

scenarios.takeaway: In FX parity, $r$ (domestic) discounts the strike and $q$ (foreign) discounts spot. The implied vol is not needed.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: Using $\sigma = 34.0\%$, BSM values a European call at USD 6.95 and the matching European put (same strike and maturity) at USD 5.12. The call actually trades at USD 7.23.
scenarios.ask: The put's market price is most likely:

options.label: Below USD 5.12
options.why: Flipped the sign of the error: $5.12 - 0.28 = 4.84$. The market pays more than BSM for the call, so it pays more for the put too.

options.label: Equal to USD 5.12
options.why: Put-call parity holds for both model and market prices, so any dollar mispricing BSM makes on the call it makes on the put.

scenarios.takeaway: Same strike, same maturity: BSM's dollar pricing error is identical for the call and the put, and so is the implied vol.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: Bilinear interpolation on a volatility surface at $K/S_0 = 1.10$ and a maturity of 4.0 years. Interpolating across strike has already given 19.80% on the 2-year row and 21.60% on the 5-year row.
scenarios.ask: The final 4-year implied volatility will be closer to:

options.label: 19.80% (the 2-year row)
options.why: Put the weight on the wrong end. The weight on the 5-year value is $(4-2)/(5-2) = 2/3$, because 4 years sits closer to 5 than to 2. Stopping at 19.80% is the other trap: that is the 2-year row, not the answer.

options.label: Exactly midway (20.70%)
options.why: The midpoint of 2 and 5 years is 3.5 years, not 4.

scenarios.takeaway: Bilinear interpolation takes two passes, one in each dimension. Put each weight on the grid point the target is nearest to.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: Normal ES as a loss: $ES = -\mu + \sigma \times \frac{e^{-Y^2/2}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,(1-X)}$. The daily mean return is $+1.0\%$, daily $\sigma = 5.0\%$, $X = 97.5\%$ and $Y = 1.96$. The tail term is already done: $5.0\% \times 2.338 = 11.69\%$.
scenarios.ask: The daily 97.5% ES, expressed as a loss, is:

options.label: Above 11.69%
options.why: Added the mean, treating the +1% expected return as if it were an expected loss. An expected profit reduces the tail loss, so it is subtracted.

options.label: Exactly 11.69%
options.why: Dropped the $-\mu$ term. The mean is small, but it is stated and it moves the answer by a full percentage point.

scenarios.takeaway: When the mean is an expected RETURN, subtract it from the tail term to get a loss.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: A USD 30m exposure is normally distributed. It is stated in loss-positive format: mean loss $+4.0\%$, $\sigma = 15.0\%$. The 97.5% ES multiplier is 2.3378, and the tail term is already done: $15.0\% \times 2.3378 = 35.07\%$.
scenarios.ask: The 97.5% ES as a percentage of the exposure is:

options.label: Below 35.07%
options.why: Subtracted the mean as if it were an expected return. In loss-positive format, +4% is an expected loss, so it adds to the tail.

options.label: Exactly 35.07%
options.why: Dropped the mean term, which here is worth four percentage points.

scenarios.takeaway: Read the format label first. A positive mean LOSS is added; a positive mean RETURN is subtracted.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: A USD 30m exposure is normally distributed. It is stated in loss-positive format: mean loss $4.0\%$, $\sigma = 15.0\%$. Use $ES_{97.5\%} = \mu + \sigma \times \phi(1.96)/(1 - 0.975)$, with $\phi(1.96) = 0.05845$.
scenarios.ask: The single-period 97.5% ES is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 1.5m
options.why: Forgot to divide the density by the tail probability $(1 - X) = 0.025$. Without that, the multiplier is 0.058 when it should be 2.34.

options.label: ≈ USD 39m
options.why: Reported the percentage (39.1%) as the dollar figure and skipped the multiply by USD 30m. An ES above the whole exposure is an instant red flag.

options.label: ≈ USD 120m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). This is four times the exposure itself.

scenarios.takeaway: The 97.5% normal ES is about $\mu + 2.34\sigma$, roughly 40% of this exposure. A figure above the whole position is a red flag.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 1 (normal, no drift): $dr = \sigma\,dw$. The current short rate is 7.18%, $\sigma = 118$ bp per year, and the step is three months ($dt = 0.25$). The realised draw is $dw = 0.18$.
scenarios.ask: The change in the short rate over the step is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Also multiplied by $dt$. The realised $dw$ already carries the time scaling, because its s.d. is $\sqrt{dt}$, so $dt$ does not appear again.
Scale slip (10×). A 2% move in one quarter would be almost twice the whole annual volatility.

scenarios.takeaway: Given a realised $dw$, the change is just $\sigma \times dw$. The time step only matters for the distribution of $dw$.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$, with $r_0 = 6.138\%$, $\lambda = 0.239\%$ per year and $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year. The horizon is one month.
scenarios.ask: The standard deviation of the one-month rate change is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scaled $\sigma$ by $dt = 1/12$. That is the drift's scaling; dispersion scales with $\sqrt{dt}$.
Left $\sigma$ at its annual value, so the one-month horizon was never applied.

scenarios.takeaway: Drift scales with $dt$ and dispersion with $\sqrt{dt}$, so write both side by side before substituting.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$, with $\lambda = 0.239\%$ per year and $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year. The horizon is one month ($dt = 1/12$).
scenarios.ask: Over the month, which is bigger: the expected drift $\lambda\,dt$ or the one-s.d. random move $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$?

options.label: The random move, by a wide margin
The drift
options.why: Compared the unscaled annual drift (0.239%) with $\sigma \times dt$ (0.10%). Each term needs its own time scaling.

options.label: They are about the same size
options.why: About 0.02% of drift against 0.35% of dispersion is a factor of roughly 17, not a match. Drift shrinks with $dt$, dispersion only with $\sqrt{dt}$.

scenarios.takeaway: At short horizons dispersion swamps drift; drift only catches up at long horizons because $t$ outgrows $\sqrt{t}$.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 2: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma\,dw$. The current rate is 5.26%, $\sigma = 115$ bp per year and $\lambda = 0.25\%$ per year. The step is one month, and the realised draw is $dw = 0.25$.
scenarios.ask: The drift contribution $\lambda\,dt$ to this month's change is closest to:

options.label: ≈ 7.2 bp
options.why: Scaled the drift by $\sqrt{dt}$. That is the dispersion's scaling; drift is linear in $dt$.

options.label: ≈ 25 bp
options.why: Used the annual drift unscaled, which is the classic Model 2 slip.

options.label: ≈ 63 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Over one month a 25 bp-a-year drift is only about 2 bp, small next to the random term.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 1 binomial tree with no drift. $r_0 = 4.00\%$, $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year, and each step is three months ($dt = 0.25$). Each node moves up or down by $\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ with probability ½.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: the up-up node's distance above 4.00% after two steps, or one standard deviation of the six-month change, $\sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$?

options.label: $\sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$
options.why: Reversed the comparison. The extreme path is $2\sigma\sqrt{dt}$, which equals $\sqrt{2} \times \sigma\sqrt{2\,dt}$.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: Treated two steps as one step of length $2dt$. The tree's extreme path widens linearly in the number of steps, while the s.d. widens with its square root.

scenarios.takeaway: A tree's outer nodes run $n\sigma\sqrt{dt}$ out, ahead of the $\sigma\sqrt{n\,dt}$ spread of the distribution.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Ho-Lee tree: $dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma\,dw$. $r_0 = 5.00\%$, $\sigma = 1.20\%$ per year, quarterly steps ($dt = 0.25$). The drift is $\lambda(1) = 0.40\%$ per year over step 1 and $\lambda(2) = 0.80\%$ per year over step 2.
scenarios.ask: The middle node after two steps sits above 5.00% by roughly:

options.label: ≈ +0.03 pp
options.why: Scale slip (0.1×).

options.label: ≈ +0.10 pp
options.why: Applied only the first step's drift, $\lambda(1)\,dt$, and dropped the second.

options.label: ≈ +1.2 pp
options.why: Added the annual drifts unscaled ($0.40 + 0.80$) without multiplying each by $dt$.

scenarios.takeaway: In a recombining tree, the up and down moves cancel on the middle path, so the middle node is just the start plus the sum of the dt-scaled drifts.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: Model 3: $dr = \lambda(t)\,dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\,dw$, with $\sigma = 1.50\%$ and $\alpha = 0.05$. At $t = 3$ years, $\lambda = 0.30\%$ per year, the step is one month and the realised $dw = 0.20$. With the undecayed $\sigma$ alone, $\sigma\,dw = 0.30\%$.
scenarios.ask: After you add the drift and apply the volatility decay, the true $dr$ is:

options.label: Above 0.30%
options.why: Added the drift (+2.5 bp) but forgot that $e^{-0.15} = 0.861$ trims the random term by about 4.2 bp. That route gives 0.325%, reading $\sigma$ as constant.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The decay effect (−4.2 bp) is about 1.7× the drift (+2.5 bp), so the net is about −1.7 bp, clearly below.

scenarios.takeaway: In Model 3, evaluate $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ first. By year 3 the decay costs more than a month of drift adds.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio is LONG asset X and SHORT asset Y. Both assets have positive volatility and the position sizes are fixed. The correlation between X and Y rises.
scenarios.ask: Variance-covariance portfolio VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: True when both positions are LONG. With one short, $w_1 w_2 < 0$, so the cross term $2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ falls as $\rho$ rises.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Correlation enters through the cross term, which is non-zero whenever both positions are non-zero.

working.label: Sign of coefficient on $\rho$
working.display: $2 w_1 w_2 \sigma_1 \sigma_2 < 0$, so variance falls as $\rho$ rises

working.label: Result
working.display: Portfolio VaR falls; it is largest at $\rho = -1$

scenarios.takeaway: Long-long: VaR rises with ρ. Long-short: the sign flips, and VaR peaks at ρ = −1.

scenarios.setup: USD 10m is split 6:4 between asset X ($\sigma = 5\%$) and asset Y ($\sigma = 10\%$), $z = 2.33$. The two assets are currently perfectly correlated. The correlation then drops to zero.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: The two calculations were done correctly but the labels were swapped. For a long-only book, ρ = 1 is always the upper bound.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Correlation only drops out when one position is zero. Here both are live, so the cross term matters.

scenarios.takeaway: For a long-only book, individual VaRs add at ρ = 1 and combine in quadrature at ρ = 0, so VaR falls as correlation falls.

scenarios.setup: USD 10m is split 6:4 between asset X ($\sigma = 5\%$) and asset Y ($\sigma = 10\%$). The assets are uncorrelated. Use the variance-covariance approach with $z = 2.33$.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio 99% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.10m
options.why: Used variances ($0.05^2$, $0.10^2$) in place of volatilities in the individual VaRs.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.40m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 12m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). That exceeds the entire USD 10m portfolio.

scenarios.takeaway: Uncorrelated VaRs combine in quadrature. Here that lands between the larger single VaR (0.93) and their sum (1.63).

scenarios.setup: A USD 10m portfolio holds USD 3m in A (daily $\sigma_A = 3\%$) and USD 7m in B (daily $\sigma_B = 5\%$), with $\rho = 0.4$. Use the variance-covariance approach with $z = 2.33$.
scenarios.ask: The one-day 99% portfolio VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.036m
options.why: Multiplied the portfolio VARIANCE (0.00156) by value and $z$ without taking its square root.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.092m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.31m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Sanity band: VaR must sit between the ρ = 0 figure (0.84) and the ρ = 1 figure (1.02).

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: There are 20 daily P&L observations (USD thousands). The ten worst are −84, −61, −47, −38, −30, −25, −19, −14, −9 and −5. At 90% confidence the tail holds $(1 - 0.90) \times 20 = 2$ observations, so the 90% VaR threshold is 61.
scenarios.ask: The 90% expected shortfall is:

options.label: Exactly 61
options.why: Reported the threshold (the VaR) instead of averaging the losses inside the tail.

options.label: Below 61
options.why: ES averages losses at or beyond the VaR threshold, so it can't come in below VaR. To get below 61 you must have averaged observations from outside the tail.

scenarios.takeaway: ES ≥ VaR at the same confidence level, always. If yours comes out lower, something is wrong.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: The 95% ES is approximated as the plain average of five tail VaRs (EUR m): 18.0 at 96%, 20.5 at 97%, 24.0 at 98%, 30.0 at 99% and 42.5 at 99.9%.
scenarios.ask: The resulting ES estimate is:

options.label: Equal to 24.0
options.why: Took the middle value of the list (the median). ES is a MEAN.

options.label: Below 24.0
options.why: The largest VaR sits 18.5 above 24.0 while the smallest is only 6.0 below. The skewed tail pulls the mean up, not down.

scenarios.takeaway: ES averages the tail, so a long right tail drags it above the middle tail VaR.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: You hold one share of a stock that closed yesterday at USD 100. The 95% historical-simulation VaR uses a 260-day window, so it reads off the $(1 - 0.95) \times 260 + 1 = 14$th worst return. Yesterday that return was −6.05% (VaR USD 6.05), and the 13th worst was −6.25%. Today the stock falls 10%, a new worst return, and a −3% day drops out of the window.
scenarios.ask: Today's 95% VaR in USD, compared with yesterday's USD 6.05:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Updated only the quantile ($6.25\% \times 100 = 6.25$) and applied it to yesterday's price. The position is now worth USD 90.

options.label: Roughly unchanged
options.why: The two updates don't cancel. The quantile worsens by about 3%, the base falls by 10%, and the net change is about −7%.

working.label: New 14th-worst return
working.display: Every rank shifts down one, so the old 13th (−6.25%) becomes the new 14th

scenarios.takeaway: A rolling HS VaR has two moving parts, the quantile AND the position value. A big loss can lower the dollar VaR.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: The 95% historical-simulation VaR uses a 260-day window, so it reads off the 14th worst return. Yesterday the 13th and 14th worst were −6.25% and −6.05%. Today a −10% return enters the window, worse than every existing observation. The return leaving is −3%, which was not in the tail.
scenarios.ask: Today's 14th-worst return, compared with −6.05%, is:

options.label: Better (a smaller loss)
options.why: Nothing leaves the tail. The departing −3% was never in the worst 16, so no rank moves up, and the new −10% pushes every rank down one.

options.label: The same
options.why: That would only hold if the new return were milder than −6.05%. At −10% it outranks all of them.

working.label: New rank of −10%
working.display: 1st worst; all others shift down one rank

scenarios.takeaway: A new worst-ever return shifts every order statistic down one place, so the VaR quantile gets worse.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: The standard error of a quantile (VaR) estimate is $se = \frac{1}{f(q)}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, with $n = 1{,}000$. Moving from 95% to 99.9% confidence, $p(1-p)$ falls from 0.0475 to 0.000999, and the density at the quantile falls from 0.1031 to 0.00337.
scenarios.ask: The net effect on the standard error is:

options.label: It falls
options.why: Looked only at $p(1-p)$, whose square-root ratio is about 0.145×, and forgot the density sits in the DENOMINATOR, where its ratio is about 30.6×.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The two effects are 0.145× and 30.6×. They net to about 4.4×, nowhere near a wash.

scenarios.takeaway: Deep-tail VaR is estimated less precisely, because the density at the quantile collapses faster than $p(1-p)$ does.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Quantile standard error: $se = \frac{1}{f(q)}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$, with $n = 1{,}000$ in both cases. At 95%: $p(1-p) = 0.0475$ and $f(q) = 0.1031$. At 99.9%: $p(1-p) = 0.000999$ and $f(q) = 0.00337$.
scenarios.ask: $se_{99.9\%} / se_{95\%}$ is closest to:

options.why: Used the density ratio (0.1031 / 0.00337) alone and dropped the offsetting $\sqrt{p(1-p)}$ term.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: The two effects multiply: roughly ×0.15 from $p(1-p)$ and ×31 from the density, so going deep into the tail costs precision.

scenarios.setup: An exchange option pays $\max(S_1 - S_2, 0)$. The correlation between $S_1$ and $S_2$ rises, and each asset's own volatility is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The exchange option's value:

options.label: Rises
options.why: That is the BASKET call, which is an option on a sum. The exchange option is an option on a DIFFERENCE, where correlation enters with a minus sign.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Option value rises with the volatility of the underlying combination, and $\text{Var}(S_1 - S_2) = \sigma_1^2 + \sigma_2^2 - 2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ moves with $\rho$.

working.label: Result
working.display: Less spread volatility, so the option is worth less

scenarios.takeaway: An option on a difference loses value as correlation rises; an option on a sum gains value.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: Volatility follows a GARCH(1,1) process, and current volatility is ABOVE its long-run level.
scenarios.ask: The term structure of volatility forecasts slopes:

options.label: Upward
options.why: That is the case when current volatility is BELOW long-run. GARCH itself imposes no upward slope.

options.label: Flat
options.why: Only if current volatility equals the long-run level. GARCH(1,1) mean-reverts, so forecasts drift toward the long-run level.

working.label: Mean reversion
working.display: Forecasts converge geometrically to the long-run variance

working.label: Result
working.display: Current > long-run, so forecasts decline with horizon: a downward slope

scenarios.takeaway: GARCH term structure: the slope points from the current volatility toward the long-run level.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: FX rates violate both lognormality conditions: their volatility is non-constant and they jump. The result is a pronounced FX volatility smile.
scenarios.ask: As option maturity increases, the implied-volatility smile becomes:

options.label: More pronounced
options.why: Non-constant volatility makes the effect on PRICES more pronounced with maturity. The smile plots IMPLIED volatilities, and there both channels weaken.

options.label: No different
options.why: The jump effect on implied volatility fades with maturity. Short-dated rows of a surface are visibly more curved than long-dated ones.

working.label: Non-constant vol, effect on implied vol

scenarios.takeaway: Smiles are sharpest at short maturities; both FX channels fade in implied-volatility terms as T grows.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: A firm's debt load is roughly fixed. Its equity value falls.
scenarios.ask: Under the capital-structure leverage argument, the equity's volatility:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Reverses the leverage effect. Lower equity against fixed debt raises the debt-to-equity ratio and amplifies swings on the residual equity claim.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: That holds only with zero debt, where equity volatility equals EBIT volatility.

working.label: Debt-to-equity
working.display: Equity down with debt fixed, so D/E rises

working.label: Result
working.display: Higher leverage amplifies equity volatility, so price down means volatility up

scenarios.takeaway: Falling equity raises leverage and so volatility. That negative price–vol link is one reason for the downward equity skew.

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: The FRTB switched from 99% VaR to 97.5% ES. Under normality, 99% VaR $= \mu + 2.326\sigma$ and 97.5% ES $= \mu + 2.338\sigma$, which are nearly equal. Now suppose losses have a heavier tail than the normal.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the 99% VaR, the 97.5% ES is:

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Focused on the lower confidence level. ES averages the whole tail beyond its quantile, so a heavy tail raises it more than it raises a single quantile.

options.label: Roughly equal
options.why: Near-equality is the normal-distribution result. Heavy tails break it.

working.label: Heavy tail
working.display: VaR ignores the shape beyond the quantile; ES averages it

working.label: Result
working.display: 97.5% ES exceeds 99% VaR, possibly by a lot

scenarios.takeaway: The switch is capital-neutral only under normality. Heavy tails make 97.5% ES bite harder than 99% VaR.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: In volatility-weighted historical simulation, one month ago the asset returned 5%. The daily volatility estimate at that time was 2%, and today's daily volatility forecast is 1.5%.
scenarios.ask: The volatility-adjusted return, compared with 5%, is:

options.label: Larger
options.why: Inverted the ratio: $5\% \times 2/1.5 = 6.67\%$. Current volatility goes on top.

options.label: The same
options.why: That is basic HS. Volatility weighting rescales by $\sigma_{\text{now}}/\sigma_{\text{then}} = 0.75$.

scenarios.takeaway: Calmer now than then means old returns get scaled DOWN. Current volatility goes in the numerator.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A USD 1m equity portfolio, one-year horizon: mean 15%, volatility 25%, $z = 2.33$. Under normal returns, 99% VaR $= (-0.15 + 0.25 \times 2.33) \times 1\text{m} = \text{USD } 432{,}500$. You switch to lognormal: $VaR = P\,[1 - \exp(\mu - \sigma z)]$.
scenarios.ask: The lognormal VaR, compared with USD 432,500, is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Since $e^{-x} > 1 - x$, the lognormal loss $1 - e^{-0.4325}$ is always below the normal $0.4325$. Lognormal also caps the loss at the full value.

options.label: The same
options.why: The exponent equals the normal bracket, $-0.4325$, but $1 - e^{-0.4325} = 0.351$, not 0.4325.

scenarios.takeaway: For the same μ and σ, lognormal VaR is always below normal VaR, because $1 - e^{-x} < x$.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Stock A's past 260 daily returns are highly NEGATIVELY skewed. P1 is long stock A; P2 is the same-size short position.
scenarios.ask: Moving from P1 (long) to P2 (short), the absolute 99% VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: That is the positive-skew case. With negative skew the long LEFT tail hurts the long position, not the short.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Long and short VaRs match only for a symmetric distribution. Skewness is exactly what breaks that.

working.label: Long's loss tail
working.display: Left tail, which is long here

working.label: Short's loss tail
working.display: Right tail, which is short here

working.label: Result
working.display: VaR(P2) < VaR(P1), so going short lowers VaR

scenarios.takeaway: The sign of skew picks the side that's penalised. With negative skew, the long position carries the bigger VaR.
