scenarios.setup: An at-the-money call has strike USD 20.00 and BSM delta 0.50. The implied distribution has a LIGHT left tail and a HEAVY right tail, so implied volatility rises with $K/S_0$. The stock now rises toward USD 21.00.
scenarios.ask: The call's TRUE delta:

options.label: Rises above 0.50
options.why: Counted only the BSM term ($N(d_1)$ rises). The smile term, vega × $\partial\sigma_{imp}/\partial S$, is negative here.

options.label: Falls below 0.50
options.why: Counted only the smile term. The standard BSM term pushes delta up.

options.label: Stays at 0.50
options.why: Ignores both terms; neither is zero here.

working.label: Term 1: BSM
working.display: $\partial c/\partial S$ rises as the option moves into the money: positive

working.label: Term 2: smile
working.display: $S$ up means $K/S_0$ down, so $\sigma_{imp}$ falls; vega > 0, so the term is negative

working.label: Net
working.display: The two terms oppose, so the direction is indeterminate

scenarios.takeaway: True delta = BSM delta + vega × ∂σ/∂S. Under a reverse skew the two terms fight, so you need magnitudes.

scenarios.reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
scenarios.setup: You are hedging USD 100m face of a bond (DV01 0.300) with an instrument whose DV01 is 0.250. The DV01-neutral hedge is USD 120m face, short. A regression of the bond's yield changes on the hedge's yield changes gives beta = 0.800.

options.label: Larger

options.label: The same

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A desk's P/L over the period is normal with mean $+14.1$ (an expected **profit**) and standard deviation $28.2$. For the 95% VaR you have already computed the volatility leg $\sigma z = 28.2 \times 1.645 = 46.39$.
scenarios.ask: Once the mean is brought in, is the 95% VaR above 46.39, below it, or equal to it?

options.label: Above 46.39
options.why: Sign slip: an expected profit was treated as extra loss ($+14.1 + 46.39 = 60.5$). In P/L terms a positive mean offsets the tail loss.

options.label: Equal to 46.39
options.why: Dropped-term slip: $\sigma z$ alone ignores the mean. It is only the whole VaR when $\mu = 0$.

scenarios.takeaway: In P/L format a positive mean is a profit: it pulls VaR below $\sigma z$.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A portfolio is worth USD 200. Its arithmetic return over the horizon is normal with mean $+5\%$ and standard deviation $10\%$. Use $z_{95} = 1.65$.
scenarios.ask: The 95% VaR is closest to…

options.label: ≈ USD 70
options.why: Scale slip (3×).

options.label: ≈ USD 230
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 2,300
options.why: Percent vs decimal: plugged 5 and 10 in as whole numbers, $(-5 + 10 \times 1.65) \times 200 = 2{,}300$.

scenarios.takeaway: Return-based VaR is a percentage until you multiply it by the position value.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A USD 100m portfolio has normally distributed **geometric** returns with $\mu = 10\%$ and $\sigma = 40\%$. For the 95% lognormal VaR $P\,[1 - e^{\mu - \sigma z}]$ you have the exponent $\mu - \sigma z = 0.10 - 0.40 \times 1.645 = -0.558$.
scenarios.ask: Is the lognormal VaR more than half the portfolio value, less than half, or too close to call?

options.label: More than half (above USD 50m)
options.why: Normal-VaR reflex: $[-\mu + \sigma z] \times P = 55.8$m, but the lognormal bracket is $1 - e^{-0.558}$, which is smaller than 0.558. Half is lost only when the exponent reaches $-\ln 2 = -0.693$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The exponent $-0.558$ is well short of $-0.693$: $e^{-0.558} \approx 0.57$, so the loss is about 43%, clearly under 50%.

scenarios.takeaway: Lognormal VaR loses $1 - e^{\mu - \sigma z}$ of value: half is gone only when $\sigma z - \mu$ exceeds $\ln 2 \approx 0.69$.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A USD 1m equity portfolio has mean return 15% and volatility 25%. Its one-year 99% VaR ($z = 2.33$) under the **normal** (arithmetic-return) assumption is USD 432,500.
scenarios.ask: Switch to the **lognormal** assumption (geometric returns normal) with the same inputs. The VaR…

options.label: Rises
options.why: Lognormal caps the loss at 100% of value; it cannot out-lose the normal. With the same inputs the lognormal bracket $1 - e^{-x}$ is always below the normal bracket $x$.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: The exponent is the same number, $-0.4325$, but $1 - e^{-0.4325} = 0.351$, not 0.4325.

scenarios.takeaway: Same inputs, lognormal VaR < normal VaR, always, because $1 - e^{-x} < x$.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Two **independent** positions: $A \sim N(0.5,\,1)$ and $B \sim N(3,\,15)$, where the second parameter is the **variance**. The portfolio is $P = A + B$. Use $z_{95} = 1.645$.
scenarios.ask: The 95% parametric VaR of $P$ is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (0.3×).

scenarios.takeaway: Independent positions: add variances, take the root, then subtract the mean.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Two **independent** positions: $A \sim N(0.5,\,1)$ and $B \sim N(3,\,15)$ (second parameter = variance). On the way to the VaR of $P = A + B$ you need $\sigma_P$. A colleague writes $\sigma_A + \sigma_B = 1 + \sqrt{15} \approx 4.87$.
scenarios.ask: Is the true $\sigma_P$ larger than 4.87, smaller, or equal?

options.label: Larger
options.why: Variances add, not standard deviations; the root of a sum is below the sum of the roots for positive terms, so independence can only shrink $\sigma_P$ below 4.87.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Adding standard deviations silently assumes correlation $+1$. Here the positions are independent.

scenarios.takeaway: Work in variance space until the last square root; adding sigmas assumes $\rho = 1$.

options.label: ≈ CAD 42m

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Bond X is CAD 20m (annual $\sigma = 9\%$) inside a CAD 150m portfolio; its correlation with the portfolio is 0.60. At 99% one-year ($z = 2.326$) its individual VaR is $20 \times 2.326 \times 0.09 = \text{CAD } 4.19$m.
scenarios.ask: Is X's **component** VaR larger than, smaller than, or equal to its individual VaR?

options.label: Larger
options.why: Component VaR = individual VaR × correlation with the portfolio; a correlation below 1 can only shrink it.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only when $\rho = 1$, the undiversified case. Here $\rho = 0.60$.

scenarios.takeaway: Component VaR = individual VaR × ρ: below individual whenever ρ < 1.

scenarios.setup: A one-year correlation swap on a three-asset basket has notional USD 12m and fixed correlation 0.18. At maturity the realised pairwise correlations are 0.24, 0.26 and 0.36.
scenarios.ask: The payoff to the buyer of correlation (the fixed-rate payer) is closest to…

options.label: ≈ USD 0.043m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.13m
options.why: Averaged with $2/n^2 = 2/9$ instead of $2/(n^2-n) = 1/3$: realised $0.86 \times 2/9 = 0.191$, so the payoff is $12 \times (0.191 - 0.18) = 0.13$m. The $n$ diagonal pairs must be excluded.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.43m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Swap payoff = notional × (average realised − fixed); net the fixed leg.

scenarios.setup: A USD 12m correlation swap on three assets has a fixed correlation of 0.18. At maturity the realised pairwise correlations are 0.10, 0.28 and 0.12.
scenarios.ask: For the buyer of correlation (payer of the fixed rate), the payoff is…

options.label: Positive (buyer receives)
options.why: Anchored on the 0.28 pair, or summed the three (0.50) instead of averaging. The average is $0.50/3 = 0.167$, below 0.18.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Zero needs the average realised correlation to equal the fixed rate exactly; 0.167 ≠ 0.18.

scenarios.takeaway: Average the pairwise correlations first; the buyer wins only if that average beats the fixed rate.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Volatility-weighted historical simulation (Hull–White). A return of $+5\%$ was observed a month ago, when daily volatility was estimated at 2%. Today's daily volatility forecast is 1.5%.
scenarios.ask: The volatility-adjusted return used today is…

options.label: Larger than 5%
options.why: Inverted ratio: $(2.0/1.5) \times 5\% = 6.67\%$. Today's volatility goes on top, because the output must live on today's scale.

options.label: Equal to 5%
options.why: That is basic historical simulation, with no volatility adjustment.

scenarios.takeaway: Calmer today than then → historical returns are scaled down (today's σ in the numerator).

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Age-weighted historical simulation with a 300-day window and decay parameter $\lambda = 0.8$. Consider the observation from 13 days ago.
scenarios.ask: The weight it receives is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Equal weighting $1/300$: that is basic historical simulation, not age weighting.
Dropped the $(1 - \lambda)$ factor: $0.8^{12} = 0.069$ on its own.

scenarios.takeaway: Age weight $w(i) = \lambda^{i-1}(1-\lambda)/(1-\lambda^n)$: newest gets $1-\lambda$, then it decays geometrically.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Age-weighted historical simulation: 300-day window, decay $\lambda = 0.8$, weight $w(i) = \lambda^{i-1}(1-\lambda)/(1-\lambda^{n})$. Basic historical simulation would give every observation $1/300 \approx 0.0033$.
scenarios.ask: Is the age weight on the observation from 13 days ago larger than, smaller than, or about the same as 0.0033?

options.label: Smaller
options.why: Thirteen days is still recent at $\lambda = 0.8$: $0.8^{12} \approx 0.069$, times 0.2 gives about 0.014, roughly 4× the equal weight. The age weight drops below $1/300$ only from about day 20 onward.

options.label: About the same
options.why: 0.0137 vs 0.0033 is a factor of about 4, not a near tie.

scenarios.takeaway: With a fast decay (λ = 0.8), recent observations get far more than 1/n; old ones get almost nothing.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Stock A's past 260 daily returns are strongly **negatively** skewed. Position P1 is long A; P2 is an equal-sized short in A.
scenarios.ask: Which position has the larger 99% VaR?

options.label: P2, the short
options.why: Polarity flip: a short loses when A rises, so it lives in the right tail, which negative skew makes short and thin.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: True only for a symmetric distribution; skew is exactly what breaks the mirror image.

options.label: Cannot be determined
options.why: The sign of the skew is given, and the sign decides which tail is long.

working.label: Tail shape
working.display: Negative skew → long **left** tail, short right tail

working.label: Exposure map
working.display: Long loses on the downside (left tail); short loses on the upside (right tail)

working.label: Answer
working.display: Long position faces the long tail → larger VaR

scenarios.takeaway: Negative skew penalises the long; positive skew penalises the short.

scenarios.reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
scenarios.setup: Regression hedge of a corporate bond yield $Y_p$ with a government futures yield $Y_h$: correlation 0.8, $\sigma(Y_p) = 0.05$, $\sigma(Y_h) = 0.04$. The slope is $\beta = \rho\,\sigma_p/\sigma_h$.
scenarios.ask: The correlation pulls β below 1 and the volatility ratio pushes it above 1. Net: is β above 1, below 1, or exactly 1?

options.label: Below 1
options.why: That is the correlation factor alone (0.8); the volatility ratio 1.25 then scales it back up.

options.label: Above 1
options.why: That is the volatility ratio alone (1.25), with the correlation dropped.

scenarios.takeaway: β = ρ × σ(hedged)/σ(hedge); here 0.8 × 1.25 cancels exactly, so regression and DV01-neutral hedges coincide.

scenarios.reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
scenarios.setup: Daily yield changes of the hedging instrument over four days (bp): 2.0, 2.5, 1.5, 3.0. The sample covariance with the hedged yield is 0.273. The hedge $\beta = \text{Cov}/\text{Var}(Y_h)$ uses the **sample** variance.
scenarios.ask: Without finishing the division: is β above 1, below 1, or too close to call?

options.label: Above 1
options.why: Inverted ratio: $\text{Var}/\text{Cov} = 0.417/0.273 = 1.53$ is the reverse slope.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: Deviations from the mean 2.25 are ±0.25 and ±0.75, so the squared deviations sum to 1.25 and the sample variance is 0.417, well above the covariance 0.273.

scenarios.takeaway: β = Cov/Var(hedge): when Var(hedge) exceeds the covariance, β < 1.

scenarios.reading: Empirical Approaches to Risk Metrics and Hedging
scenarios.setup: You are hedging USD 100m face of a bond with DV01 0.300 using an instrument with DV01 0.250. The estimated regression hedge factor is $\beta = 0.80$.
scenarios.ask: In absolute size, is the regression hedge's face value larger than, smaller than, or equal to the DV01-neutral hedge's face value?

options.label: Larger
options.why: Divided by β instead of multiplying ($120/0.8 = 150$m). β < 1 means the hedged yield moves less than the hedge yield, so less hedge is needed.

options.label: Equal
options.why: Only when β = 1, the DV01-neutral special case.

scenarios.takeaway: Regression hedge = DV01-neutral hedge × β; with β < 1 it must be the smaller position.

scenarios.setup: A peaks-over-threshold (GPD) fit gives scale $\beta = 0.60$, shape $\xi = 0.30$, threshold $u = 1\%$, and a share of observations above the threshold of $N_u/n = 5\%$.
scenarios.ask: The 99% VaR is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip (3×).
Used $N_u/n = 0.05$ where its reciprocal $n/N_u = 20$ belongs: $(0.05 \times 0.01)^{-0.3} = 9.78$, so VaR $= 1 + 2 \times 8.78 = 18.6\%$.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: GPD VaR $= u + \frac{\beta}{\xi}\{[\frac{n}{N_u}(1-c)]^{-\xi} - 1\}$; it must land above $u$.

scenarios.setup: GPD tail model: $\beta = 0.60$, $\xi = 0.30$, threshold $u = 1\%$, $N_u/n = 5\%$. The 99% VaR is $u + \frac{\beta}{\xi}\{[\frac{n}{N_u}(1-c)]^{-\xi} - 1\}$, and you have the inner term $\frac{n}{N_u}(1-c) = 20 \times 0.01 = 0.20$.
scenarios.ask: Is the curly-bracket term $\{0.20^{-0.30} - 1\}$ positive, negative, or approximately zero?

options.label: Negative: VaR sits below u
options.why: A number below 1 raised to a **negative** power exceeds 1. The negative bracket comes from flipping the sign of $\xi$ ($0.20^{+0.30} = 0.617$).

options.label: Approximately zero: VaR ≈ u
options.why: $0.20^{-0.30} = 1.62$, so the bracket is 0.62, not near zero.

scenarios.takeaway: In the GPD VaR, $(\text{small number})^{-\xi} > 1$, so VaR always sits above the threshold.

scenarios.setup: A benchmark index has 95% VaR of USD 2.080m; the active portfolio's tracking-error VaR against it is USD 1.090m. The ratio is $1.090/2.080 = 0.524$. Variance improvement is the share of index **variance** eliminated.
scenarios.ask: Is the variance improvement above 50%, below 50%, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 50%
options.why: Forgot to square: $1 - 0.524 = 47.6\%$. VaR is in standard-deviation units, so the ratio must be squared before comparing variances.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: That near-50% number is the unsquared one. Squared, the ratio is 0.275, far from 0.5.

scenarios.takeaway: VaRs are standard deviations: square their ratio before talking variance.

scenarios.setup: Backtesting a daily 98% VaR over $T = 252$ days with a two-tailed 95% test (accept if $|z| \le 1.96$). Expected exceptions $Tp = 5.04$; standard deviation $\sqrt{Tp(1-p)} = 2.22$. The model produced 10 exceptions.
scenarios.ask: Is the z-statistic for 10 exceptions above the 1.96 cutoff, below it, or too close to call?

options.label: Below 1.96: accept
options.why: The acceptance bound is $5.04 + 1.96 \times 2.22 = 9.40$; rounding that bound up to 10 makes 10 look acceptable, but the largest acceptable count is 9. Dividing by the variance 4.94 instead of the s.d. gives the same wrong accept.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: $z = 4.96/2.22 = 2.23$, clearly past 1.96; 10 exceptions is 0.6 above the 9.40 bound.

scenarios.takeaway: The largest acceptable exception count is the integer below the bound, not the nearest one.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: One monthly step of a CIR short-rate model, $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$: $r = 4\%$, $\theta = 6\%$, $k = 0.40$, $\sigma = 0.08$, $dt = 1/12$, realised $dw = 0.15$ (rates in decimals).
scenarios.ask: Which term contributes more to $dr$ this month: the drift or the diffusion?

options.label: The drift term
options.why: Drift scales linearly with $dt$: $0.40 \times 0.02 \times \tfrac{1}{12} = 0.00067$, tiny over one month.

options.label: Roughly equal
options.why: $0.0024$ vs $0.00067$: the diffusion term is about 3.6× the drift.

scenarios.takeaway: Over short steps the random term dominates the drift; in CIR take $\sqrt{r}$ on the decimal rate.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: You estimate the 95% quantile (VaR) from $n = 1{,}000$ observations assumed standard normal. The density at that quantile is $f(q) = 0.1031$.
scenarios.ask: The standard error of the quantile estimate, in return units, is closest to…

options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Left $n$ out of the root: $\sqrt{0.0475}/0.1031 = 2.11$.

scenarios.takeaway: Quantile s.e. $= \frac{1}{f(q)}\sqrt{p(1-p)/n}$: the density divides, so thin tails mean noisy VaR.

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: Analyst A (250 obs) estimates a 95% VaR of 2.10% with standard error 0.134%. Analyst B (1,000 obs) gets 2.31% with standard error 0.067%. The gap between the point estimates is 0.21 percentage points.
scenarios.ask: Is the 0.21pp gap larger than, smaller than, or too close to call against the half-width of A's 95% confidence interval?

options.label: Smaller: B's estimate sits inside A's interval
Larger
options.why: Compared the gap to one standard error (0.134) instead of $1.96 \times 0.134 = 0.263$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The half-width is 0.263 against a 0.21 gap. B's 2.31% sits clearly inside [1.84%, 2.36%].

scenarios.takeaway: A gap between estimates means nothing until it is measured in standard errors.

scenarios.setup: You redraw a volatility smile against actual European **call** deltas, keeping the axis ordered so that the **strike increases** from left to right across five points.
scenarios.ask: Reading left to right, the call delta…

options.label: Rises steadily (near 0 → near 1)
options.why: Low strikes are deep in the money, with call delta near 1; high strikes are out of the money, with delta near 0.

options.label: Falls to 0.50, then rises again (10-25-50-25-10)
options.why: That is the market shorthand, which switches from puts to calls at the money. Call delta $N(d_1)$ is strictly decreasing in strike, so no value can repeat.

scenarios.takeaway: Call delta falls as strike rises; the symmetric 10-25-50-25 labels mix puts and calls.

scenarios.setup: A one-year at-the-money equity call has BSM delta 0.60, so the matching put's BSM delta is $-0.40$. The market shows the standard equity skew: implied volatility **decreases** in $K/S(0)$ (heavy left tail).
scenarios.ask: Relative to $-0.40$, the put's TRUE delta (including the smile effect) is…

options.label: Lower, i.e. more negative (e.g. −0.45)
options.why: This reads 'more sensitive' as 'more negative'. Parity forces put delta = call delta − 1, and the call's true delta rises above 0.60, so the put's delta also rises.

options.label: Equal to −0.40
options.why: This drops the smile term vega × ∂σ/∂S, which is positive under an equity skew.

scenarios.takeaway: Equity skew raises both true deltas by the same amount: the call's above 0.60, the put's toward zero.

scenarios.setup: A call struck at USD 20 is at the money (BSM delta 0.50). The implied distribution has a **light left tail and a heavy right tail**, so implied volatility **rises** with $K/S(0)$. The stock drifts up toward USD 21.
scenarios.ask: Relative to 0.50, the call's TRUE delta (BSM term plus smile term)…

options.label: Rises above 0.50
options.why: That counts only the BSM term. Under a reverse skew the smile term is negative and pulls the other way.

options.label: Falls below 0.50
options.why: That counts only the smile term; nothing in the setup says it outweighs the BSM move.

options.label: Stays at 0.50
options.why: This ignores both terms, and they are not zero.

working.label: BSM term
working.display: Moving into the money: $N(d_1)$ rises above 0.50 (positive)

working.label: Net
working.display: Opposite signs → indeterminate without skew steepness and vega

scenarios.takeaway: Sign each delta term separately; call a direction only when the signs agree (equity skew yes, reverse skew no).

scenarios.reading: Volatility Smiles and the Fundamental Review of the Trading Book
scenarios.setup: An analyst believes an asset's volatility is uncertain and **positively** correlated with its price.
scenarios.ask: Relative to constant-volatility (BSM) prices, out-of-the-money **puts** are…

options.label: More expensive
options.why: That is the equity pattern, which comes from **negative** correlation. Positive correlation thins the left tail, and OTM puts (low strikes) are priced off that tail.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Stochastic volatility that is correlated with price reshapes the implied distribution's tails, so low-strike options are no longer priced at the constant-volatility value.

working.label: Correlation → tails
working.display: High price with high vol → heavy right tail, light left tail

working.label: Tails → strikes
working.display: OTM puts are struck low → priced off the light left tail → cheaper

scenarios.takeaway: Positive price–vol correlation: upward skew, OTM puts cheap, OTM calls dear.

scenarios.reading: Tuckman, The Science of Term Structure Models
scenarios.setup: A normal (Gaussian) short-rate tree produces some negative nodes. The modeller replaces every negative node with zero and leaves all other nodes unchanged.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the unfloored tree, the mean of the modelled short rate…

options.label: Falls
options.why: Wrong direction: the only values changed were negatives, and each one moved **up** to zero.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Tempting because negative nodes are rare, but truncating the left tail is a systematic change that moves the mean up (and the volatility down).

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Negative nodes move up to 0; nothing moves down

working.label: Moments
working.display: Mean ↑, volatility ↓ vs the unadjusted model

scenarios.takeaway: Flooring at zero raises the mean and lowers the volatility of the modelled rate.

scenarios.setup: A domestic investor holds a quanto **call** on a foreign equity index, with the payoff converted at a fixed exchange rate. Let $\rho$ be the correlation between the index and the FX rate (domestic currency per unit of foreign).
scenarios.ask: If $\rho$ increases, the value of the quanto call…

options.label: Rises
options.why: Wrong sign: $\rho$ enters the quanto drift with a minus sign.

options.label: Is unchanged, because the rate is fixed
options.why: The fixed rate is the source of the exposure, not a hedge against it.

options.label: Can't be signed without the FX volatility
options.why: Volatilities multiply $\rho$ and are non-negative, so they set the size of the effect, not its sign.

scenarios.takeaway: Higher index–FX correlation lowers the quanto drift: quanto calls lose value, quanto puts gain.

scenarios.setup: A portfolio is **long** two assets with fixed weights and volatilities. VaR is computed with the variance–covariance approach. The correlation between the assets rises from 0 to 0.5.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio VaR…

options.label: Falls
options.why: For two longs the cross term $2w_1w_2\rho\sigma_1\sigma_2$ has a positive coefficient. VaR falls with $\rho$ only if one leg is short.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Correlation enters portfolio variance directly through the cross term.

options.label: Depends on the two volatilities
options.why: The volatilities set the size of the change, not its sign: the coefficient on $\rho$ is positive whatever they are.

working.label: Sign
working.display: Coefficient on $\rho$ $> 0$ for long/long → VaR increasing in $\rho$

scenarios.takeaway: Long/long: VaR rises with correlation, maximal at ρ = 1 (sum of individual VaRs).

scenarios.setup: A bank spreads its loan book across more borrowers, lowering its concentration ratio. The default correlation between the loans is strictly **below one**.
scenarios.ask: The joint probability of default across the portfolio…

options.label: Rises
options.why: More names with $\rho < 1$ add independent variation; simultaneous failure becomes less likely.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Only at $\rho = 1$, where obligors fail as a block. The setup rules that out.

options.label: Cannot be determined
options.why: The $\rho < 1$ condition is exactly what makes the sign determinable.

working.label: Direction
working.display: $\rho < 1$ → diversification works → joint default probability falls

scenarios.takeaway: Lower concentration with ρ < 1 → lower joint default probability; at ρ = 1 diversification does nothing.

scenarios.setup: A risk manager adds several new **general** risk factors to an existing mapped VaR model.
scenarios.ask: The specific risk in the model…

options.label: Increases
options.why: More factors can mean more estimation error, but the specific term is the residual, and a residual cannot grow when regressors are added.

options.label: Is unaffected
options.why: General and specific risk split one fixed total; they are not measured independently.

options.label: Can't be signed without knowing the factors
options.why: The factors chosen set the **size** of the drop, not its sign.

working.label: Direction
working.display: Total fixed; more explained by general factors → residual (specific) shrinks

scenarios.takeaway: Adding general factors moves variance from specific to general risk: specific risk falls.

scenarios.setup: A two-bond portfolio's VaR is computed with **duration mapping**, which collapses it onto one vertex. The analyst re-maps it with **cash-flow mapping** onto several vertices whose correlations are high but below one.
scenarios.ask: The VaR…

options.label: Rises
options.why: Cash-flow mapping captures diversification that duration mapping assumes away; it cannot add risk here.

options.label: Is unchanged
options.why: Only if all vertex correlations were 1 and risk were linear in maturity; neither holds.

working.label: Duration mapping
working.display: One vertex → cash flows implicitly perfectly correlated: VaR 2.80

scenarios.takeaway: The finer the mapping, the more diversification it recognises: duration mapping is conservative.

scenarios.setup: A VaR model's PIT values (where each realised P&L fell within the model's predicted distribution) bunch heavily around 0.5, with very few near 0 or 1.
scenarios.ask: The model…

options.label: Understates risk
options.why: That is the signature of excess mass in the tails of the PIT histogram (outcomes landing at the extremes).

options.label: Is well calibrated
options.why: A correct model gives a **flat** PIT histogram, not one peaked in the middle.

working.label: Reading
working.display: Outcomes keep landing near the centre → predicted distribution too wide

working.label: Verdict
working.display: Risk overstated; capital tied up unnecessarily

scenarios.takeaway: PIT peaked in the middle = forecast too wide (overstates); mass in the ends = too narrow (understates).

scenarios.reading: Dowd, Estimating Market Risk Measures: An Introduction and Overview
scenarios.setup: A QQ plot of daily equity returns (empirical quantiles on the vertical axis) against a normal reference: the middle hugs the line, the left end falls **below** it and the right end rises **above** it.
scenarios.ask: Relative to the normal, the tails are…

options.label: Lighter
options.why: Lighter tails bend the ends **toward** the line. Here the extremes are larger in magnitude than the normal predicts at both ends.

options.label: Neither: it is a mean shift
options.why: A location shift moves the whole line (non-zero intercept); it doesn't bend both ends in opposite directions.

working.label: Left end
working.display: Empirical quantile more negative than normal → bigger losses

working.label: Right end
working.display: Empirical quantile more positive than normal → bigger gains

working.label: Verdict
working.display: S-shape bending outward → excess kurtosis (heavy tails)

scenarios.takeaway: QQ ends bending away from the line = heavy tails; bending toward it = light tails.

scenarios.setup: An asset's implied distribution has a **lighter left tail and a heavier right tail** than lognormal. The risk reversal is $RR = \sigma_{imp}(0.25\Delta\text{ call}) - \sigma_{imp}(-0.25\Delta\text{ put})$.
scenarios.ask: The risk reversal is…

options.label: Negative
options.why: That is the standard equity-skew case (heavy left tail). This setup describes the reverse skew.

options.label: Zero
options.why: Zero needs a symmetric smile; the tails here are asymmetric.

working.label: Tails → slope
working.display: Light left, heavy right → implied vol increasing in strike

working.label: Legs
working.display: 25Δ call is struck high (high vol); −25Δ put is struck low (low vol)

scenarios.takeaway: Risk reversal sign = direction of skew: negative for equity skew, positive for reverse skew.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A USD 1.0bn loan portfolio yields 5.0% a year. Operating cost is USD 6.0m, the deposit transfer charge is 1.40% on the full USD 1.0bn, and expected loss is 1.0% (USD 10m). Economic capital of USD 80m (8% of the loan) is invested at the 1.0% risk-free rate. Tax rate 25%.
scenarios.ask: After-tax RAROC is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip (3×). That would need about USD 47m after tax, but only USD 15.6m survives funding, costs, EL and tax.
Economic capital entered as 8 (the 8% ratio) instead of USD 80m, a percent-vs-amount slip.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: RAROC = after-tax risk-adjusted income / economic capital. With capital at 8% of the loan, a 1.5% after-tax margin comes out near 20%.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Same portfolio: revenue USD 50.0m, operating cost 6.0m, transfer charge 14.0m, expected loss 10.0m, return on EC 0.8m, giving a pre-tax numerator of USD 20.8m. Tax 25%, economic capital USD 80m (RAROC 19.5%). Two classic slips: dropping the $(1-t)$ factor, or dropping the expected loss.
scenarios.ask: Which slip inflates RAROC more?

options.label: Dropping the tax factor
options.why: The tax haircut is only 25% × 20.8 = USD 5.2m, but the EL is still USD 7.5m after tax. Dropping EL does more damage.

options.label: They inflate it equally
options.why: They add back different amounts: USD 5.2m (tax) and USD 7.5m (EL after tax), which is 6.5pp against 9.4pp of RAROC.

scenarios.takeaway: A deduction still matters after tax: 10m of EL is worth 7.5m of numerator, more than the whole 5.2m tax bite.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A single loan: value USD 2,000,000, gross revenue USD 250,000, expected loss 300bp, interest expense USD 100,000, operating costs USD 60,000, return on invested economic capital USD 10,000, and economic capital USD 400,000. No tax.
scenarios.ask: Once expected loss is in dollars, which is larger: expected loss or operating costs?

options.label: Operating costs are larger
options.why: That comes from applying 300bp to the USD 400,000 of capital (USD 12,000). Expected loss is a reserve on the exposure, so the base is the USD 2m loan.

options.label: Expected loss is larger
options.why: 300bp of USD 2,000,000 is exactly USD 60,000, the same as operating costs.

scenarios.takeaway: A rate quoted in bp needs its base named first. For expected loss that base is the exposure, never the capital.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: The same loan: USD 2,000,000 exposure earning USD 250,000 gross, so the headline yield is 12.5%. Deductions are expected loss of 300bp on the loan, USD 100,000 of interest and USD 60,000 of operating costs; add back USD 10,000 of return on capital. Economic capital is USD 400,000 (a fifth of the loan).
scenarios.ask: The loan's RAROC compared with its 12.5% gross yield is:

options.label: Higher
options.why: Capital is only a fifth of the loan, which multiplies the return by 5. But the deductions leave USD 40k of the USD 250k (16%), so 12.5% × 5 × 0.16 = 10%.

options.label: About the same
options.why: 10% against 12.5% is a fifth lower, not a rounding difference.

working.label: Comparison
working.display: $10.0\% < 12.5\%$: after funding, costs and EL the shareholder return is lower

scenarios.takeaway: The capital leverage (×5) cannot rescue a margin that funding, costs and EL have cut to 16% of revenue.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A bank cuts the confidence level behind its RAROC economic capital from 99.97% to 99.5%. Nothing else changes, and the activity's risk is dominated by rare, large operational and credit losses.
scenarios.ask: The risk capital allocated to the activity:

options.label: Rises, because more of the loss distribution is captured
options.why: Polarity flip. A lower confidence level reads the worst-case loss closer to the body of the distribution, so capital shrinks.

options.label: Stays the same, and only its year-to-year volatility changes
options.why: Role slip. The PIT vs TTC choice drives volatility; the confidence level sets the level.

options.label: Falls, so the measure is less conservative

working.label: Conservatism
working.display: Less capital against the same exposure is less conservative, not more

scenarios.takeaway: Lowering the confidence level always releases capital, and releasing capital is never conservative.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A bank switches the default probabilities feeding its economic capital from through-the-cycle (rating-agency style) estimates to point-in-time (structural, KMV-style) estimates.
scenarios.ask: Year-to-year volatility of economic capital, and so of RAROC:

options.label: Falls
options.why: The direction is backwards. PIT PDs track current conditions and ratings stay put less often, so capital moves more.

options.label: Unchanged, because only the level of capital moves
options.why: Role slip. The level is set by the confidence level; the PIT vs TTC choice is what drives volatility.

working.label: PIT
working.display: PIT PDs follow the current cycle $\Rightarrow$ more rating migration

working.label: Result
working.display: PIT $\Rightarrow$ higher volatility of EC; TTC $\Rightarrow$ lower volatility of EC

scenarios.takeaway: PIT → volatile capital and RAROC; TTC → stable. Volatility belongs to the PD method, level to the confidence level.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A project's RAROC is 10.00%. Its beta is 1.18, $r_f = 2.00\%$ and the expected market return is 7.932%, so the market premium $R_M - r_f$ is 5.932%.
scenarios.ask: Adjusted RAROC minus the risk-free rate is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: That only happens if r_f is dropped from the bracket: 1.18 × 7.932% = 9.36% leaves 0.64%, which is below 2%. The charge is 1.18 × 5.932% ≈ 7.0%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The margin is a full 1.00pp (3.00% against 2.00%).

scenarios.takeaway: Test the condition before computing a gap: here adjusted RAROC already beats r_f, so the required increase is zero.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A loan portfolio's traditional RAROC works out at 13.50%. The firm's equity beta is 1.60, the risk-free rate is 1.0% and the expected market return is 8.0%.
scenarios.ask: The RAROC adjusted for systematic risk is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (0.1×).
The risk-free rate was dropped from the bracket: 13.5% − 1.6 × 8.0% = 0.7%. The premium is R_M − r_f = 7.0%.

scenarios.takeaway: A high beta can swallow most of a healthy-looking RAROC; the adjusted figure is then compared with r_f, not the hurdle.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A USD 200m loan portfolio has an unadjusted RORAC of 6.39%, just above the firm's 6% hurdle rate. Equity beta is 1.05, $r_f = 3\%$ and the expected market return is 7%.
scenarios.ask: Adjusted RORAC minus the risk-free rate is:

options.label: Positive
options.why: That comes from comparing the unadjusted 6.39% with the 6% hurdle. After the 1.05 × 4% = 4.20% charge, 2.19% is below 3%.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The gap is −0.81pp, which is clearly negative.

scenarios.takeaway: Once returns are beta-adjusted, the bar is the risk-free rate, and 'above the hurdle' can turn into a reject.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A leveraged fund (portfolio USD 2,000m, expected loss USD 50m) sizes economic capital at 99.5% confidence. Its 99.5% worst-case loss is revised up from USD 500m to USD 1,000m.
scenarios.ask: The increase in required economic capital is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 2,000m
options.why: Treated the whole portfolio as capital, as if solvency had to be guaranteed at 100%.

options.label: ≈ USD 5,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 15,000m
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Capital = worst-case loss − EL. With EL unchanged, the change in capital is the change in the tail.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Same fund: expected loss USD 50m, unchanged. The 99.5% worst-case loss rises from USD 500m to USD 1,000m, and economic capital is sized as worst-case loss minus EL, before and after.
scenarios.ask: Which is larger: the increase in economic capital or the increase in worst-case loss?

options.label: The capital increase is smaller, by the USD 50m of EL
options.why: EL is subtracted from both the before and the after figure, so it cancels in the difference.

options.label: The capital increase is larger
options.why: Nothing adds to capital beyond the deeper tail, and EL is unchanged.

scenarios.takeaway: A constant EL cancels in any before/after comparison. Read the final noun ('increase') before computing levels.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A bank's Business Indicator is EUR 18.0bn. Marginal coefficients: 12% on the first EUR 1bn, 15% from EUR 1bn to 30bn, 18% above EUR 30bn. A colleague shortcuts the BIC as $18.0 \times 15\% = 2.70$.
scenarios.ask: The correct BIC is:

options.label: Above 2.70
options.why: The 18% bucket only starts at EUR 30bn. At BI = 18bn no coefficient above 15% applies.

options.label: Exactly 2.70
options.why: The first EUR 1bn is charged 12%, not 15%, which takes 0.03bn off.

scenarios.takeaway: Marginal, not average: each coefficient applies only to the slice of BI inside its bucket, like tax brackets.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A bank's Business Indicator is EUR 18.0bn. Marginal coefficients: 12% up to EUR 1bn, 15% from EUR 1bn to 30bn, 18% above EUR 30bn.
scenarios.ask: The Business Indicator Component is closest to?

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.090bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.27bn
options.why: Percent/decimal slip: 15% read as 1.5% (18 × 0.015).

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.9bn
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

scenarios.takeaway: BIC is roughly 15% of BI for a mid-sized bank, so a BI of 18bn means a BIC of about 2.7bn.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: Marginal BIC coefficients: 12% on the first EUR 1bn of BI, 15% from 1bn to 30bn, 18% above 30bn. At BI = EUR 18bn the BIC is EUR 2.67bn. Now consider a bank with BI = EUR 35bn.
scenarios.ask: BIC as a percentage of BI at 35bn, compared with 18bn, is:

options.label: Lower
options.why: The direction is backwards. The extra BI above 30bn is charged 18%, which pulls the average rate up, not down.

options.label: The same
options.why: Only a single flat coefficient keeps BIC/BI constant. Marginal coefficients rise with size.

scenarios.takeaway: Rising marginal coefficients mean op-risk capital grows faster than proportionally with bank size.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: Acme Bank's Business Indicator is EUR 56.0bn, which gives a BIC of EUR 9.15bn after the 12%/15%/18% marginal coefficients. Its Internal Loss Multiplier is 0.8050.
scenarios.ask: Acme's operational-risk RWA is closest to?

options.label: ≈ EUR 7.4bn
options.why: That is the capital charge (ORC). You stopped one step early.

options.label: ≈ EUR 276bn
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 700bn
options.why: Applied 12.5 to the BI itself (56 × 12.5) and skipped the BIC and ILM.

scenarios.takeaway: Op-risk RWA = 12.5 × ORC. Once you have the capital charge, multiply by 12.5; don't stop at the capital figure.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: Acme's BI of EUR 56.0bn spans all three buckets: the first EUR 1bn at 12%, EUR 1bn to 30bn at 15%, and everything above EUR 30bn at 18%.
scenarios.ask: Which bucket's slice adds more to the BIC?

options.label: Bucket 2 (EUR 1bn to 30bn)
options.why: Bucket 2 covers more BI (29bn against 26bn), but the 18% coefficient more than makes up the gap: 4.68 against 4.35.

options.label: They contribute exactly the same
options.why: 29 × 15% = 4.35 and 26 × 18% = 4.68, so they are not equal.

scenarios.takeaway: For big banks the top bucket dominates: its higher coefficient outweighs a slightly narrower slice.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A bank's BIC is EUR 2.67bn. Its average annual operational-risk losses over the past ten years are EUR 200m. The Loss Component is $LC = 15 \times$ average annual loss, and $ILM = \ln\left(e - 1 + LC/BIC\right)$. The national regulator has not set ILM = 1.
scenarios.ask: The sign of ILM − 1 is:

options.label: Negative
options.why: That only happens if the ×15 is forgotten: LC = 0.2 < 2.67. The correct LC = 3.00 is above BIC, so the log argument is above e.

options.label: Zero
options.why: ILM = 1 only when LC equals BIC exactly, or when the regulator sets it to 1 (ruled out here).

scenarios.takeaway: LC > BIC ⇒ ILM > 1 ⇒ more capital; LC < BIC ⇒ ILM < 1. Settle the direction before taking any logs.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: BIC is EUR 2.67bn and the Loss Component is EUR 3.00bn, so $LC/BIC = 1.124$. The multiplier is $ILM = \ln\left(e - 1 + LC/BIC\right)$ and ORC = BIC × ILM.
scenarios.ask: ORC exceeds BIC by roughly what percentage?

options.why: Used LC/BIC = 1.124 as the multiplier. The log exists to damp the adjustment: 12% excess losses give only about a 4.4% capital uplift.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Added LC on top of BIC (2.67 + 3.00) instead of scaling BIC by the ILM.

scenarios.takeaway: The ILM is log-damped: losses running about 12% above BIC lift capital by only about 4.4%.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 24: Basel III: Finalising Post-Crisis Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: Under the Basel III standardised approach, a bank with BI well above EUR 1bn has a Loss Component (15 × average annual op-risk loss over ten years) below its BIC, and its regulator applies the ILM. A large old loss now drops out of the ten-year window, which lowers LC further. BI is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The bank's operational-risk capital charge:

options.label: Unchanged, because internal loss history no longer enters the calculation
options.why: Scope slip. The reform removed internal models, not internal loss data. Losses enter through ILM = ln(e − 1 + LC/BIC).

options.label: Rises
options.why: Polarity flip. A lower LC/BIC lowers the ILM, and with it the capital.

scenarios.takeaway: Loss experience still counts through the ILM: lower losses relative to BIC mean lower capital, higher losses mean higher capital.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A bank's RWA under its approved approaches (including internal models) is EUR 180.0bn. Its RWA using only the standardised approaches is EUR 260.0bn. The Basel III output floor is 72.5%.
scenarios.ask: Approved-approach RWA minus the floored standardised figure is:

options.label: Positive, so the floor is slack
options.why: That comes from putting the 72.5% on the modelled leg (0.725 × 180 = 130.5). The percentage belongs to the standardised leg: 0.725 × 260 = 188.5.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The gap is −8.5bn, about 5% of RWA, which is decisive.

scenarios.takeaway: Output floor: RWA = max(modelled, 72.5% × standardised). The 72.5% always goes on the standardised leg.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A bank's RWA under its approved approaches is EUR 180.0bn. Its standardised-only RWA is EUR 260.0bn. The Basel III output floor is 72.5%.
scenarios.ask: The floor adds roughly how much to reported RWA?

options.label: ≈ EUR 0.85bn
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 2.6bn
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

options.label: ≈ EUR 50bn
options.why: Put the 72.5% on the bank's own 180 (130.5) and measured 180 − 130.5. That is the wrong leg, and a cushion rather than an uplift.

scenarios.takeaway: The floor can only raise RWA. When it binds, the uplift is the gap to 72.5% of standardised RWA, not the whole modelling benefit.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: Same bank: standardised-only RWA is EUR 260.0bn and the output floor is 72.5%. Model refinements cut its approved-approach RWA from EUR 180.0bn to EUR 170.0bn.
scenarios.ask: Reported RWA:

options.label: Falls by about EUR 10bn
options.why: The floor already binds at 188.5, both before and after. A lower modelled figure only widens the gap below the floor.

options.label: Rises
options.why: The floor lifts reported RWA to 72.5% of standardised and no further. Extra modelling benefit isn't penalised beyond that.

scenarios.takeaway: Once the output floor binds, further model-driven RWA cuts are worth nothing to the bank.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 25: High-Level Summary of Basel III Reforms (BCBS)
scenarios.setup: A G-SIB faces a risk-weighted higher loss-absorbency (HLA) requirement of 2.5%. The Basel III leverage ratio minimum is 3% Tier 1, and G-SIBs add a leverage ratio buffer on top. A colleague writes 3% + 2.5% = 5.5%.
scenarios.ask: The correct Tier 1 leverage requirement, including the buffer, compared with 5.5% is:

options.label: The same
options.why: The HLA isn't carried over in full. The leverage buffer is calibrated at 50% of it.

options.label: Higher
options.why: Nothing is added beyond the 3% minimum and the buffer, and the buffer is smaller than the HLA.

scenarios.takeaway: G-SIB leverage buffer = half the risk-weighted HLA, on top of the 3% minimum (for example 2% HLA gives a 1% buffer).

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Two candidate businesses; the cost of equity is 6.2%. Tarragona: expected net profit EUR 3.0m on economic capital of EUR 50m. Valencia: EUR 1.5m on EUR 22m.
scenarios.ask: Which has the higher RAROC?

options.label: Tarragona
options.why: It earns twice the profit but uses more than twice the capital: 3.0/50 = 6.0% against 1.5/22 = 6.8%.

options.label: They are equal
options.why: 6.0% against 6.8%: the gap is 0.8pp, and it straddles the 6.2% cost of equity.

working.label: vs 6.2%
working.display: Only Valencia clears the cost of equity

scenarios.takeaway: Putting capital in the denominator can reverse a profit ranking. Compare profit to capital, not profit to profit.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Per USD 100 of loans: expected revenue 7.0, expected credit loss 3.0, budgeted operating costs 2.5, return on economic capital 0.2 (EC = 40), tax 30%. Operating costs actually came in at double the budget.
scenarios.ask: With EL included and operating costs doubled, the pre-tax RAROC numerator is:

options.label: Positive
options.why: Positive only if the 3.0 of expected loss is left out (7 − 5 + 0.2 = 2.2). EL is a cost of doing business and always comes off the numerator.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The numerator is −0.8 per 100 against revenue of 7.0, which gives RAROC = −1.40%. That is clearly negative.

scenarios.takeaway: EL (3.0) plus a 2.5 cost overrun is more than the whole 4.7 of margin before EL, so the sign flips.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A bank's rating-migration matrix is estimated on 2009–2024 data (growth and mild recessions) and applied uniformly, which makes it a through-the-cycle construction. A severe recession, deeper than any since the 1990s, is expected in 2025.
scenarios.ask: The matrix's 2025 default probabilities will be:

options.label: Overstated
options.why: Polarity flip. TTC smooths toward the cycle average, and in a severe recession realised defaults run above that average.

options.label: About right, because TTC is designed to be stable
options.why: Stable is not the same as accurate. TTC deliberately ignores the coming downturn.

working.label: TTC
working.display: Estimates sit near the cycle average and do not condition on current conditions

working.label: Severe recession
working.display: actual defaults $>$ cycle-average rates $\Rightarrow$ TTC PDs too low

working.label: Knock-on
working.display: EL and economic capital are both understated, so RAROC is flattered

scenarios.takeaway: TTC PDs lag a downturn: in a severe recession they underestimate default, which flatters capital and RAROC.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: A liquid proprietary trading desk reports a one-day VaR. The naive one-year figure is $\text{VaR}_{1d} \times \sqrt{\text{business days}}$. In a crisis the desk would run its position down, in an orderly way over a 'time to reduce', to a core risk level and hold it there for the rest of the year.
scenarios.ask: Appropriate one-year risk capital, compared with the naive annualised VaR, is:

options.label: Above it, because volatility clustering makes √T too low
options.why: The adjustment that matters here is the shrinking position, not clustering. Exposure falls to the core level.

options.label: Equal to it
options.why: √T scaling assumes the full position is held all year, which a desk in a crisis would not do.

working.label: Realistic path
working.display: Exposure declines to the core risk level over the time to reduce, then stays there

scenarios.takeaway: For liquid trading desks, risk capital sits below √T-scaled VaR. Over-attributing it can push a value-creating desk below the hurdle.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: The hurdle rate is the market-value-weighted cost of equity. Common equity is USD 200m with a CAPM cost of 8.75%. Preferred equity is USD 800m and pays USD 48m of dividends a year.
scenarios.ask: The blended hurdle rate will sit closer to:

options.why: Common equity is only 20% of the equity by market value, so the preferred cost dominates.

options.label: The midpoint of the two costs (≈7.4%)
options.why: That needs equal weights, but market values are 200 against 800.

scenarios.takeaway: A weighted hurdle leans toward the heavier weight: 80% preferred at 6% pulls it to 6.55%.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Activities X and Y have stand-alone risk capital of USD 70m and USD 80m. The business unit's combined risk capital, after all diversification effects, is USD 120m.
scenarios.ask: The implied correlation between X and Y is:

options.label: Zero
options.why: Zero correlation gives √(70² + 80²) ≈ 106m. At 120m the unit sits above that floor.

options.label: Negative
options.why: Negative correlation would pull combined capital below about 106m, not up to 120m.

scenarios.takeaway: Aggregate capital sits between √Σ(RC²) (ρ = 0) and ΣRC (ρ = 1); anywhere above the floor means positive correlation.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Two departments with less than perfect correlation share a combined risk capital figure. Each department's marginal capital is the combined capital minus the combined capital without that department.
scenarios.ask: The sum of the two marginal capitals, compared with the combined risk capital, is:

options.label: Exactly equal to it
options.why: Sibling mix-up. It is the fully diversified (pro rata) capitals that reconcile exactly.

options.label: More than it
options.why: Direction slip. Marginal capital credits each department with the full diversification benefit, so the sum falls short.

working.label: Marginal
working.display: $\sum \text{marginal capital} < \text{combined capital}$: the benefit is counted twice

scenarios.takeaway: Fully diversified capital adds up; marginal capital doesn't. That is why marginal capital drives business-mix decisions, not reconciliation.

scenarios.reading: Operational Risk and Resilience, Ch. 18: Risk Capital Attribution and Risk-Adjusted Performance Measurement (Crouhy, Galai and Mark)
scenarios.setup: Consumer Credit Cards (stand-alone capital USD 90m) and Consumer Purchase Loans (USD 110m) are negatively correlated, so their combined capital is USD 150m. In a crisis, their correlation shifts sharply toward +1.
scenarios.ask: Combined risk capital:

options.label: Falls further below USD 150m
options.why: Polarity flip. Higher correlation shrinks the diversification benefit and does not add to it.

options.label: Stays at USD 150m, because the allocated benefit is fixed
options.why: The portfolio effect depends on correlation, which is unstable and can disappear in a crisis.

scenarios.takeaway: Diversification benefits evaporate when correlations jump in a crisis, so be careful how generously you allocate them.

scenarios.setup: Altman Z-score, $Z = 1.2X_1 + 1.4X_2 + 3.3X_3 + 0.6X_4 + 0.999X_5$. A firm has total assets 670,000, working capital 170,000, retained earnings 300,000, EBIT 60,000, market equity 380,000, total liabilities 240,000 and sales 2,200,000.
scenarios.ask: Which is bigger: the $0.999X_5$ (sales/assets) term alone, or the other four terms combined?

options.label: The other four combined
options.why: The four together come to only about 2.18. Sales are 3.3× total assets, so $X_5 \approx 3.28$ on its own outweighs them.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: 3.28 versus 2.18 is a 50% gap. Asset turnover (3.28) is by far the largest ratio, and its weight of 0.999 barely shrinks it.

scenarios.takeaway: For a high-turnover firm, X5 (sales/assets) can carry most of the Z-score. Check it first.

scenarios.setup: S&P cumulative default rates for a **B**-rated issuer: 3.34% by year 1, 7.80% by year 2, 11.75% by year 3. The cumulative figure keeps climbing.
scenarios.ask: Is the marginal (unconditional) PD in year 3 larger or smaller than in year 2?

options.label: Larger in year 3
options.why: A rising cumulative PD tells you nothing about whether the yearly increments are rising. Year 2 adds 4.46 points and year 3 adds only 3.95.

options.label: Equal
options.why: The increments are 4.46 and 3.95. They differ by about half a point, so they are not equal.

working.label: Comparison
working.display: $3.95\% < 4.46\%$: the B-rated marginal profile peaks in year 2 and then falls

scenarios.takeaway: Speculative-grade marginal PDs peak early and then decline once the issuer survives. Investment-grade marginal PDs tend to rise over time.

scenarios.setup: Constant hazard rate $\lambda = 2\%$. Cumulative PD is $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 4} = 7.69\%$ by year 4 and $1 - e^{-0.02 \times 5} = 9.52\%$ by year 5. So the unconditional PD during year 5 is $1.83\%$.
scenarios.ask: The PD in year 5 *conditional on surviving to year 4*: higher than, lower than, or equal to 1.83%?

options.label: Lower than 1.83%
options.why: Conditioning divides by the survival probability $1 - 0.0769 < 1$, which can only make the number larger.

options.label: Equal to 1.83%
options.why: The two coincide only in year 1, when survival to the start of the year is 100%. By year 5 the survival factor is 92.3%.

scenarios.takeaway: Conditional PD = marginal / survival, so it is always at least as large as the unconditional PD. Under a constant hazard it stays flat at 1 − e^(−λ).

scenarios.setup: CDS spreads: 5-year 90 bp, 10-year 110 bp. Expected recovery is 65%. Average hazard rates are bootstrapped with $\bar\lambda = s/(1-RR)$.
scenarios.ask: The average hazard rate between year 5 and year 10 is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip (0.1×), e.g. a decimal slip when converting bp to percent.
You bootstrapped the raw spreads, $(10 \times 1.10\% - 5 \times 0.90\%)/5$, without dividing by $LGD = 0.35$.

scenarios.takeaway: Forward hazard = time-weighted difference of cumulative averages, divided by the gap in years. Gross spreads up by LGD first.

scenarios.setup: 5-year iTraxx Europe is quoted bid 150 bp / ask 152 bp. The index has 125 names. An investor buys EUR 500,000 of protection on *each* name.
scenarios.ask: The annual premium paid is closest to?

options.label: ≈ EUR 2,850,000
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 9,500,000
options.why: Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ EUR 28,500,000
options.why: Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

working.label: Rate
working.display: Buyer of protection pays the ask: $152 \text{ bp} = 0.0152$

scenarios.takeaway: Index premium = ask spread × notional per name × number of names. A protection buyer pays the ask.

scenarios.setup: Merton model. Equity $E_0 = 3$, equity volatility $\sigma_E = 80\%$, solved firm value $V_0 = 12.40$, and equity delta $N(d_1) = 0.912$. Use $\sigma_E E_0 = N(d_1)\,\sigma_V V_0$.
scenarios.ask: Asset volatility $\sigma_V$ is closest to?

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).
That is the equity volatility. Equity is a levered claim, so $\sigma_V$ must be much lower than $\sigma_E$.
You inverted the leverage ratio: $\sigma_E \times V_0/E_0 = 0.8 \times 12.4/3$. Asset vol cannot exceed equity vol here.

scenarios.takeaway: Asset vol = equity vol × (E/V) ÷ delta. With leverage it comes out far below equity vol.

scenarios.setup: The CDS-bond basis is defined as $\text{CDS spread} - \text{bond yield spread}$. A CDS contract lets the protection buyer deliver the *cheapest-to-deliver* bond on default.
scenarios.ask: This feature pushes the basis: positive, negative, or no effect?

options.label: Negative
options.why: Negative-basis drivers make CDS protection worth less than it looks: counterparty risk, accrued interest excluded from the payoff, bonds above par. The CTD option works the other way.

options.label: No effect
options.why: The CTD option has value to the protection buyer, and the seller charges for it in the spread.

working.label: Who holds the option
working.display: The protection buyer chooses what to deliver, which is an extra option

working.label: Effect
working.display: Protection is worth more → CDS spread rises relative to the bond spread → basis > 0

scenarios.takeaway: Anything that hands the protection buyer an extra option (CTD, restructuring clause) pushes the basis positive.

scenarios.setup: A counterparty's credit spread is 2%. The implied hazard rate is $\lambda = s/(1-RR)$. The desk revises its recovery assumption from 40% to 60%, with the spread unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The implied hazard rate: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: Intuition says 'better recovery, safer name', but the spread is fixed. A smaller LGD means a larger default probability is needed to explain the same spread.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The spread is unchanged, but it is divided by LGD. LGD moves from 0.60 to 0.40, so the ratio moves too.

working.label: CVA side
working.display: LGD falls from 60% to 40%. Per the reading, the LGD effect dominates, so CVA falls even though the implied PD rises

scenarios.takeaway: Holding the spread fixed, higher recovery → higher implied PD but lower CVA.

scenarios.setup: $EPE = 100$, $ENE = -80$, both LGDs 60%, counterparty $PD_C = 2\%$, own $PD_I = 1.5\%$. You have computed $CVA = -0.6(100)(0.02) = -1.20$. Next comes $DVA = -LGD_I \times ENE \times PD_I$, and then $BCVA = CVA + DVA$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with CVA alone (−1.20), is BCVA more negative, less negative, or the same?

options.label: More negative
options.why: You treated DVA as another cost. With $ENE < 0$ the product $-LGD \times ENE \times PD$ is **positive**, so DVA is a benefit. Taking it as negative gives −1.92.

options.label: The same
options.why: That is unilateral CVA, which ignores your own default. BCVA admits both defaults, so the DVA term is switched on.

scenarios.takeaway: ENE is negative, so DVA comes out positive. BCVA is less negative than UCVA.

scenarios.setup: A swap with notional USD 100m and risky duration 3.75 carries a CVA of $-90{,}000$. The desk wants it as a running spread.
scenarios.ask: The running spread is closest to?

options.label: ≈ −9.0 bp
options.why: You divided by notional only ($-90{,}000/100\text{m}$). The upfront CVA must also be spread over the risky duration.

options.label: ≈ −34 bp
options.why: You multiplied by the risky duration instead of dividing.

options.label: ≈ 240 bp
options.why: Scale slip: 100× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Running spread = CVA ÷ (risky duration × notional). A negative CVA gives a negative spread, charged to the counterparty.

scenarios.setup: You have a bilateral trade. Your exposure to the counterparty tends to *increase* as its credit quality *worsens* (wrong-way risk).
scenarios.ask: Relative to the independence case, your DVA: increases, decreases, or unaffected?

options.label: Increases
options.why: That is the CVA effect: wrong-way risk increases CVA. DVA moves the opposite way. The same correlation reduces DVA.

options.label: Unaffected
options.why: CVA and DVA are driven by the same exposure paths. A dependence between exposure and default changes both.

working.label: Wrong-way risk
working.display: Positive correlation between your exposure and the counterparty's default probability

working.label: Directions
working.display: CVA ↑ (cost grows), DVA ↓ (benefit shrinks). Right-way risk flips both

scenarios.takeaway: Wrong-way risk: CVA up, DVA down. Right-way risk: CVA down, DVA up.

scenarios.setup: A securitization has equity, mezzanine and senior tranches. Default probabilities are held fixed while the default correlation across the loan pool increases.
scenarios.ask: The value of the **equity** tranche: rises, falls, or depends on the default rate?

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is the senior tranche. Higher correlation makes the extreme pool-wide losses that reach a senior note more likely.

options.label: Depends on the default rate
options.why: That describes the mezzanine tranche, which flips: down at low default rates, up at high ones.

working.label: Low correlation
working.display: Defaults cluster near their expected value, so the equity writedown is near-certain

working.label: High correlation
working.display: Outcomes spread out, including more scenarios with zero or very few defaults. That upside goes to equity

scenarios.takeaway: Correlation is a bet on dispersion: equity is long it, senior is short it, and mezzanine flips.

scenarios.setup: A CLO has 100 loans of USD 1m at 8.5%. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 a year. Up to USD 1,750,000 of excess spread a year goes to the OC account and the rest goes to equity. 5% of surviving loans default each year, paying no interest, and are not replaced. 95 loans survived year 1.
scenarios.ask: Cash paid to equity in year 2 is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 0.0083m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.025m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.074m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×).

scenarios.takeaway: Equity gets only what excess spread leaves above the OC cap, and each year's defaults shrink the base.

scenarios.setup: Same CLO. Year 1: 95 loans paid 8.5% on USD 1m each, excess spread was USD 2,400,000, and equity got USD 650,000 after the USD 1,750,000 OC diversion. Year 2: 4.75 more loans default. Bond coupons due stay at USD 5,675,000.
scenarios.ask: In year 2, how does the excess spread compare with the USD 1.75m cap?

options.label: Above the cap: equity still gets a small residual
Below the cap: all of it goes to the OC account
options.why: Excess spread falls but is still about USD 2.0m: $90.25 \times 85{,}000 - 5{,}675{,}000$. It is USD 246k above the cap.

options.label: Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Excess spread turns negative only once fewer than $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ loans survive. There are 90.25 here.

scenarios.takeaway: Two custodian tests each year: is excess spread > 0, and is it > the cap K? Equity is paid only if both are yes.

scenarios.setup: Same CLO, same 5% annual default rate on surviving loans. At the start of year 5, $100 \times 0.95^4 = 81.45$ loans survive, each USD 1m at 8.5%; loans that default during year 5 pay no interest that year. Bond coupons due are USD 5,675,000 and the OC cap is USD 1,750,000.
scenarios.ask: Year-5 excess spread is:

options.label: Above the cap: equity gets the residual
options.why: About 77.4 loans pay interest, giving USD 6.58m. That leaves only about USD 0.90m of excess spread, well short of the USD 1.75m cap.

options.label: Positive but below the cap: all of it goes to OC, equity gets nothing
Negative: the OC account pays the shortfall
options.why: Negative only below $5{,}675{,}000/85{,}000 = 66.8$ surviving loans. At 77.4 the structure still covers its coupons.

working.label: vs cap
working.display: $902{,}150 < 1{,}750{,}000$ → all diverted to OC, equity gets 0

scenarios.takeaway: Excess spread shrinks with the pool. Equity cash dries up well before the structure fails to cover coupons.

scenarios.setup: Next week a bank expects USD 150m of new qualifying loan requests and a USD 75m Treasury purchase. It also expects USD 135m of drawings on existing credit lines. You've already totalled sources: USD 185m received today plus USD 100m expected = USD 285m.
scenarios.ask: The available funds gap: a shortfall (positive), a surplus (negative), or about zero?

options.label: A surplus
options.why: You dropped the credit-line drawings: $150 + 75 - 285 = -60$. Drawings on committed lines are a use of funds.

options.label: About zero
options.why: You dropped the securities purchase: $150 + 135 - 285 = 0$. Planned investments are a use too.

scenarios.takeaway: AFG = (loans + investments + expected line drawings) − (current + expected inflows). Positive means a shortfall.

scenarios.setup: Historical average cost approach. Total funds raised USD 1,000m, total interest paid USD 65m, other operating costs USD 10m, earning assets USD 750m.
scenarios.ask: Which is bigger: the weighted average interest expense (step 1) or the break-even cost rate on earning assets (step 2)?

options.label: The weighted interest expense
options.why: Step 2 adds USD 10m of operating costs to the numerator and divides by the smaller earning-asset base. Both push it up.

options.label: About equal
options.why: Even with the wrong USD 1,000m denominator, step 2 would be 7.5%. With the correct USD 750m it is 10%, well above 6.5%.

scenarios.takeaway: The denominator switches from total funds (step 1) to earning assets (steps 2–3). 6.5%, 10% and 12.46% are all correct answers to different questions.

scenarios.setup: Pooled-funds approach. New funds: USD 100m transaction deposits (50% placeable), USD 100m time deposits (60% placeable) and USD 100m new equity (90% placeable). Total operating cost is USD 30m. Suppose the time-deposit placeable share drops to 40%, with costs unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The hurdle rate on earning assets: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Falls
options.why: A smaller placeable base cannot lower the hurdle. The same USD 30m must be recovered from fewer earning dollars.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The pooled funds *expense* (30/300 = 10%) is unchanged. The hurdle, though, divides by dollars placeable, which fall from 200 to 180.

scenarios.takeaway: Pooled-funds hurdle = operating costs ÷ dollars placeable in earning assets. Less placeable money means a higher hurdle.

scenarios.setup: A repo: bonds with face USD 10m and market value USD 11m are sold for USD 11m and repurchased after 31 days. The repo rate is 0.3% (actual/360), with no haircut or accrued interest.
scenarios.ask: The repo interest (settlement minus USD 11m) is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 280
options.why: You read 0.3% as 0.03%, a slip by a factor of 10.

options.label: ≈ USD 33,000
options.why: You applied the annual rate for a full year ($0.003 \times 11\text{m}$) and forgot the $31/360$ day fraction.

options.label: ≈ USD 280,000
options.why: You used 0.3 (30%) instead of 0.003, a percent-to-decimal slip.

working.label: Contract price
working.display: USD 11m market value (not the USD 10m face)

scenarios.takeaway: Repo settlement = contract price × (1 + rate × days/360), on market value. At 0.3% a month's interest is tiny.

scenarios.setup: The OTR 10-year trades special: the special spread is 0.22% for 125 days (actual/360). Price is 101.90 and DV01 is 0.085 per 100 face.
scenarios.ask: The financing advantage, in yield terms, is closest to?

options.label: ≈ 0.0066 bp
options.why: You multiplied the dollar value by DV01 instead of dividing. Dollar value ÷ DV01 gives basis points.

options.label: ≈ 9 bp
options.why: Scale slip (10×).

options.label: ≈ 92 bp
options.why: You used 0.22 as the decimal spread instead of 0.0022.

scenarios.takeaway: Financing value: spread × days/360 → scale by price/100 → divide by DV01. It comes out at under a basis point.

scenarios.setup: The OTR 10-year trades about 2.00 per 100 face rich to the C-STRIPS curve. You've valued its financing advantage (lending it at the special rate for 125 days) at 7.7 cents per 100 face.
scenarios.ask: The rest of the premium (richness minus financing), attributed to liquidity: bigger or smaller than the financing value?

options.label: Smaller: richness is mostly financing
options.why: 7.7 cents out of about 2 dollars is under 4%. Specialness explains only a sliver of OTR richness.

options.label: Much bigger: richness is mostly liquidity
About the same
options.why: About 1.92 of liquidity against 0.077 of financing is a ratio of roughly 25 to 1.

scenarios.takeaway: OTR premium = liquidity advantage + financing advantage, and the liquidity part is usually by far the larger.

scenarios.setup: Since 2009 a failed delivery of a Treasury incurs a penalty rate of $\max(3\% - \text{FFR},\, 0)$. The fed funds rate rises from 1% to 2%.
scenarios.ask: The penalty rate, and so the cap on the special spread: rises, falls, or unchanged?

options.label: Rises
options.why: The penalty moves inversely with the fed funds rate. It is largest (3%) when rates are zero.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The 0 floor binds only once FFR ≥ 3%. At 1–2% the penalty is still falling one-for-one with FFR.

scenarios.takeaway: Fails penalty = max(3% − FFR, 0): high rates mean a low penalty, and zero rates mean the full 3%.

scenarios.setup: Special spread = GC repo rate − special repo rate for the on-the-run Treasury. Compare the days just before the next auction with the days just after it.
scenarios.ask: Just before the auction, the OTR special spread is: wider, narrower, or the same?

options.label: Narrower
options.why: Right after an auction the new OTR issue is in surplus supply, which narrows specialness. Before the auction, demand for the scarce issue pushes it wider.

options.label: The same
options.why: Special spreads follow a systematic auction-cycle pattern; they are not flat.

working.label: After auction
working.display: New supply of the OTR issue → less scarce as collateral → special rate nearer GC → narrower

working.label: Before auction
working.display: Rising demand for the issue to borrow → special rate falls further below GC → wider

scenarios.takeaway: OTR special spreads: wide before an auction, narrow just after (new supply).

scenarios.setup: A portfolio holds five positions of USD 2 million each. Every position has return volatility $\sigma = 30\%$ and every pair is correlated at $\rho = 0.2$. Use $z = 2.33$ and $\sigma_P = \sigma\sqrt{1/N + (1 - 1/N)\rho}$.
scenarios.ask: Portfolio VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.84m
options.why: Used one USD 2m position as the portfolio value. Five positions of USD 2m is a USD 10m portfolio.

options.label: ≈ USD 13m
options.why: Scale slip (3×). Even with no diversification at all ($\sigma_P = 30\%$) VaR is only $2.33 \times 0.30 \times 10 = \text{USD } 7.0\text{m}$, so the answer must sit below that.

options.label: ≈ USD 42m
options.why: Scale slip (10×). The undiversified ceiling is USD 7.0m; nothing with $\rho < 1$ can exceed it.

scenarios.takeaway: Equal-weight VaR sits between the large-$N$ floor $z\sigma\sqrt{\rho}\,P$ and the undiversified ceiling $z\sigma P$, and $P$ is the whole portfolio, not one position.

scenarios.setup: Portfolio X has a VaR of EUR 400,000 and holds four equally weighted assets of EUR 1,000,000 each. Asset A has a beta of 1.2 against the portfolio.
scenarios.ask: Asset A's marginal VaR (change in portfolio VaR per extra euro in A) is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/10 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Also multiplied by A's 25% weight. $\text{MVaR}_A \times w_A$ is A's component VaR per euro of portfolio, not the per-euro marginal VaR.
Divided by one asset's EUR 1m instead of the EUR 4m portfolio.

scenarios.takeaway: Marginal VaR is a per-dollar number, $(\text{VaR}_P / P) \times \beta_i$. It sits near 0.1, not in the thousands.
