working.display: High-beta stocks are more volatile, so the Sharpe ratio drops from 0.9 to 0.4 through a larger denominator

scenarios.takeaway: Beta anomaly: the numerator stays flat and the denominator grows. Volatility anomaly: the numerator collapses.

scenarios.setup: A loan has a USD 2,000,000 commitment, of which USD 1,800,000 is drawn. $PD = 1\%$, loss rate $LR = 40\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 10\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 30\%$.
scenarios.ask: Unexpected loss on the loan is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 7,200
options.why: That is expected loss, $EA \times PD \times LR$. UL is the standard deviation of loss, not its mean.

options.label: ≈ USD 250,000
options.why: Used $\sigma$ instead of $\sigma^2$ inside the root: $1.8\text{m} \times \sqrt{0.01 \times 0.3 + 0.16 \times 0.1} \approx 248{,}000$.

options.label: ≈ USD 900,000
options.why: Scale slip (10×): 1.8m × 0.5 instead of 1.8m × 0.05, i.e. a misplaced decimal in the square root.

scenarios.takeaway: UL = EA × √(PD·σ²_LR + LR²·σ²_PD) on the drawn amount; it dwarfs EL for a low-PD loan.

scenarios.setup: Same loan: drawn USD 1,800,000, $PD = 1\%$, $LR = 40\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 10\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 30\%$. You are filling in $UL = EA\sqrt{PD \cdot \sigma_{LR}^2 + LR^2 \cdot \sigma_{PD}^2}$.
scenarios.ask: Which term under the root is bigger?

options.label: The loss-rate-uncertainty term, $PD\,\sigma_{LR}^2$
options.why: $\sigma_{LR} = 30\%$ looks big, but it is multiplied by $PD = 0.01$ (unsquared): $0.0009$ against $0.0016$.

options.label: Roughly equal
options.why: $0.0016$ is about $1.8\times$ $0.0009$; the default-uncertainty term clearly leads.

scenarios.takeaway: PD enters the first UL term unsquared; LR enters the second squared. A small PD shrinks the recovery-uncertainty term.

scenarios.setup: Two loans. A: USD 8.25m, $PD = 0.5\%$, $LR = 50\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 7.05\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 25\%$. B: USD 1.8m, $PD = 1\%$, $LR = 40\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 10\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 30\%$. Default correlation $\rho = 0.3$.

options.label: ≈ USD 933

scenarios.setup: Two loans. A: USD 8.25m, $PD = 0.5\%$, $LR = 50\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 7.05\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 25\%$. B: USD 1.8m, $PD = 1\%$, $LR = 40\%$, $\sigma_{PD} = 10\%$, $\sigma_{LR} = 30\%$. Default correlation $\rho = 0.3$. At $\rho = 0.3$, $EL_P = 27{,}825$ and $UL_P = 362{,}642$. The correlation now drops to $0.1$.
scenarios.ask: What happens to portfolio expected loss $EL_P$?

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is $UL_P$ (to $346{,}118$). EL is a sum of stand-alone expected losses; correlation never enters it.

options.label: Rises
options.why: Lower correlation cuts concentration risk; it cannot raise any loss measure here, and EL does not move at all.

working.label: Effect of ρ
working.display: $EL_P$ has no $\rho$ term, so it stays $27{,}825$; only $UL_P$ falls ($362{,}642 \to 346{,}118$)

scenarios.setup: Bigger Bank has $UL_A = \text{USD } 325{,}333$ and $UL_B = \text{USD } 90{,}000$ with default correlation $\rho = 0.3$. You are about to take $UL_P = \sqrt{UL_A^2 + UL_B^2 + 2\rho\,UL_A UL_B}$.
scenarios.ask: Where will $UL_P$ land?

options.label: Above $UL_A + UL_B$
options.why: The simple sum is the $\rho = 1$ ceiling; any $\rho < 1$ lands below it.

options.label: Below $UL_A$
options.why: With $\rho \ge 0$, $UL_P \ge \sqrt{UL_A^2 + UL_B^2} \approx 337{,}600 > UL_A$; adding a risky asset cannot cut UL below the larger stand-alone UL here.

scenarios.takeaway: 0 < ρ < 1 puts UL_P between the root-sum-of-squares and the simple sum of stand-alone ULs.

scenarios.setup: A large portfolio of loans with roughly the same size and characteristics. Each loan's stand-alone UL is USD 10,500; constant pairwise default correlation $\rho = 0.32$.
scenarios.ask: Each loan's UL contribution to portfolio UL is closest to?

options.label: ≈ USD 197
options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 1,100
options.why: Squared the correlation: $10{,}500 \times 0.32^2 \approx 1{,}075$. The shortcut uses $\sqrt{\rho}$.

options.label: ≈ USD 19,000
options.why: Divided by $\sqrt{\rho}$ instead of multiplying: $10{,}500 / 0.566 \approx 18{,}560$. A contribution cannot exceed the stand-alone UL.

scenarios.takeaway: Large homogeneous book: ULC_i = UL_i × √ρ, always less than UL_i.

scenarios.setup: Banks ABC and XYZ have the same exposure, duration, rating and expected loss. ABC's average pairwise default correlation is lower than XYZ's. Both raise the confidence level used to set economic capital.
scenarios.ask: Economic capital needed:

options.label: Rises at XYZ, falls at ABC
options.why: Correlation sets the level of $UL_P$, not the direction of the change. A higher confidence level raises the capital multiplier for both.

options.label: Unchanged at both
options.why: Economic capital $= UL_P \times CM$. $UL_P$ is unchanged, but $CM$ rises with the confidence level.

working.label: Effect
working.display: Higher confidence level $\Rightarrow$ larger $CM$ $\Rightarrow$ higher $EC$ at both banks (ABC's is lower in level because its $UL_P$ is lower)

scenarios.takeaway: Raise the confidence level → bigger capital multiplier → more economic capital, whatever the correlation.

scenarios.setup: A trading book holds USD 10m in asset 1 (daily $\sigma = 2\%$) and USD 5m in asset 2 (daily $\sigma = 1\%$). Correlation $0.7$. VaR at 99% ($z = 2.3264$). Stand-alone daily σ in USD m: $10 \times 2\% = 0.20$ and $5 \times 1\% = 0.05$, so their sum is $0.25$.

scenarios.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
scenarios.setup: A trading book holds USD 10m in asset 1 (daily $\sigma = 2\%$) and USD 5m in asset 2 (daily $\sigma = 1\%$). Correlation $0.7$. VaR at 99% ($z = 2.3264$). At correlation 0.7 the 10-day VaR is USD 1.75m. The correlation assumption is cut to 0, positions and volatilities unchanged.

options.label: Unchanged

scenarios.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
scenarios.setup: A correlation-swap buyer pays fixed $\rho = 0.20$ on USD 1m notional, three assets. Realized pairwise correlations: $\rho_{2,1} = 0.6$, $\rho_{3,1} = 0.2$, $\rho_{3,2} = 0.04$. You have the pairwise sum $0.84$ and will scale it by $\tfrac{2}{n^2 - n}$.
scenarios.ask: Will realized correlation beat the fixed 0.20, i.e. is the buyer's payoff positive, negative, or zero?

options.label: Negative
options.why: You divided by $n^2 - n = 6$ and forgot the 2: $0.84/6 = 0.14 < 0.20$. The factor is $2/6 = 1/3$, giving 0.28.

scenarios.takeaway: 2/(n²−n) is just 1 / (number of pairs): with 3 assets, average the 3 pairwise ρs.

scenarios.setup: Two USD 2.5m loans, each $PD = 5\%$, default correlation $\rho = 0.5$. Joint default: $P(AB) = \rho\sqrt{PD_A(1-PD_A)PD_B(1-PD_B)} + PD_A PD_B$.
scenarios.ask: Which piece of $P(AB)$ is bigger: the correlation term or the independence term $PD_A PD_B$?

options.label: The independence term $PD_A PD_B$

options.label: About equal

scenarios.takeaway: At realistic default correlations the ρ term, not PD_A × PD_B, drives joint default.

scenarios.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
scenarios.setup: An investor holds Spanish government bonds and buys CDS protection on Spain from BNP Paribas. The default correlation between Spain and BNP Paribas rises; Spain's own default probability is unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The value of the CDS to the buyer (the fair fixed spread):

options.label: Rises
options.why: Higher correlation means BNP is more likely to be down when Spain defaults, so the protection is less likely to pay. That is wrong-way risk.

options.label: Unchanged, since the reference PD did not move
options.why: The spread depends on the reference PD and on the joint default correlation between reference entity and seller.

working.label: Driver
working.display: The fixed spread depends on the reference PD and $\rho(\text{Spain}, \text{BNP})$

working.label: Effect
working.display: $\rho \uparrow$: if both default the buyer gets nothing, so the CDS value (spread) falls

scenarios.takeaway: Higher reference–seller correlation → wrong-way risk → CDS protection worth less.

scenarios.reading: MR-8: Correlation Basics: Definitions, Applications, and Terminology
scenarios.setup: Five annual returns for $X$ and $Y$. The sum of cross-products of deviations is $-0.5135$; sample standard deviations are $\sigma_X = 0.4207$ and $\sigma_Y = 0.4068$ (divide by $n - 1 = 4$).
scenarios.ask: The correlation between X and Y is:

options.label: Mildly negative, between $-0.6$ and $0$
options.why: $-0.5135$ is the sum of cross-products, not $\rho$. Covariance is $-0.1284$, and dividing by $\sigma_X\sigma_Y = 0.171$ scales it up to $-0.75$.

options.label: Positive
options.why: The cross-product sum is negative, so the covariance is negative; dividing by two positive σs cannot flip the sign.

scenarios.takeaway: Covariance / (σ_X σ_Y): when both σs are below 1, ρ is larger in size than the covariance.

scenarios.reading: CR-5: Introduction to Credit Risk Modeling and Assessment

scenarios.setup: In CreditRisk+, the expected number of defaults $qn$ is itself uncertain and modelled as gamma-distributed, turning the Poisson into a negative binomial. The standard deviation of $qn$ is increased, with its mean unchanged.

scenarios.setup: Ashanti Goldfields hedged its future production by selling gold forward. The hedge generated margin calls it could not meet, because its underlying gold was illiquid.
scenarios.ask: Which gold-price move triggered the crisis?

options.label: Gold price fell
options.why: A fall would have paid on the short forwards. A falling price is the Metallgesellschaft story (oil), the classic sibling swap.

options.label: Either direction, since any large move forces margin calls
options.why: Only the move against the short forward position creates margin calls: a rise.

working.label: Position
working.display: Short gold forwards (a hedge against falling prices)

working.label: Loss side
working.display: Gold rises → forwards lose → margin calls → cash crisis

scenarios.takeaway: Ashanti: gold ROSE. Metallgesellschaft: oil FELL. Both were hedgers hit by cash timing.

scenarios.setup: After an initial price drop, trading in a market is dominated by trend followers, stop-loss rules and dynamic hedgers.
scenarios.ask: The subsequent price move:

options.label: Amplified, with the fall feeding on itself
Damped, with prices stabilising
options.why: That is negative-feedback (value) trading, buying into falls. These three all sell as prices fall.

options.label: Reversed
options.why: Nothing here buys the dip. Each rule mechanically requires selling as the price falls.

working.label: Classification
working.display: Trend trading, stop-loss rules and dynamic hedging are positive-feedback trading

working.label: Effect
working.display: Sell on falls → more falls → a one-sided, illiquid market (a liquidity black hole)

scenarios.takeaway: Positive feedback = sell on falls = destabilising.

options.label: Yes, automatically, because $LR_{ind} > 3.84$

scenarios.reading: MR-7: Beyond Exceedance-Based Backtesting of VaR Models
scenarios.setup: A VaR model's forecast P&L distribution is systematically too narrow compared with the true distribution. You histogram a long series of its PITs by decile.

options.label: Bunches in the middle deciles, thin at the ends
options.why: That is the signature of a forecast that is too WIDE.

options.why: It has the larger PV, but its VaR% is about a fifth of the 5-year figure. PV is only 1.3 times larger, so the VaR% gap wins.

options.label: About equal
options.why: The VaR% gap (about 5×) swamps the PV gap (about 1.3×). The 5-year bucket carries roughly four times the risk.

scenarios.takeaway: In cash-flow mapping, the long bucket's VaR% dominates even when its PV is smaller.

scenarios.setup: You sold a $6 \times 12$ FRA on USD 100m, mapped as a 180-day leg of $x_1 = -97.991$ (VaR% 0.1629%) and a 360-day leg of $x_2 = +97.991$ (VaR% 0.4696%). The two rates have correlation 0.79. Diversified variance $= (x_1V_1)^2 + (x_2V_2)^2 + 2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$.
scenarios.ask: The cross term $2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$ is:

options.label: Positive, so it adds to VaR
options.why: That would need both legs on the same side. Here $x_1 < 0$ and $x_2 > 0$, so with $\rho > 0$ the product is negative and the legs hedge each other.

options.label: Roughly zero
options.why: The correlation is 0.79, far from zero, and the cross term (−0.116) is about half the size of the squared long leg (0.212).

scenarios.takeaway: Opposite-signed legs + positive correlation = negative cross term: the FRA's two legs largely hedge each other.

scenarios.setup: A sold $6 \times 12$ FRA maps to a short 180-day leg (risk $x_1V_1 = -0.160$) and a long 360-day leg (risk $x_2V_2 = +0.460$), in USD millions. At a correlation of 0.79 the diversified VaR is 0.348. The correlation between the 180-day and 360-day rates now rises to 0.95.
scenarios.ask: The FRA's diversified VaR:

options.label: Rises
options.why: True for two same-signed exposures. These legs have opposite signs, so higher correlation makes the hedge tighter.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: Diversified VaR depends on the correlation through the cross term $2\rho\,(x_1V_1)(x_2V_2)$, which changes here. Only the undiversified sum (0.620) ignores it.

scenarios.takeaway: Higher correlation raises VaR for same-sign exposures but lowers it for hedged (opposite-sign) ones.

scenarios.setup: A 1-year forward to buy EUR 100m for USD 126.5m maps into three legs, each with present value USD 122.911m: EUR spot (monthly VaR% $4.5381\%$), a long 1-year EUR bill ($0.1396\%$) and a short 1-year USD bill ($0.2121\%$). Undiversified VaR $= \sum |x_i|V_i$.
scenarios.ask: Undiversified monthly VaR of the forward is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.060m
options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 0.43m
options.why: Counted only the two bill legs and left out the EUR spot leg, which carries almost all the risk.

options.label: ≈ USD 1.8m
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The spot leg alone is 4.5% of USD 123m, which is already about USD 5.6m.

scenarios.takeaway: A currency forward's VaR is almost all spot FX risk; the two interest-rate legs are rounding.

scenarios.setup: Annual P/L for XYZ is normal with mean profit USD 15m and standard deviation USD 10m. Use $z_{95\%} = 1.645$ and $\mathrm{VaR} = -\mu + \sigma z$.
scenarios.ask: The 95% VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 4.5m
options.why: Scale slip: 3× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

options.label: ≈ USD 16m
options.why: Dropped the mean. A USD 15m expected profit offsets almost all of the $1.645\sigma$ tail move.

options.label: ≈ USD 150m
options.why: Used the variance, $\sigma^2 = 100$, in place of $\sigma = 10$.

scenarios.takeaway: A large positive mean eats most of the tail move: VaR = −μ + σz can be small, even negative.

scenarios.setup: Annual P/L is normal with mean profit USD 20m and standard deviation USD 10m. You're about to compute the 5% VaR as $-\mu + \sigma z$ with $z = 1.65$, then choose between the loss reading and the profit reading.
scenarios.ask: The sign of the computed VaR figure is:

options.label: Negative, so the 5% tail is still a profit
Positive, so the 5% tail is a loss
options.why: The tail move $\sigma z = 16.5$ is smaller than the USD 20m mean, so $-20 + 16.5 < 0$.

options.label: Too close to call
options.why: The gap is USD 3.5m, a third of a standard deviation. That is clear-cut.

working.label: Reading
working.display: 5% chance that earnings fall below USD 3.5m (still a profit)

scenarios.takeaway: If μ > σz, VaR is negative: read it as a minimum profit, not a loss.

scenarios.setup: A USD 100 portfolio has returns with mean 10% and standard deviation 20%. Treating them as normal arithmetic returns gives a 99% VaR of $(-0.10 + 0.20 \times 2.326) \times 100 = 36.52$. Now treat the same 10% / 20% as normal geometric returns and use lognormal VaR, $P(1 - e^{\mu - \sigma z})$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with 36.52, the 99% lognormal VaR:

options.label: Is higher
options.why: Exponentiating caps the loss: $1 - e^{-0.365} = 0.306$ is less than 0.365, because $1 - e^{-y} < y$ for any $y > 0$.

options.label: Is the same
options.why: The two only match for tiny moves. At $y = 0.365$ the gap between $y$ and $1 - e^{-y}$ is about 6 points.

scenarios.takeaway: Lognormal VaR ≤ normal VaR for the same μ and σ: a log-return loss can never exceed 100%.

scenarios.setup: Geometric returns on a USD 100 portfolio are normal with mean 10% and standard deviation 20%. Use lognormal VaR, $P_{t-1}\,(1 - e^{\mu_R - \sigma_R z})$, with $z_{95\%} = 1.645$.
scenarios.ask: The 95% lognormal VaR is closest to:

options.label: ≈ USD 0.20
options.why: Stopped at the fraction $1 - e^{-0.229} = 0.205$ and never multiplied by the USD 100 starting value.

options.label: ≈ USD 6.1
options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). The exponent is −0.229, so roughly a fifth of the portfolio is at risk.

options.label: ≈ USD 80
options.why: Reported $100\,e^{-0.229} = 79.5$, the value left in the tail, and forgot the $1 -$.

scenarios.takeaway: Lognormal VaR ≈ P × |exponent| for small exponents, trimmed a little: −0.229 gives ≈ 20%.

scenarios.setup: You estimate the 95% ES of a standard normal by slicing the 5% tail into 5 equal slices and averaging the 4 VaRs at the boundaries: 1.7507, 1.8808, 2.0537, 2.3263 (96% to 99%). Their average is 2.003.
scenarios.ask: The exact ES (the limit as the number of slices grows) minus 2.003 is:

options.label: Negative: 2.003 overstates ES
options.why: The four boundaries stop at 99%; the thinnest and deepest part of the tail, beyond 2.33, is never sampled. Adding it can only raise the average.

options.label: Zero: slicing is exact
options.why: It converges only as $n \to \infty$. With $n = 5$ the estimate is 0.06 short of the true value.

scenarios.takeaway: Tail-slicing ES rises toward the true value as n grows: coarse slices understate it.

scenarios.setup: Expected shortfall of a standard normal ($\mu = 0$, $\sigma = 1$) at the 95% level, using $\mathrm{ES} = \mu + \sigma\,\dfrac{e^{-z^2/2}}{(1-x)\sqrt{2\pi}}$ with $z = 1.645$ and $x = 0.95$.
scenarios.ask: ES is closest to:

options.why: Dropped the $e^{-z^2/2}$ factor, i.e. used the density at 0 instead of at the quantile.
Scale slip: 10× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Scale slip: 30× the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: Normal ES at 95% ≈ 2.06σ, just beyond the 1.645σ VaR. Anything below the VaR is wrong on sight.

scenarios.setup: A desk's VaR is estimated from the portfolio's own historical returns (the P&L it actually earned). Today the trader adds a derivatives overlay that hedges most of the position. A second VaR uses pseudo returns: today's hedged portfolio revalued over the past.
scenarios.ask: The VaR built from actual historical returns:

options.label: Falls
options.why: That is what the pseudo-return VaR does. The actual return history was earned by the unhedged book, so it cannot see today's hedge.

options.label: Rises
options.why: Nothing in the past returns changes. The hedge only lowers risk going forward, which the historical series doesn't reflect.

working.label: Historical-return VaR
working.display: Built from past P&L of the old, unhedged book: unchanged

working.label: Pseudo-return VaR
working.display: Revalues the current hedged book over history: falls

working.label: Result
working.display: Historical VaR now overstates risk (conceptual soundness failure)

scenarios.takeaway: Historical-return VaR is blind to position changes; pseudo returns are what capture a new hedge.

scenarios.setup: A bank puts confidence intervals around its historical-simulation VaR estimate, once in a calm period and once during a market stress period.
scenarios.ask: Moving from the calm period to the stress period, the confidence interval:

options.label: Narrows
options.why: Stress scatters the tail observations, so the quantile is pinned down less precisely. The empirical finding is wider intervals.

options.label: Stays the same width
options.why: Interval width depends on how dispersed the tail observations are, and that changes sharply in stress.

working.label: Finding
working.display: Historical-simulation VaR gives wider (less precise) confidence intervals during stress periods

working.label: Contrast
working.display: More data and GARCH VaR of P&L both give tighter intervals

scenarios.takeaway: Stress widens HS VaR confidence intervals; more data and GARCH P&L VaR tighten them.

scenarios.setup: Model 3: $dr = \lambda\,dt + \sigma e^{-\alpha t}\,dw$. Short rate 5%, drift $\lambda = 0.24\%$ a year, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, $\alpha = 0.3$, one month ($dt = t = 1/12$). The monthly shock $dw$ is drawn from $N(0, \sqrt{1/12})$ and came out at 0.2.
scenarios.ask: The one-month change in the short rate is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/100 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Drift only: $0.24\%/12$. The volatility term is more than ten times bigger.
Scaled $dw$ by $\sqrt{1/12}$ a second time. The draw 0.2 already comes from the monthly distribution.

scenarios.takeaway: Monthly rate moves are tens of bp: the shock term dominates, and dw already carries the √dt.

scenarios.setup: CIR: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$ with $r = 5\%$, $\theta = 24\%$, $k = 0.04$, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, $dt = 1/12$ and a draw $dw = 0.2$. Before adding, size the drift term against the shock term.
scenarios.ask: Compared with each other, the drift and shock terms are:

options.label: Shock about 10× the drift
options.why: Took $\sqrt{5} = 2.236$ instead of $\sqrt{0.05} = 0.224$. That inflates the shock to 0.67% against a 0.063% drift.

options.label: Drift about 10× the shock
options.why: Forgot the $dt = 1/12$ on the drift. $0.04 \times 19\% = 0.76\%$ is the annual drift, not the monthly one.

scenarios.takeaway: In CIR, take √r with r as a decimal; here the drift and shock come out nearly equal.

scenarios.setup: CIR short-rate step: $dr = k(\theta - r)\,dt + \sigma\sqrt{r}\,dw$. Current rate 5%, long-run level 24%, $k = 0.04$, $\sigma = 1.50\%$, one month ($dt = 1/12$), random draw $dw = 0.2$.
scenarios.ask: The one-month change in the short rate is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip (0.3×). Each term is about 0.06–0.07%, so the sum is near 0.13%.
Took $\sqrt{5}$ instead of $\sqrt{0.05}$ in the volatility term, which makes the shock ten times too big.
Plugged 24 − 5 = 19 into the drift as a whole number, then read the 0.063 result as a decimal (6.3%).

scenarios.takeaway: A one-month CIR step at a 5% rate is around 13 bp; a result of 70+ bp means √5 crept in.

scenarios.setup: Model 3 with $\sigma = 126$ bp and decay $\alpha = 0.025$: the short rate's instantaneous volatility $\sigma e^{-\alpha t}$ keeps shrinking toward zero. At a 20-year horizon the standard deviation of the terminal short rate is 4.48%.
scenarios.ask: Extending the horizon from 20 to 30 years, that terminal standard deviation:

options.label: Falls
options.why: Falling instantaneous volatility means each extra year adds less variance, not negative variance. Cumulative uncertainty cannot shrink.

options.label: Still rises, but toward a ceiling
Stays flat
options.why: It only flattens in the limit ($\sigma/\sqrt{2\alpha} = 5.63\%$). At 30 years it is still well short of that.

scenarios.takeaway: Decaying volatility slows the growth of terminal SD; it doesn't reverse it. SD climbs toward σ/√(2α).

scenarios.setup: A mortgage pool is 5 months old and prepays at 150 PSA. The 100 PSA benchmark CPR is $0.2\% \times$ month (up to month 30), and $\mathrm{SMM} = 1 - (1 - \mathrm{CPR})^{1/12}$.
scenarios.ask: The single monthly mortality (SMM) is closest to:

options.why: Scale slip: 1/30 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.
Converted twice: took the twelfth root of the SMM as well, so a monthly rate got de-annualized again.
Scale slip: 1/3 the right size, the kind of error a unit, percent or decimal-place mix-up produces.

scenarios.takeaway: SMM ≈ CPR/12 in size: a 1.5% CPR means about 0.13% a month.

scenarios.setup: A pool's CPR is 1.5%. You need the monthly rate. The exact route is $\mathrm{SMM} = 1 - (1 - 0.015)^{1/12}$; the shortcut is $0.015/12 = 0.125\%$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the $\mathrm{CPR}/12$ shortcut, the exact SMM is:

options.label: Slightly smaller
options.why: Survival compounds: twelve months at 0.125% each leave $(1 - 0.00125)^{12} = 0.98512$, i.e. a CPR of only 1.49%. The monthly rate must be a touch higher to reach 1.5%.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.why: Only for simple (non-compounding) rates. SMM and CPR are linked by a twelfth root, which is not linear.

scenarios.takeaway: SMM from CPR is a twelfth root, not a divide-by-12; the root gives a slightly bigger monthly rate.

scenarios.setup: A pool prepays at 200 PSA. The 100 PSA benchmark CPR is $0.2\% \times$ month for months 1 to 29, then 6% from month 30 onward. The pool ages from month 40 to month 60.
scenarios.ask: Its CPR over that period:

options.label: Rises
options.why: Both months are past the month-30 cutoff, so the ramp no longer applies. The 200 PSA multiple scales the plateau height, not the ramp length.

options.label: Falls
options.why: PSA assumes prepayment speeds climb over the first 30 months and then level off. They don't decline with age.

scenarios.takeaway: After month 30 the PSA CPR is flat: 6% × the PSA multiple, whatever the age.

scenarios.setup: The one-year transition matrix gives an AAA issuer an 89.85% chance of staying AAA. Assume the matrix can be rooted to shorter horizons.
scenarios.ask: The probability that an AAA issuer leaves AAA within three months is closest to:

options.why: Took the twelfth root (a one-month horizon) instead of the fourth root.
Used the one-year figure, 10.15%, without shortening the horizon.
Raised to the fourth power, which projects four years ahead instead of a quarter of a year.

scenarios.takeaway: Shorter horizon → take a root of the matrix; longer → a power. A quarter-year leave rate is roughly a quarter of the annual one.

scenarios.setup: An AAA issuer stays AAA over one year with probability 89.85%. For a three-month horizon the notes take the fourth root, $0.8985^{1/4}$. A shortcut would split the 10.15% annual leave rate evenly: $1 - 10.15\%/4 = 97.46\%$.
scenarios.ask: Compared with the 97.46% shortcut, the fourth-root stay probability is:

options.label: Slightly higher
options.why: Staying compounds: $0.9746^4 = 0.9022$, which is above 0.8985. To end the year at 89.85% the quarterly stay probability must be a bit below 97.46%.

options.label: Exactly equal
options.why: A root is not a straight division. They only coincide when the leave rate is tiny.

scenarios.takeaway: Rooting a survival probability gives a lower per-period survival than dividing the loss rate evenly.

scenarios.setup: Vasicek worst-case default rate at 99.9%: $\mathrm{WCDR} = N\!\left(\dfrac{N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)}{\sqrt{1-\rho}}\right)$. PD = 1%, so $N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) = -2.326$; $N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$; correlation $\rho = 0.20$.
scenarios.ask: WCDR is closest to:

options.why: Subtracted $\sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$ instead of adding it, so you get the best case rather than the worst case.
Returned the PD itself, which is the $\rho = 0$ answer. Correlation is the whole point of the stress.
Used $\rho = 0.20$ in the numerator instead of $\sqrt{\rho} = 0.447$.

scenarios.takeaway: A modest ρ = 0.20 turns a 1% PD into a ~15% worst-case default rate; that is why capital is so ρ-sensitive.

scenarios.setup: Building the Vasicek WCDR for PD = 1% ($N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) = -2.326$), $\rho = 0.20$ and 99.9% confidence ($N^{-1}(0.999) = 3.090$). First compute the numerator $N^{-1}(\mathrm{PD}) + \sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$.
scenarios.ask: The sign of that numerator is:

options.label: Positive, so WCDR is above 50%
options.why: $\sqrt{0.20} \times 3.090 = 1.38$ is not enough to offset −2.326. The numerator only turns positive when $\rho$ exceeds about 0.57.

options.label: Roughly zero
options.why: The numerator is −0.94, nearly one full unit below zero, which still leaves WCDR well under 50%.

scenarios.takeaway: For low PDs the WCDR numerator stays negative, so the worst case is high but still under 50%.

scenarios.setup: A loan portfolio has PD = 1% and a Vasicek correlation of $\rho = 0.20$, giving a 99.9% worst-case default rate of 14.6%. The correlation assumption is raised to 0.30, with PD and confidence level unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The worst-case default rate (and so the IRB capital charge):

options.label: Falls
options.why: The numerator is negative, so the smaller $\sqrt{1-\rho}$ does push the ratio down a little. But the $\sqrt{\rho}\,N^{-1}(0.999)$ term grows much faster, and the net effect is up.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: WCDR depends directly on $\rho$. Only at $\rho = 0$ does it collapse to the PD.

scenarios.takeaway: More asset correlation → fatter default-rate tail → higher WCDR and higher capital.

scenarios.setup: CreditRisk+ treats the expected number of defaults $qn$ as gamma-distributed with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$, which turns the Poisson default count into a negative binomial. The analyst raises $\sigma$ and leaves $\mu$ unchanged.
scenarios.ask: The probability of an extreme year with a very large number of defaults:

options.label: Falls
options.why: More uncertainty about the default rate spreads the default-count distribution, putting more mass in the right tail.

options.label: Unchanged
options.why: The mean number of defaults is unchanged, but the tail isn't. $\sigma$ is how CreditRisk+ builds in default correlation, and $\sigma \to 0$ recovers the thin-tailed Poisson.

working.label: Mechanism
working.display: Higher $\sigma$ = more uncertainty in the default rate = implied default correlation

working.label: Result
working.display: Right tail of the default-count distribution fattens: extreme outcomes more likely

scenarios.takeaway: In CreditRisk+, default-rate volatility σ plays the role of correlation: raise it and the tail fattens.
